subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Greek Art I: The Archaic Period (CLASSICS 161)
description: The class considers the development of Greek art from 1000-480 and poses the question, how Greek was Greek art? In the beginning, as Greece emerges from 200 years of Dark Ages, their art is cautious, conservative and more abstract than life-like, closer to Calder than Michelangelo. While Homer describes the rippling muscles (and egos) of Bronze Age heroes, his fellow painters and sculptors prefer abstraction. This changes in the 7th century, when travel to and trade with the Near East transform Greek culture. What had been an insular society becomes cosmopolitan, enriched by the sophisticated artistic traditions of lands beyond the Aegean "frog pond." Imported Near Eastern bronzes and ivories awaken Greek artists to a wider range of subjects, techniques and ambitions. Later in the century, Greeks in Egypt learn to quarry and carve hard stone from Egyptian masters. Throughout the 6th century, Greek artists absorb what they had borrowed, compete with one another, defy their teachers, test the tolerance of the gods and eventually produce works of art that speak with a Greek accent. By the end of the archaic period, images of gods and mortals bear little trace of alien influence or imprint, yet without the contributions of Egypt and the Near East, Greek art as we know it would have been unthinkable.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Greek Art II: From the Parthenon to Scopas (CLASSICS 162)
description: The class begins with the art, architecture and political ideals of Periclean Athens, from the emergence of the city as the political and cultural center of Greece in 450 to its defeat in the Peloponnesian War in 404. It then considers how the Athenians (shell-shocked from war and three outbreaks of plague) and the rest of 4th century Greece rebuild their lives and the monuments that define them.  Earlier 5th century traditions endure, with subtle changes, in the work of sculptors such as Kephisodotos.  Less subtle are the outlook and output of his son Praxiteles. In collaboration with Phryne, his muse and mistress, Praxiteles challenged the canons and constraints of the past with the first female nude in the history of Greek sculpture. His gender-bending gods and men were equally audacious, their shiny surfaces reflecting Plato's discussion of Eros and androgyny. Scopas was also a man of his time, but pursued different interests. Drawn to the interior lives of men and woman, his tormented Trojan War heroes and victims are still scarred by memories of the Peloponnesian War, and a world away from the serene faces of the Parthenon. His Maenad, who has left this world for another, belongs to the same years as Euripides' Bacchae and, at the same time, anticipates the torsion and turbulence of Bernini and the Italian Baroque.  The history and visual culture of these years remind us that we are not alone, that the Greeks grappled as we do with the inevitability and consequences of war, disease and inner daemons.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Designing How We Live: Why Architecture is More Than Just Building
description: Think about the spaces you visit daily: the dorm room that shapes every interaction with your roommate, the coffee shop that somehow makes you feel focused, or the museum that forces you to walk more slowly. Anyone with an engineering degree can calculate the weight a pillar can hold, but it takes an architect to ask: How will this very pillar shape the ways people live around it? In this seminar, we are moving past the myth that architecture is just about choosing fabrics for a new living room. Instead, we will treat it as a revolutionary activity that, starting in the 20th century, transformed modern lifestyles. We'll dive into big, pressing questions: How can a neighborhood's design improve mental health? What does a truly climate-resilient home look like? And are skyscrapers really the only way to meet the demands of overpopulation? You don't need any prior background to attend this course, just a curiosity about how the world around you is shaped and how it could be different. To understand the difference between good and bad architecture, we will make full use of the many resources right here on campus. We'll explore historical maps, learn how to read blueprints, and deconstruct the hidden psychology of our own campus buildings. By the end of this seminar, you will never look at a room or a corner shop the same way again. You'll walk away with a toolkit to critically read the built environment, understand the deep intersection of design and societal ideals, and possess the foundation to start imagining the future spaces of our world.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Byzantine Art and Architecture, 300-1453 C.E. (ARTHIST 306, CLASSICS 171)
description: This course explores the art and architecture of the Eastern Mediterranean: Constantinople, Jerusalem, Alexandria, Antioch, Damascus, Thessaloniki, and Palermo, 4th-15th centuries. Applying an innovative approach, we will probe questions of phenomenology and aesthetics, focusing our discussion on the performance and appearance of spaces and objects in the changing diurnal light, in the glitter of mosaics and in the mirror reflection and translucency of marble.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Art Worlds: Museum, Studio, Gallery, Archive
description: How does a work of art get from the artist's studio to the museum wall? Who makes these choices, and why? This class will introduce students to the spaces and institutions where art is made, sold, exhibited, viewed, and researched. We will visit museums and community art spaces, galleries and auction houses, conservation labs and artist studios, and speak with the people who work there. These visits will illuminate the many paths one can take to make a life in art. We will also ask ourselves how these places--and the choices that are made behind closed doors--shape what we think we know, see, and like.

subject: ARTHIST
title: The American Civil War: A Ghost Story (AMSTUD 116A)
description: How does the past persist? How does it haunt us, making us who we are? What is it like to visit the sites of violence, the places of despair, and to find in them a source of contemplation, of perspective, and ultimately of a deepened faith in what is possible; to become, in short, a graver, deeper person? Considering the poetry, photography, and painting of the American Civil War--thinking of the work of Walt Whitman, Frederick Douglass, Emily Dickinson, Abraham Lincoln, and many others--this course explores an urgent question: what is our ethical relation to the American past?

subject: ARTHIST
title: Love at First Sight: Visual Desire, Attraction, and the Pleasures of Art (ARTHIST 319, FRENCH 149, FRENCH 349, ITALIAN 149, ITALIAN 349)
description: Why do dating sites rely on photographs? Why do we believe that love is above all a visual force? How is pleasure, even erotic pleasure, achieved through looking? While the psychology of impressions offers some answers, this course uncovers the ways poets, songwriters, and especially artists have explored myths and promoted ideas about the coupling of love and seeing. Week by week, we will be reflecting on love as political critique, social disruption, and magical force. And we will do so by examining some of the most iconic works of art, from Dante's writings on lovesickness to Caravaggio's Narcissus, studying the ways that objects have shifted from keepsakes to targets of our cares. While exploring the visual roots and evolutions of what has become one of life's fundamental drives, this course offers a passionate survey of European art from Giotto's kiss to Fragonard's swing that elicits stimulating questions about the sensorial nature of desire and the human struggle to control emotions.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Islam and Water
description: Water plays a central role in Islamic religious practice, and in the lifeworlds the Islamic world, from late antiquity to the present. This course examines water in relation to the artistic production of the Islamic world, encompassing architecture, portable objects, and paintings (mostly in books).  Indoor and outdoor fountains in residence and mosques, bathhouses, basins and channels in gardens, and cisterns to store water are only some examples of water architecture. Objects used for transportation, storage, and consumption of water were highly adorned, and designed for complex tasks such as water filtering. Paintings depict scenes of bathing, and seafarers braving the ocean, while portolan charts help navigation. Contemporary architects and artists in the Islamic world and Muslim diaspora communities react to challenges raised by climate change in buildings and artworks. This course will delve on historical and contemporary approaches to water, and introduce students to eco-critical art history.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Modern Africa: Art and Decolonization (AFRICAAM 128C, ARTHIST 328)
description: This course surveys modern African art from the colonial period through the early post-independence decades. Modern forms of African art developed as early as the 1920s and '30s among scattered independent practitioners and in schools and workshops run by colonial educators. Following World War II, a new generation of artists and theorists rose to prominence in conjunction with the growing influence of Negritude. By the 1960s and '70s, modernist movements flourished in some African countries with support from new national governments, while socialist cultural policies often sought to modernize and nationalize local art practices, even as alarms began to sound over new patterns of authoritarianism and foreign intervention. Because classificatory orders in Africa were never so commanding as they tend to be in the West, modern African art stands to be studied in this context through a cross-genre and multi-media lens that examines drawing, painting, and sculpture alongside performance, photography, and film, and that recognizes how divisions between "high" and "low" forms often blurred or were nonexistent.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Global Modern Art (ARTHIST 333)
description: This course explores major developments in modern art around the world, including historical avant-garde movements in Europe and their points of intersection with movements and practices from Latin America, the Caribbean, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. While making no claim to comprising a totality, the course offers an introduction to modernism - mainly in painting, sculpture, photography, and critical writing - as a global phenomenon. While looking closely at a range of individual artists, artworks, and movements, the course contends with ways of conceptualizing modernism and modernity from the late 19th century through the mid 20th century in global terms, considering issues of periodization and temporal disjuncture, power asymmetry and decolonization, provincialism and cosmopolitanism, cultural particularity and comparison, international relations and exhibition politics.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Experiencing Campus Architecture (CEE 33L)
description: This introductory course will increase students' awareness of architecture, space, and design through experiencing the buildings on Stanford's campus as a spatial laboratory. Each week students will visit an area on campus or group of buildings, understand their historical significance, spatial experience, architectonic expression, and how they fit into the architectural discourse of their day. Walking tours will be supplemented by weekly readings and responses to contextualize the architecture and expand on the understanding of their history.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Early Andean Visual Culture: Interspecies Value and More-than-Human Presence (ARCHLGY 54, NATIVEAM 134A)
description: This course chronologically surveys the visual and material culture of the Andes region of South America from approximately 3000 BCE to 1500 CE. We will study Indigenous Andean worldviews as conveyed through primary source materials, such as fiber objects, ceramics and stonework, metallurgy, the built environment, performance, ritual. A throughline in the class is how an attention to more-than-human or other-than-human entities and animal natures converged with human socio-cultural value systems - and how this comes across in visual culture. Within this scope we will discuss early Andean notions of sacred geography, spiritual and political power, tensions between individual and collective identity, labor and class hierarchies, legacy, and cultural memory. We will approach material through visual analysis, cultural context, ethnohistorical references, contemporary interdisciplinary scholarship, and popular media.

subject: ARTHIST
title: East Asian Buddhist Painting: Visions and Practices (ARTHIST 339, CHINA 139, CHINA 339, EASTASN 339A)
description: This course will explore the rich and diverse history of Chinese  and Japanese Buddhist painting, from 4th century CE cave-shrines to modern eras. Along with introducing major Buddhist iconographic types, narratives, doctrines, painting styles and techniques, the course will emphasize the functions of painting in religious practices in monasteries and among communities of lay believers. While painting will be the primary focus, we will also consider the spatial and architectural contexts and functions of paintings in cave-shrines and monasteries, the interplay of paintings with sculpture, and other pictorial media such as print illustrations.

subject: ARTHIST
title: An Architectural Imagination (FILMEDIA 140)
description:
What is architecture? What questions and needs does it respond to? What kind of an imagination does it provoke? What is it about our relationship to architecture that has led to so many forms of cultural expression to draw from its theoretical and practical frameworks? Drawing from the work of thinkers and practitioners from across a wide variety of mediums, including film, fashion, performance, and visual art, this course will examine these questions in an effort to unpack how this modality of imagination shapes our knowledge of ourselves, others (human and non-human), and the cosmos. 
This course introduces students to the histories and theories of architecture as one of the earliest forms of interdisciplinary thought. Students without a background in art or architecture are encouraged to enroll.

subject: ARTHIST
title: The Life and Legends of Cleopatra VII (AFRICAAM 48C, CLASSICS 48, FEMGEN 48)
description: Ways certification pending for Aesthetic and Interpretative Inquiry (AII) and Exploring Difference and Power (EDP). The heir of a murderous and flagging dynasty, Cleopatra VII rose to be queen of Egypt when she was just a teenager. She solidified her power by defeating three of her siblings, branding herself a living goddess, and allying diplomatically and romantically with two of the most powerful Roman generals of the age: Julius Caesar and Mark Antony. After losing a war to the future Roman emperor, Augustus Caesar, she chose suicide over being displayed as a war prize in his military parade. Roman poets called her "the whore queen," "the Egyptian wife," and "drunk on luck and wine." But even enemies found something fascinating about the charismatic queen. "No humble woman," admits the Roman poet Horace, she was "fiercer for choosing her own death." In this class, we will assess depictions of Cleopatra in literature and art, starting with ancient poetry and historical texts before moving through Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra and finally to twentieth century media. In American film, Cleopatra shifts from Shakespeare's lovesick and capricious heroine to the conniving femme fatale, most famously in Joseph Mankiewicz' 1963 epic Cleopatra, starring Elizabeth Taylor. A consistent presence in Civil Rights activism, she simultaneously arises in Black American literature and art as a symbol of resistance against imperial domination. "I refuse to be eclipsed by Caesar's shadow and Caesar's sex," writes prolific poet and sculptor Barbara Chase-Riboud, "Rome, don't cross me." Throughout this class, we will look closely at depictions of Cleopatra's race and gender, which authors and artists from antiquity onward adapted to their own ends. With consideration of Edward Said's concept of "Orientalism," or pervasive stereotypes about the East as intellectually and morally inferior to the West, and W. E. B. Du Bois' assertion that "all art is propaganda," we will recognize the political aims of each version of Cleopatra and ask whom they benefit. No prior study of the ancient world is required. All readings are in English.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Thinking with Leonardo da Vinci:  Creativity and Invention in the Renaissance (HISTORY 14Q, ITALIAN 14Q)
description: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) is emblematic of creativity and innovation. His art is iconic, his inventions legendary. His understanding of nature, the human body, and machines made him a scientist and engineer as well as an artist. Leonardo's incessant curiosity about many things made him a lifelong learner and inveterate scribbler of ideas. His way of looking at and representing the world through his paintings and drawings continues to capture our imagination. This seminar explores the historical Leonardo, considering his interests and accomplishments as a product of the society of Renaissance Italy. Why did this world produce a Leonardo? Special attention will be given to interdisciplinary connections between art, science, and technology and we will look at original artifacts from Renaissance Italy in Special Collections, Cantor Arts Center, and Legion of Honor in San Francisco.

subject: ARTHIST
title: The American West (AMSTUD 124A, ENGLISH 124, HISTORY 151, POLISCI 124A)
description: The American West is characterized by frontier mythology, vast distances, marked aridity, and unique political and economic characteristics. This course integrates several disciplinary perspectives into a comprehensive examination of Western North America: its history, physical geography, climate, literature, art, film, institutions, politics, demography, economy, and continuing policy challenges. Students examine themes fundamental to understanding the region: time, space, water, peoples, and boom and bust cycles.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Queer America: Art, Photography, and Politics (AMSTUD 163A, AMSTUD 363, ARTHIST 363, FEMGEN 163, FEMGEN 363)
description: This class explores queer art, photography and politics in the United States since 1930. Our approach will be grounded in close attention to the history and visual representation of sexual minorities in particular historical moments and social contexts. We will consider the cultural and political effects of World War II, the Cold War, the civil rights movement, psychedelics, hippie culture and sexual liberation, lesbian separatism, the AIDS crisis, and marriage equality.

subject: ARTHIST
title: History of World Cinema III: Queer Cinemas Around the World (ARTHIST 364, CSRE 102C, CSRE 302C, FEMGEN 100C, FEMGEN 300C, FILMEDIA 100C, FILMEDIA 300C, GLOBAL 193, GLOBAL 390, TAPS 100C, TAPS 300C)
description: This course provides an overview of cinema from around the world since 1960, highlighting the cultural, political, and economic forces that have shaped various film movements over the last six decades. Specific topics may vary by term/year/instructor. This term's topic, Queer Cinemas around the World, engages with a range of queer cinematic forms and queer spectatorial practices in different parts of the world, as well as BIPOC media from North America. Through film and video from Kenya, Malaysia, India, The Dominican Republic, China, Brazil, Palestine, Japan, Morocco, the US etc., we will examine varied narratives about trans experience, same-sex desire, LGBTQI2S+ rights, censorship, precarity, and hopefulness. This course will attune us to regional cultural specificities in queer expression and representation, prompting us to move away from hegemonic and homogenizing understandings of queer life and media. Notes: Screenings will be held on Fridays at 1:30PM in Oshman Hall. Screening times will vary slightly from week to week.

subject: ARTHIST
title: AI 360: What's Critical to Know about AI (AFRICAAM 106C, AMSTUD 106B, CSRE 106A, ENGLISH 106A, SYMSYS 168A)
description: This interdisciplinary course analyzes 'artificial intelligence' as both a powerful tool and a subject of live inquiry. Our interactive course will not only engage these technologies in real-world real-time applied environments but also examine many of the urgent sociotechnical implications and evolving impact of AI. The aim of the course is to provide you with some important technical literacy as well as essential grounding in the broader cultural, social and political questions of the day related to AI. Going beyond the news headlines, beyond generic approaches to ethics, and beyond the hype and doom, we will examine research and use-cases on AI and privacy; surveillance; mental health; disability; medicine; higher education; the arts, humanities, and creative industries; impacts on environment and human labor; in-depth look at bias-mitigation and equity issues; and AI policies around the globe, including the African continent, among other subjects. Open to all students, the expansive topics and hands-on activities are designed to more fully support your education, your career, and your role in society as an informed citizen. Fieldtrips may include the AI Tinkery, the Robotics Lab, CESTA, the Center for Teaching & Learning and the AI Mis-Alignment Museum among others. Our class also includes a special public lecture series with AI experts, thanks to support from the Office of the Vice Provost of Undergraduate Education. Invited speakers from Stanford faculty and alumni, industry, philanthropy, public policy, investigative journalism, the arts, and civil society.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Asian American Art (AMSTUD 186D, ARTHIST 386B, ASNAMST 186B)
description: This lecture course explores the work of artists and makers of Asian descent from 1850-present. Rather than a discrete identity category, we approach 'Asian American' as an expansive, relational term that encompasses heterogenous experiences of racialization and migration. Key themes include the history of immigration and displacement; diasporic geographies; art, activism, and community; feminist/queer perspectives; and interethnic conflict and solidarity. The course is structured around the Asian American Art Initiative's Fall exhibition Spirit House: Haunting and the Asian Diaspora at the Cantor Arts Center; sections will be held in the museum and at Stanford Special Collections.

subject: ARTHIST
title: From Shanghai Modern to Global Contemporary: Frontiers of Modern Chinese Art (ARTHIST 388B, CHINA 188B, CHINA 388B, EASTASN 388B)
description: Chinese artistic developments in an era of revolution and modernization, from Shanghai Modern and New National Painting though the politicized art of the Cultural Revolution and post-Mao era re-entry into international arenas.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Close Cinematic Analysis: Poetic Cinema (ASNAMST 108, FEMGEN 104, FILMEDIA 101, FILMEDIA 301, TAPS 101F)
description: "What is poetic cinema?" This course begins with theoretical attempts at a definition by such thinkers as Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky, writer and filmmaker Pier Paolo Pasolini, and film scholars Tom Gunning and P. Adams Sitney - along with some of their examples such as Dziga Vertov's documentary A Sixth Part of the World (1926), Michelangelo Antonioni's Red Desert (1964), and the early films of Maya Deren.  We will continue to consider these definitions of the poetic mode in relation to specific elements of film such as sound, and films historically proclaimed as "poetic," including Surrealist films, films of the American avant-garde, and the "Poetic School" of Soviet cinema.  Other potential sites of poetic cinema we may consider include the Griot poetry system in Nollywood films, song lyrics in Hindi films, and adaptations of long poems such as The Shahnameh. The course has three main goals:  to chart and familiarize ourselves with the history of poetic cinema; to recognize and analyze the qualities and elements that tip a film - or part of a film - into the category of film poetry; and, more broadly, to hone our skills of close attention and analysis.

subject: ARTHIST
title: What is Art: Introduction to Early Global Art and Architecture (CLASSICS 56)
description: This course explores the concepts of "image" and "art" across cultures and historical periods from pre-historic cave paintings, Egyptian pyramids, and Assyrian reliefs to medieval palaces and monasteries.

subject: ARTHIST
title: How to Look at Art and Why: An Introduction to the History of Western Painting
description: This course explores the relation of art to life - how and why works of art, even from hundreds of years ago, matter in a person's life. It trains students to find the words to share their thoughts about art with their peers, friends, and family. Some fundamental questions the course considers: How do we get beyond the idea that the study and making of art are elite, 'privileged' activities apart from the real world? How do we develop a sense of discernment - of deciding for ourselves which artists matter, and which don't - without being a snob? How can works of art teach us to feel the wonder of being alive and our deep debt to the past, to the dead? Focusing on painters such as Michelangelo, Rembrandt, Goya, Manet, Morisot, and Charlotte Salomon, this course will pursue these questions with the aim of challenging and encouraging students to develop their own ways of thinking and feeling - generously and ethically - about the past and the present. Sections will focus on original works of art at the Cantor Arts Center. No prerequisites required.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Soren Kierkegaard and the Visual Arts (ARTHIST 401A)
description: Soren Kierkegaard (1813-1855), the Danish philosopher and theologian, espoused the importance of the individual's relation to God, the need to forsake different forms of group-think ("the crowd is untruth"), and the necessity of overcoming despair as a means to finding one's own spirit or "infinitization." In dense but accessible prose, dedicating his books always to his readers (of whom he had almost none during his lifetime), he wrote beautiful and tormented texts psychoanalyzing himself as a first patient, a first agent, of the truth he saw for others. Reading famous Kierkegaard texts such as Fear and Trembling, The Seducer's Diary, The Concept of Anxiety, The Sickness unto Death, and The Point of View for My Work as an Author, we will consider the challenging and open question of the philosopher's relation to works of visual art. In our own moment of artistic norms and conventions, profound personal seeking is as shunned and forbidden as it was in Kierkegaard time. Considering art from then and now, each student will write on a work of art of their own choosing, exploring it in a Kierkegaardian fashion.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Artists, Athletes, Courtesans and Crooks (CLASSICS 163)
description: The seminar examines a range of topics devoted to the makers of Greek art and artifacts, the men and women who used them in life and the afterlife, and the miscreants - from Lord Elgin to contemporary tomb-looters and dealers - whose deeds have damaged, deracinated and desecrated temples, sculptures and grave goods.  Readings include ancient texts in translation, books and articles by classicists and art historians, legal texts and lively page-turners. Students will discuss weekly readings, give brief slide lectures and a final presentation on a topic of their choice, which need not be confined to the ancient Mediterranean.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Dialogues with the Dead (CLASSICS 127)
description: This seminar considers the dynamism and resilience of Greek art and culture. The dialogues in question are not with ancient shades in the underworld but with later artists who build on the creative vision (and blind spots) of the past to addressthe issues of their day.Roman philhellenes, Renaissance humanists and Neoclassical loyalists have received much attention. More remains to be explored in the work of modern and contemporary artists such as Romare Bearden, Robert Mapplethorpe, Lawrence Argent, Daniel Arsham, Yinka Shonibare and Xu Zhen.In the Cantor Center and the Rodin Garden, the artist's debts to antiquity run deep; freed from his shadow, Camille Claudel's bronzes reflect the sunlit surfaces of Greek sculpture. On Meyer Green, the capital puns of Xu Zhen reverberate from Shanghai to Athens, from archetypes in the Louvre to galleries around the world, where classical "icons" - subverted, inverted and recharged - engage contemporary eyes. Classical tragedy spoke to war-weary Greeks in the 5th century. Today, Sophocles and Bryan Doerries' Theatre of War Productions help veterans to feel less alone as they return to civilian life bearing the wounds of war, visible and invisible. The vibrant and varied afterlife of Greek art is the subject of the seminar, but we will not ignore the sinister aspects of its legacy: the advertising industry's Botoxic embrace of "Greek perfection," the quest for fitness at any price and the persistence of white, western, ableist ideals of male and female beauty. Darker still is the lethal appropriation of classical art and architecture by genocidal tyrants and racists. These dialogues are deadly.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Hagia Sophia (ARTHIST 408, CLASSICS 173, CLASSICS 273)
description: This course explores the architecture, art, and music of Hagia Sophia, the cathedral of Constantinople. This building presents the largest domed interior in the Mediterranean. The architecture, while it evokes the Pantheon, surpasses the Roman precedents with its size, light, and acoustics. Employing an interdisciplinary approach, this course teaches students how to work across the fields of art and architectural history, acoustics, liturgy, music, and poetry.

subject: ARTHIST
title: War and Art
description: How can art show new ways to live? People have lived and worked amongst the ruins of war throughout history, creating work that has gone on to define Western art. Our course will reveal the different anxieties of wartime and postwar worlds, where artists like Goya and Picasso attempted to come to terms with newly reshaped societies. In moments of rupture, artists ask questions which seem to be on everyone's lips: how can we build a better world? How can art change politics and society? We will tackle conflicts from the Battle of San Romano (1432) to the Napoleonic Wars, the World Wars of the 20th century, and the Algerian War of Independence. To understand how art responds to war over time, we will consider the historical, cultural, and sociopolitical contexts, looking at artists such as Paolo Uccello, Antoine-Jean Gros, and Lee Miller, while we will read texts by Sun Tzu, Niccolò Machiavelli, and Paul Fussell. Art will be the focus of each seminar and students will develop their critical ability to respond thoughtfully and incisively towards some of the most astonishing (and harrowing) imagery ever created.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Love's Reach: A Visual and Poetic History (ARTHIST 414A, COMPLIT 214A, COMPLIT 318)
description: This seminar explores love in its manifold expressions - erotic and parental, filial and friendly, queer and political - asking how each form illuminates, contests, and deepens the others. We extend our inquiry from love of persons to love of world and fate: Arendt's amor mundi and Nietzsche's amor fati, the difficult yes to existence as it is. Our materials move between philosophy, literature, and the visual arts: Plato's Symposium, Kierkegaard's Works of Love, Fromm's The Art of Loving, Weil and Murdoch on attention as love's discipline, Eva Illouz, Why Love Hurts, Sophocles' Antigone and Ovid's Orpheus; the Song of Songs, Shakespeare's sonnets, Cavafy's poems of memory and the body; Morrison's Beloved, Baldwin on love and justice, Strout's My Name Is Lucy Barton, Didion's Blue Nights, Maggie Nelson's The Argonauts, Ocean Vuong; Rembrandt's Jewish Bride, Hine's Ellis Island portraits, Goldin's Ballad of Sexual Dependency, Leibovitz's photographs of Sontag dying, Deana Lawson's tableaux of Black kinship and desire. At the heart of the seminar lies the cultivation of attention, care, resonance, dwelling, and seeing. Can love be commanded - as the v'ahavta insists ("You shall love"), as Buddhist metta is cultivated, as Sufi mahabba is practiced - or does command betray love's nature? How does love unsettle us, and how does it return us to ourselves?

subject: ARTHIST
title: Design Theory (ARTHIST 417B)
description: This seminar focuses on the key themes, histories, and methods of architectural theory -- a form of architectural practice that establishes the aims and philosophies of architecture.  Architectural theory is primarily written, but it also incorporates drawing, photography, film, and other media.  One of the distinctive features of modern and contemporary architecture is its pronounced use of theory to articulate its aims. One might argue that modern architecture is modern because of its incorporation of theory. This course focuses on those early-modern, modern, and late-modern writings that have been and remain entangled with contemporary architectural thought and design practice.  Rather than examine the development of modern architectural theory chronologically, it is explored architectural through thematic topics. These themes enable the student to understand how certain architectural theoretical concepts endure, are transformed, and can be furthered through his/her own explorations.CEE 32B is a crosslisting of ARTHIST 217B/417B.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Michelangelo: Gateway to Early Modern Italy (ARTHIST 418A, HISTORY 237B, HISTORY 337B, ITALIAN 237, ITALIAN 337)
description: Revered as one of the greatest artists in history, Michelangelo Buonarroti's extraordinarily long and prodigious existence (1475-1564) spanned the Renaissance and the Reformation in Italy. The celebrity artist left behind not only sculptures, paintings, drawings, and architectural designs, but also an abundantly rich and heterogeneous collection of artifacts, including direct and indirect correspondence (approximately 1400 letters), an eclectic assortment of personal notes, documents and contracts, and 302 poems and 41 poetic fragments. This course will explore the life and production of Michelangelo in relation to those of his contemporaries. Using the biography of the artist as a thread, this interdisciplinary course will draw on a range of critical methodologies and approaches to investigate the civilization and culture of Italy in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Course themes will follow key tensions that defined the period and that found expression in Michelangelo: physical-spiritual, classical-Christian, tradition-innovation, individual-collective.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Field Works: Contemporary Chinese Landscape Arts across Cultures (ARTHIST 426, CHINA 226, CHINA 426, EASTASN 326A)
description: An exploration of new forms of landscape art in China's contemporary era, 1980s-present. Studies of new media platforms for landscape related imagery, imagined landscapes, and expanded concepts of landscape in an era of heightened ecological consciousness.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Otherized and Organized: The Politicization of Indigeneity in Colonial Latin America (ARTHIST 431A, NATIVEAM 231A)
description: This course focuses on Indigenous visual, material, and cultural production of early colonial Latin America (Viceroyalty of Peru and Viceroyalty of New Spain) from the mid-1500s through the mid-1700s, with some content on the very late precontact period before colonization. During this period, Indigenous Latin American peoples experienced dramatic changes to their autonomy and lifeways, with implications for their languages, social organization, and relationship to the landscape. The class will review artifacts, texts, and other cultural expressions to bring forward the complexity of cultural clash between various Indigenous and European actors and to sort through how material and cultural value--and changing value--factored into questions of political and social order. Study of cross-cultural shifts incorporates emerging discourses on race, ethnicity, and social justice. In this scope, we will address discourses and debates regarding difference, alterity, the hybrid, the transcultural, etc., and analyze how visual and material culture examples bring forward Indigenous identities as perceived and politicized in relation to questions of self and other, with attention mainly to Indigenous creators and audiences but also their European counterparts. Furthermore, a component of the class will include contemporary artworks that reflect on the reverberations of colonization of the Americas.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Rome: From Pilgrimage to the Grand Tour (ARTHIST 432D, HISTORY 232D, HISTORY 332D, HISTORY 432D, ITALIAN 232D, ITALIAN 332D)
description: Imagine yourself in Rome. What do you see beyond the ruins of an ancient city? In the fourteenth century the city of over one million ancient Roman inhabitants had shrunk to a paltry population of less than twenty thousand. With the return of the papacy in the fifteenth century the rebuilding and revival of Rome began in earnest. By the late sixteenth century it was the center of global missions, an expanding state, and a nascent tourist industry. This course explores the history of the "Eternal City" from the late Middle Ages through the age of the Grand Tour. It examines the political, diplomatic, and religious history of the papacy, Roman society and cultural life, the everyday world of Roman citizens, the relationship between the city and the surrounding countryside, the material transformation of Rome as a city, and its meaning for foreigners.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Aura, AI, and Sports (AFRICAAM 155, ENGLISH 155A, TAPS 155A)
description: The course explores the idea of aura in sports, performance, and art. How does a performer, athlete, or artwork have aura? What is aura and why does it have value? The course will think about the idea of aura in art theory, religious practice, and current performance theory. Aura has been described as a special quality of artwork that carries religious power in a secular setting. Aura has also been linked to a special human quality. The course will explore the ways athletes and performers carry a special quality to their movements, expressions, and performances. We will look at how Black literature, poetry, and visual arts portray athletes and performances to unveil a special quality to their work. And we will ask questions about the relation between aura and race, authenticity and Black performances across sports, music, and art. We will also ask the question of whether aura is a human quality or if creative work made by AI can also produce "aura."

subject: ARTHIST
title: Making Art History: Black Mountain College (ARTHIST 457A, ARTSINST 257)
description: In 1933, artists Anni and Josef Albers arrived in rural North Carolina to teach at Black Mountain College. Drawing on their years of experience teaching at the Bauhaus, the Albers emphasized practice before theory, learning by doing.  Their lessons shaped generations of experimental artists, including Ruth Asawa, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly, and John Cage, among many others.  Co-taught by an art historian and a physicist/artist, this course takes the Albers' pedagogy as its starting point.  Our class sessions will recreate some of the Albers' foundational lessons in materials, design, drawing, and paper folding.  What emerges when we begin art history with making rather than theory?  How does the intelligence of the hand relate to knowledge of the past?

subject: ARTHIST
title: The Mongol Empire (ARTHIST 459A, HISTORY 289A, HISTORY 389A)
description: This course examines the artistic production of the Mongol Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, stretching from the Middle East to East Asia. Under the vast umbrella of an empire built by Chinggis Khan and his successors, artistic exchange brought the introduction of Chinese motifs into Islamic art; increased production of illustrated manuscripts of histories and epics such as the Shahname; production of brocaded silks in Iran and China. Islamic, Buddhist, and Christian religious monuments were built, and new cities founded.  This course looks at architecture, textiles, manuscripts, ceramics, and metalwork in this global, pre-modern Empire.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Word and Image (ARTHIST 465A, COMPLIT 225, ITALIAN 265, ITALIAN 365)
description: What impact do images have on our reading of a text? How do words influence our understanding of images or our reading of pictures? What makes a visual interpretation of written words or a verbal rendering of an image successful? These questions will guide our investigation of the manifold connections between words and images in this course on intermediality and the relations and interrelations between writing and art from classical antiquity to the present. Readings and discussions will include such topics as the life and afterlife in word and image of Ovid's "Metamorphoses," Dante's "Divine Comedy," Ludovico Ariosto's "Orlando Furioso," and John Milton's "Paradise Lost;" the writings and creative production of poet-artists Michelangelo Buonarroti, William Blake, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; innovations in and correspondences between literature and art in the modern period, from symbolism in the nineteenth century through the flourishing of European avant-garde movements in the twentieth century.

subject: ARTHIST
title: What is Contemporary Art?
description: What is Contemporary Art

subject: ARTHIST
title: The Russian and Soviet Avant-Garde (ARTHIST 475A, FILMEDIA 275, FILMEDIA 475, REES 275A)
description: This course approaches the Russian and Soviet avant-gardes through three central themes:  things, forms, and thinking. 'Things' speaks to such key concepts as dialectical materialism, nonobjective art, and faktura.  'Forms' encompasses the intricate paths of Russian Formalism as well as Constructivist design. 'Thinking' threads through things and forms as they were understood to shape subjectivities.  We will consider many arts:  literature and poetry, visual arts, fashion, architecture and film, placing the greatest emphasis on film.  Our reading will be wide-ranging in terms of time and discipline.  It will include, among others, avant-garde artists such as Kazimir Malevich and Sergei Eisenstein and their contemporaries Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Eikhenbaum. We will also read more contemporary art historians such as Christina Lodder, Yves-Alain Bois, John Bowlt, T. J. Clark, Christina Kaier, and Aglaya Glebova; film and literary scholars such as Jessica Merrill, Nariman Skakov, and Emma Widdis; and Russian historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick, Terry Martin, and Yuri Slezkine.  Films range from melodrama (Olga Preobrazhenskaya's 1927 The Peasant Women of Ryazan) to Dziga Vertov's documentaries and Eisenstein's Ivan the Terrible (1945 and 1958).  We will also make time to look at archival materials in Special Collections.

subject: ARTHIST
title: From Aksum to Athens: African Antiquity (AFRICAAM 278C, CLASSICS 278, CLASSICS 378A)
description: Located in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, the ancient city of Aksum is a site of cultural exchange and cosmopolitanism. In this course, students will learn more about Aksum's art, language, and history; they will also situate Aksum alongside Greece and Rome as another ancient empire focused on expansion. As the course title suggests, this course presents Aksum an important starting point ("from") from which inclusive studies of antiquity can emerge. By discarding the Greco-Roman hegemony of "antiquity," students will learn to make way for a plural model of the past.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Museum Practice (ANTHRO 134D, ARCHLGY 134, ARCHLGY 234)
description: This is a hands-on museum practicum course open to students of all levels that will culminate in a student-curated exhibit. It entails a survey of the range of museum responsibilities and professions including the purpose, potential, and challenges of curating collections. While based at the Stanford University Archaeology Collections (SUAC), we will visit other campus collections and sites. Students will plan and realize an exhibition at the Stanford Archaeology Center, gaining skills in collections management, research, interpretation, and installation.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Putting It Together: The Art of Curating (AMSTUD 288, ARTHIST 488A)
description: This course will focus on the production, criticism, and curating of art. Through a series of required readings, intensive class discussions, class trips, and first-hand encounters with art objects, collections, and exhibitions, we will investigate the history and practice of museum and gallery display. Our work together will depart from "Morris Hirshfield Rediscovered" the exhibition currently at the Cantor Arts Center. As the curator of the exhibition, Prof. Meyer will provide behind the scenes knowledge of how such a project is conceived and realized as well as the challenges encountered along the way.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Curricular Practical Training
description: CPT course required for international students completing degree.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Writing and the Visual: The Art of Art Writing
description: This course explores some approaches and techniques for writing about visual art and material culture. As a Writing in the Major (WIM) course, it is intended to be helpful to your academic writing for projects such as presentations, reports, essays, research papers, and theses. We will consider forms, practices, and problems of writing about art and visual culture of the sort encountered both in scholarly and professional settings - including research papers, gallery texts, and art criticism. The course will be structured in part as a writing workshop, with a series of writing exercises, brief presentations, discussions, and critiques. We will also discuss some readings, including examples of various genres and modes of art writing as well as methodological or theoretical accounts of relationships between language/texts and images/objects. We will also consider some critical issues surrounding art writing.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Visual Arts Internship
description: Professional experience in a field related to the Visual Arts for six to ten weeks. Internships may include work for galleries, museums, art centers, and art publications. Students arrange the internship, provide a confirmation letter from the hosting institution, and must receive consent from the faculty coordinator to enroll in units. To supplement the internship students maintain a journal.  Evaluations from the student and the supervisor, together with the journal, are submitted at the end of the internship.  Restricted to declared majors and minors. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Junior Seminar: Methods & Historiography of Art History
description: Historiography and methodology. Through a series of case studies, this course introduces a range of influential critical perspectives in art history as a discipline and a practice. The goal is to stimulate thinking about what it means to explore the history of art today, to expose and examine our assumptions, expectations and predilections as we undertake to learn and write about works of art, their meanings and their status in the world.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Honors Thesis Writing
description: May be repeated for credit.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Individual Work: Art History
description: Prerequisite: student must have taken a course with the instructor and/or completed relevant introductory course(s). Instructor consent and completion of the Independent Study Form are required prior to enrollment.  All necessary forms and payment are required by the end of Week 2 of each quarter. Please contact the Undergraduate Coordinator in McMurtry 108 for more information. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Islamic Art (ISLAMST 149C)
description: This course surveys the art and architecture of societies where Muslims were dominant or where they formed significant minorities from the emergence of Islam until the present.  It examines the form and function of architecture and works of art as well as the social, historical and cultural contexts, patterns of use, and evolving meanings attributed to art by the users.  The course follows a chronological order, where selected visual materials are treated along chosen themes.  Themes include the creation of a distinctive visual culture in the emerging Islamic polity; the development of urban institutions; key architectural types such as the mosque, madrasa, caravanserai, dervish lodge and mausoleum; art objects and the arts of the illustrated book; self-representation; cultural interconnections along trade and pilgrimage routes; westernization and modernization in art and architecture.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Byzantine Art and Architecture, 300-1453 C.E. (ARTHIST 106, CLASSICS 171)
description: This course explores the art and architecture of the Eastern Mediterranean: Constantinople, Jerusalem, Alexandria, Antioch, Damascus, Thessaloniki, and Palermo, 4th-15th centuries. Applying an innovative approach, we will probe questions of phenomenology and aesthetics, focusing our discussion on the performance and appearance of spaces and objects in the changing diurnal light, in the glitter of mosaics and in the mirror reflection and translucency of marble.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Performance and Performativity (ENGLISH 313, FEMGEN 313, TAPS 313)
description: Performance theory through topics including: affect/trauma, embodiment, empathy, theatricality/performativity, specularity/visibility, liveness/disappearance, belonging/abjection, and utopias and dystopias. Readings from Schechner, Phelan, Austin, Butler, Conquergood, Roach, Schneider, Silverman, Caruth, Fanon, Moten, Anzaldúa, Agamben, Freud, and Lacan. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Love at First Sight: Visual Desire, Attraction, and the Pleasures of Art (ARTHIST 119, FRENCH 149, FRENCH 349, ITALIAN 149, ITALIAN 349)
description: Why do dating sites rely on photographs? Why do we believe that love is above all a visual force? How is pleasure, even erotic pleasure, achieved through looking? While the psychology of impressions offers some answers, this course uncovers the ways poets, songwriters, and especially artists have explored myths and promoted ideas about the coupling of love and seeing. Week by week, we will be reflecting on love as political critique, social disruption, and magical force. And we will do so by examining some of the most iconic works of art, from Dante's writings on lovesickness to Caravaggio's Narcissus, studying the ways that objects have shifted from keepsakes to targets of our cares. While exploring the visual roots and evolutions of what has become one of life's fundamental drives, this course offers a passionate survey of European art from Giotto's kiss to Fragonard's swing that elicits stimulating questions about the sensorial nature of desire and the human struggle to control emotions.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Modern Africa: Art and Decolonization (AFRICAAM 128C, ARTHIST 128)
description: This course surveys modern African art from the colonial period through the early post-independence decades. Modern forms of African art developed as early as the 1920s and '30s among scattered independent practitioners and in schools and workshops run by colonial educators. Following World War II, a new generation of artists and theorists rose to prominence in conjunction with the growing influence of Negritude. By the 1960s and '70s, modernist movements flourished in some African countries with support from new national governments, while socialist cultural policies often sought to modernize and nationalize local art practices, even as alarms began to sound over new patterns of authoritarianism and foreign intervention. Because classificatory orders in Africa were never so commanding as they tend to be in the West, modern African art stands to be studied in this context through a cross-genre and multi-media lens that examines drawing, painting, and sculpture alongside performance, photography, and film, and that recognizes how divisions between "high" and "low" forms often blurred or were nonexistent.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Introduction to Global Modern Art (ARTHIST 133)
description: This course explores major developments in modern art around the world, including historical avant-garde movements in Europe and their points of intersection with movements and practices from Latin America, the Caribbean, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. While making no claim to comprising a totality, the course offers an introduction to modernism - mainly in painting, sculpture, photography, and critical writing - as a global phenomenon. While looking closely at a range of individual artists, artworks, and movements, the course contends with ways of conceptualizing modernism and modernity from the late 19th century through the mid 20th century in global terms, considering issues of periodization and temporal disjuncture, power asymmetry and decolonization, provincialism and cosmopolitanism, cultural particularity and comparison, international relations and exhibition politics.

subject: ARTHIST
title: East Asian Buddhist Painting: Visions and Practices (ARTHIST 139, CHINA 139, CHINA 339, EASTASN 339A)
description: This course will explore the rich and diverse history of Chinese  and Japanese Buddhist painting, from 4th century CE cave-shrines to modern eras. Along with introducing major Buddhist iconographic types, narratives, doctrines, painting styles and techniques, the course will emphasize the functions of painting in religious practices in monasteries and among communities of lay believers. While painting will be the primary focus, we will also consider the spatial and architectural contexts and functions of paintings in cave-shrines and monasteries, the interplay of paintings with sculpture, and other pictorial media such as print illustrations.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Queer America: Art, Photography, and Politics (AMSTUD 163A, AMSTUD 363, ARTHIST 163, FEMGEN 163, FEMGEN 363)
description: This class explores queer art, photography and politics in the United States since 1930. Our approach will be grounded in close attention to the history and visual representation of sexual minorities in particular historical moments and social contexts. We will consider the cultural and political effects of World War II, the Cold War, the civil rights movement, psychedelics, hippie culture and sexual liberation, lesbian separatism, the AIDS crisis, and marriage equality.

subject: ARTHIST
title: History of World Cinema III: Queer Cinemas Around the World (ARTHIST 164, CSRE 102C, CSRE 302C, FEMGEN 100C, FEMGEN 300C, FILMEDIA 100C, FILMEDIA 300C, GLOBAL 193, GLOBAL 390, TAPS 100C, TAPS 300C)
description: This course provides an overview of cinema from around the world since 1960, highlighting the cultural, political, and economic forces that have shaped various film movements over the last six decades. Specific topics may vary by term/year/instructor. This term's topic, Queer Cinemas around the World, engages with a range of queer cinematic forms and queer spectatorial practices in different parts of the world, as well as BIPOC media from North America. Through film and video from Kenya, Malaysia, India, The Dominican Republic, China, Brazil, Palestine, Japan, Morocco, the US etc., we will examine varied narratives about trans experience, same-sex desire, LGBTQI2S+ rights, censorship, precarity, and hopefulness. This course will attune us to regional cultural specificities in queer expression and representation, prompting us to move away from hegemonic and homogenizing understandings of queer life and media. Notes: Screenings will be held on Fridays at 1:30PM in Oshman Hall. Screening times will vary slightly from week to week.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Blackness/Gender/Sexuality & Dis-ease: HIV/AIDS Art History (ARTHIST 466A, CSRE 366A, FEMGEN 466A)
description: Since the emergence of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), artists have been central to the fight against the state's violence and neglect of those with HIV/AIDS. In this story, however, race and gender are marginalized as frameworks that shape this arts activism. This course takes up black art production that responds to the HIV/AIDS crisis to provide a longer, fuller, and more vital cultural narrative. By centering blackness in this story, we can ask how does dis-ease,referencing both infection and an aesthetically and structurally anxious relation to death,shape black art practices and lives? How have race and gender been used to conceptualize disease? And how do filmmakers, abstract painters, photographers, and poets help us to better comprehend blackness, gender, and sexuality under the threat of disease? After providing an overview of the relation between blackness, sexuality, and dis-ease and the emergence of the AIDS crisis, we will consider canonical works from the height of the crisis produced by filmmaker Marlon Riggs and poet Essex Hemphill. From there, we will move to themes of black art and mourning, black women's under cited activism, the controversial use of documentary photography in the crisis, black masculinity, diasporic responses, and the urgency and erasure of the ongoing crisis. Each week we will focus on a cultural text (film, painting, photograph, poem), a reading to provide historical context, and critical theories that will illuminate the art works' formal qualities and importance for our now.

subject: ARTHIST
title: From Shanghai Modern to Global Contemporary: Frontiers of Modern Chinese Art (ARTHIST 188B, CHINA 188B, CHINA 388B, EASTASN 388B)
description: Chinese artistic developments in an era of revolution and modernization, from Shanghai Modern and New National Painting though the politicized art of the Cultural Revolution and post-Mao era re-entry into international arenas.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Soren Kierkegaard and the Visual Arts (ARTHIST 201A)
description: Soren Kierkegaard (1813-1855), the Danish philosopher and theologian, espoused the importance of the individual's relation to God, the need to forsake different forms of group-think ("the crowd is untruth"), and the necessity of overcoming despair as a means to finding one's own spirit or "infinitization." In dense but accessible prose, dedicating his books always to his readers (of whom he had almost none during his lifetime), he wrote beautiful and tormented texts psychoanalyzing himself as a first patient, a first agent, of the truth he saw for others. Reading famous Kierkegaard texts such as Fear and Trembling, The Seducer's Diary, The Concept of Anxiety, The Sickness unto Death, and The Point of View for My Work as an Author, we will consider the challenging and open question of the philosopher's relation to works of visual art. In our own moment of artistic norms and conventions, profound personal seeking is as shunned and forbidden as it was in Kierkegaard time. Considering art from then and now, each student will write on a work of art of their own choosing, exploring it in a Kierkegaardian fashion.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Global Arts of Guinea, West Africa
description: Designed as a curatorial practicum, this seminar offers an introduction to the field of African art history, building both theoretical and practical expertise related to the arts of Africa and postcolonial art histories more broadly. We will examine globally circulating arts from Guinea, West Africa, as a means of honing curatorial research and writing; engaging with key issues in museology; and developing the intellectual versatility needed to deal responsibly with arts and material culture dating from the late 19th century to the present. It may be generally convenient to slot the arts of Africa into neat categories determined by culture and geography (ethnic/national, African/diaspora) or by medium and period or type (traditional, popular, modern, contemporary). But artistic practices rarely conformed to such classifications. Not only have masks and other canonical works of Guinean sculpture made their way into collections around the world, but also Fodeba Keita (1921-1969), a central figure in Guinean art history who is today best remembered via Frantz Fanon as an exemplary literary producer of "national culture," was in fact active internationally in multiple artistic domains: music, poetry, theater, cinema, and choreography, as well as pan-Africanist anticolonial activism and postcolonial nation-building. In 1960, Keita's Paris- and Dakar-based internationally touring performance company Les Ballets Africains relocated to Conakry and became the top ensemble in Guinea's socialist-inspired national arts system, which mandated youth participation from around the country and transferred many ethnically specific art forms - notably masks and masquerade - to the national stage. When the socialist period ended in 1984, state arts patronage dwindled and many artists left for cities in Europe, the Americas, Japan, and elsewhere, inaugurating the contemporary phase in the global story of Guinean arts. Work for the seminar will include close study of objects in the Cantor Arts Center and other local collections; reading across periods, art forms, and disciplines; and short curatorial writing assignments. Final projects will take the form of position papers on proposed curatorial interventions.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Graduate Pedagogy
description: This course is designed for graduate students in Art History and Film Studies preparing to work as teaching assistants in the Department of Art and Art History. The seminar will focus on a range of theoretical and practical  concerns pertaining to the successful conceptualization, organization, and execution of class lectures and discussion sections.  Students will be exposed to a variety of perspectives and strategies related to quality teaching at the college level.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Hagia Sophia (ARTHIST 208, CLASSICS 173, CLASSICS 273)
description: This course explores the architecture, art, and music of Hagia Sophia, the cathedral of Constantinople. This building presents the largest domed interior in the Mediterranean. The architecture, while it evokes the Pantheon, surpasses the Roman precedents with its size, light, and acoustics. Employing an interdisciplinary approach, this course teaches students how to work across the fields of art and architectural history, acoustics, liturgy, music, and poetry.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Love's Reach: A Visual and Poetic History (ARTHIST 214A, COMPLIT 214A, COMPLIT 318)
description: This seminar explores love in its manifold expressions - erotic and parental, filial and friendly, queer and political - asking how each form illuminates, contests, and deepens the others. We extend our inquiry from love of persons to love of world and fate: Arendt's amor mundi and Nietzsche's amor fati, the difficult yes to existence as it is. Our materials move between philosophy, literature, and the visual arts: Plato's Symposium, Kierkegaard's Works of Love, Fromm's The Art of Loving, Weil and Murdoch on attention as love's discipline, Eva Illouz, Why Love Hurts, Sophocles' Antigone and Ovid's Orpheus; the Song of Songs, Shakespeare's sonnets, Cavafy's poems of memory and the body; Morrison's Beloved, Baldwin on love and justice, Strout's My Name Is Lucy Barton, Didion's Blue Nights, Maggie Nelson's The Argonauts, Ocean Vuong; Rembrandt's Jewish Bride, Hine's Ellis Island portraits, Goldin's Ballad of Sexual Dependency, Leibovitz's photographs of Sontag dying, Deana Lawson's tableaux of Black kinship and desire. At the heart of the seminar lies the cultivation of attention, care, resonance, dwelling, and seeing. Can love be commanded - as the v'ahavta insists ("You shall love"), as Buddhist metta is cultivated, as Sufi mahabba is practiced - or does command betray love's nature? How does love unsettle us, and how does it return us to ourselves?

subject: ARTHIST
title: Design Theory (ARTHIST 217B)
description: This seminar focuses on the key themes, histories, and methods of architectural theory -- a form of architectural practice that establishes the aims and philosophies of architecture.  Architectural theory is primarily written, but it also incorporates drawing, photography, film, and other media.  One of the distinctive features of modern and contemporary architecture is its pronounced use of theory to articulate its aims. One might argue that modern architecture is modern because of its incorporation of theory. This course focuses on those early-modern, modern, and late-modern writings that have been and remain entangled with contemporary architectural thought and design practice.  Rather than examine the development of modern architectural theory chronologically, it is explored architectural through thematic topics. These themes enable the student to understand how certain architectural theoretical concepts endure, are transformed, and can be furthered through his/her own explorations.CEE 32B is a crosslisting of ARTHIST 217B/417B.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Michelangelo: Gateway to Early Modern Italy (ARTHIST 218A, HISTORY 237B, HISTORY 337B, ITALIAN 237, ITALIAN 337)
description: Revered as one of the greatest artists in history, Michelangelo Buonarroti's extraordinarily long and prodigious existence (1475-1564) spanned the Renaissance and the Reformation in Italy. The celebrity artist left behind not only sculptures, paintings, drawings, and architectural designs, but also an abundantly rich and heterogeneous collection of artifacts, including direct and indirect correspondence (approximately 1400 letters), an eclectic assortment of personal notes, documents and contracts, and 302 poems and 41 poetic fragments. This course will explore the life and production of Michelangelo in relation to those of his contemporaries. Using the biography of the artist as a thread, this interdisciplinary course will draw on a range of critical methodologies and approaches to investigate the civilization and culture of Italy in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Course themes will follow key tensions that defined the period and that found expression in Michelangelo: physical-spiritual, classical-Christian, tradition-innovation, individual-collective.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Field Works: Contemporary Chinese Landscape Arts across Cultures (ARTHIST 226, CHINA 226, CHINA 426, EASTASN 326A)
description: An exploration of new forms of landscape art in China's contemporary era, 1980s-present. Studies of new media platforms for landscape related imagery, imagined landscapes, and expanded concepts of landscape in an era of heightened ecological consciousness.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Magic
description: In the early modern world, art and magic operated on shared principles: both could strike the viewer with sudden wonder, both sought to conjure the invisible - whether gods or natural forces - and both required esoteric training that doubled as a transformative process of initiation. This seminar examines the deep connection between visual culture and occult practices from the 15th through the 17th centuries. Through thinkers like Ficino, Agrippa, Boehme, and Bruno, the course argues that magical thinking was essentially artistic  thinking. We will explore how artists' manipulation of raw materials brought their work into close alignment with the practices of witches and healers. Through an interdisciplinary lens - examining objects ranging from early Afro-European trade fetishes and sculptors' experiments with quicksilver to the mystical hearts of Paul Kaym - we will trace how images were crafted not just to represent reality, but to actively alter it.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Otherized and Organized: The Politicization of Indigeneity in Colonial Latin America (ARTHIST 231A, NATIVEAM 231A)
description: This course focuses on Indigenous visual, material, and cultural production of early colonial Latin America (Viceroyalty of Peru and Viceroyalty of New Spain) from the mid-1500s through the mid-1700s, with some content on the very late precontact period before colonization. During this period, Indigenous Latin American peoples experienced dramatic changes to their autonomy and lifeways, with implications for their languages, social organization, and relationship to the landscape. The class will review artifacts, texts, and other cultural expressions to bring forward the complexity of cultural clash between various Indigenous and European actors and to sort through how material and cultural value--and changing value--factored into questions of political and social order. Study of cross-cultural shifts incorporates emerging discourses on race, ethnicity, and social justice. In this scope, we will address discourses and debates regarding difference, alterity, the hybrid, the transcultural, etc., and analyze how visual and material culture examples bring forward Indigenous identities as perceived and politicized in relation to questions of self and other, with attention mainly to Indigenous creators and audiences but also their European counterparts. Furthermore, a component of the class will include contemporary artworks that reflect on the reverberations of colonization of the Americas.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Rome: From Pilgrimage to the Grand Tour (ARTHIST 232, HISTORY 232D, HISTORY 332D, HISTORY 432D, ITALIAN 232D, ITALIAN 332D)
description: Imagine yourself in Rome. What do you see beyond the ruins of an ancient city? In the fourteenth century the city of over one million ancient Roman inhabitants had shrunk to a paltry population of less than twenty thousand. With the return of the papacy in the fifteenth century the rebuilding and revival of Rome began in earnest. By the late sixteenth century it was the center of global missions, an expanding state, and a nascent tourist industry. This course explores the history of the "Eternal City" from the late Middle Ages through the age of the Grand Tour. It examines the political, diplomatic, and religious history of the papacy, Roman society and cultural life, the everyday world of Roman citizens, the relationship between the city and the surrounding countryside, the material transformation of Rome as a city, and its meaning for foreigners.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Philosophy, Literature, and the Arts Core Seminar (DLCL 333, ENGLISH 333, MUSIC 332, PHIL 333)
description: This course serves as the Core Seminar for the PhD Minor in Philosophy, Literature, and the Arts. It introduces students to a wide range of topics at the intersection of philosophy with literary and arts criticism. The seminar is intended for graduate students. It is suitable for theoretically ambitious students of literature and the arts, philosophers with interests in value theory, aesthetics, and topics in language and mind, and other students with strong interest in the psychological importance of engagement with the arts. In this year's installment, we will focus on issues about the nature of fiction, about the experience of appreciation and what it does for us, about the ethical consequences of imaginative fictions, and about different conceptions of the importance of the arts in life more broadly. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Millennium Approaches: The Art of the 1990s (ARTHIST 240)
description: This seminar will examine the art historical legacy of the 1990s, the decade of Bill Clinton, Beavis and Butthead, and Y2K.  By placing art in conversation with music, popular culture, and political events, we will explore the dark underbelly of the decade's facade of sunny optimism.  Key topics will include the the end of the Cold War, multiculturalism, American interventionism, the AIDS crisis, and early internet culture.  Artists covered will include Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Kim Gordon, Mike Kelly, the Young British Artists, Gregg Bordowitz, Lorna Simpson, Zoe Leonard, Byron Kim, and Glenn Ligon.  What is the relationship between art, popular culture, and history?  How did the 1990s help shape our current culture?

subject: ARTHIST
title: Making Art History: Black Mountain College (ARTHIST 257, ARTSINST 257)
description: In 1933, artists Anni and Josef Albers arrived in rural North Carolina to teach at Black Mountain College. Drawing on their years of experience teaching at the Bauhaus, the Albers emphasized practice before theory, learning by doing.  Their lessons shaped generations of experimental artists, including Ruth Asawa, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly, and John Cage, among many others.  Co-taught by an art historian and a physicist/artist, this course takes the Albers' pedagogy as its starting point.  Our class sessions will recreate some of the Albers' foundational lessons in materials, design, drawing, and paper folding.  What emerges when we begin art history with making rather than theory?  How does the intelligence of the hand relate to knowledge of the past?

subject: ARTHIST
title: The Mongol Empire (ARTHIST 259A, HISTORY 289A, HISTORY 389A)
description: This course examines the artistic production of the Mongol Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, stretching from the Middle East to East Asia. Under the vast umbrella of an empire built by Chinggis Khan and his successors, artistic exchange brought the introduction of Chinese motifs into Islamic art; increased production of illustrated manuscripts of histories and epics such as the Shahname; production of brocaded silks in Iran and China. Islamic, Buddhist, and Christian religious monuments were built, and new cities founded.  This course looks at architecture, textiles, manuscripts, ceramics, and metalwork in this global, pre-modern Empire.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Word and Image (ARTHIST 265A, COMPLIT 225, ITALIAN 265, ITALIAN 365)
description: What impact do images have on our reading of a text? How do words influence our understanding of images or our reading of pictures? What makes a visual interpretation of written words or a verbal rendering of an image successful? These questions will guide our investigation of the manifold connections between words and images in this course on intermediality and the relations and interrelations between writing and art from classical antiquity to the present. Readings and discussions will include such topics as the life and afterlife in word and image of Ovid's "Metamorphoses," Dante's "Divine Comedy," Ludovico Ariosto's "Orlando Furioso," and John Milton's "Paradise Lost;" the writings and creative production of poet-artists Michelangelo Buonarroti, William Blake, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; innovations in and correspondences between literature and art in the modern period, from symbolism in the nineteenth century through the flourishing of European avant-garde movements in the twentieth century.

subject: ARTHIST
title: The Russian and Soviet Avant-Garde (ARTHIST 275, FILMEDIA 275, FILMEDIA 475, REES 275A)
description: This course approaches the Russian and Soviet avant-gardes through three central themes:  things, forms, and thinking. 'Things' speaks to such key concepts as dialectical materialism, nonobjective art, and faktura.  'Forms' encompasses the intricate paths of Russian Formalism as well as Constructivist design. 'Thinking' threads through things and forms as they were understood to shape subjectivities.  We will consider many arts:  literature and poetry, visual arts, fashion, architecture and film, placing the greatest emphasis on film.  Our reading will be wide-ranging in terms of time and discipline.  It will include, among others, avant-garde artists such as Kazimir Malevich and Sergei Eisenstein and their contemporaries Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Eikhenbaum. We will also read more contemporary art historians such as Christina Lodder, Yves-Alain Bois, John Bowlt, T. J. Clark, Christina Kaier, and Aglaya Glebova; film and literary scholars such as Jessica Merrill, Nariman Skakov, and Emma Widdis; and Russian historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick, Terry Martin, and Yuri Slezkine.  Films range from melodrama (Olga Preobrazhenskaya's 1927 The Peasant Women of Ryazan) to Dziga Vertov's documentaries and Eisenstein's Ivan the Terrible (1945 and 1958).  We will also make time to look at archival materials in Special Collections.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Putting It Together: The Art of Curating (AMSTUD 288, ARTHIST 288)
description: This course will focus on the production, criticism, and curating of art. Through a series of required readings, intensive class discussions, class trips, and first-hand encounters with art objects, collections, and exhibitions, we will investigate the history and practice of museum and gallery display. Our work together will depart from "Morris Hirshfield Rediscovered" the exhibition currently at the Cantor Arts Center. As the curator of the exhibition, Prof. Meyer will provide behind the scenes knowledge of how such a project is conceived and realized as well as the challenges encountered along the way.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Methods and Debates
description: This course introduces graduate students to a range of interpretive methods within art history and visual culture studies.  In addition to scrutinizing multiple schools of thought and critical debates within the field, the seminar pays particular attention to the style and strategies of writing taken up by individual critics and scholars.  How and to whom does the art historian's voice speak in different moments, visual contexts, and interpretive communities?

subject: ARTHIST
title: Qualifying Examination Preparation
description: For Art History Ph.D. candidates. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.

subject: ARTHIST
title: Dissertation Proposal Preparation
description: (Staff)
