This class is enrollment by permission only. To request a spot in the class, please fill out the survey:  https://forms.gle/S1CqZn8XcLrc5vb66

subject: ENGLISH
title: Literary Text Mining 2: Studies in Cultural Analytics
description: In this course, students will learn how to apply quantitative and computational methods for analyzing text to questions that are of significance to Literary Studies, and the humanities more broadly. Beginning with a series of readings and discussions on the theoretical implications of using quantitative methods for literary analysis, we will move to in-depth instruction in more advanced methods for computational text analysis, including topic models, word embeddings, and large language models. Students will not only become familiar with training and querying these models, but, more importantly, will gain hands-on experience in how to build these analytical techniques into humanities-based research.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Information Technologies: A History
description: Beginning with cave painting, inscription, cuneiform, hieroglyph, and other early textual innovations, this course will survey the creation, production and functionality of writing systems, images, print, sound, bytes and social media - all text technologies employed to communicate. The course will focus on the recording of language, on remembrance and on ideas explicating significant themes seen throughout history: these include censorship, propaganda, authenticity, apocalypticism, technophobia, reader response, skeumorphism, democratization, and authority. We'll learn about the production, transmission and reception of tablet technology, the scroll, the handmade book, the machine-made book, newspapers and ephemera; and we shall investigate the emergence of image, sound, and digital multimedia. We'll examine the impact of these various text technologies on their users, and try to draw out similarities and differences in our cultural and intellectual responses to evolving technologies of communication.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Mad Fiction: Literature of Mental Illness (CSRE 184B, FEMGEN 185B)
description: How have literary traditions of madness informed modern fiction's portrayals of the human mind, particularly in the context of rapidly shifting cultural frameworks about the origins and manifestations of mental illness? What are the repercussions of new forms, trends and genres for parsing (or blurring) the line between condition and personhood? Using the novels of Akwaeke Emezi, Toni Morrison, Virginia Woolf, and Leslie Marmon Silko to guide our inquiries, we'll consider inherited and new metaphors of madness in light of emerging theoretical interpretations of disability, identity, gender and trauma.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Intermediate Fiction Writing
description: Intermediate course in the craft and art of fiction writing. Students read a diverse range of short stories and novel excerpts, complete writing exercises, and submit a short and longer story to be workshopped and revised.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Fiction into Film
description: Workshop. For screenwriting students. Story craft, structure, and dialogue. Assignments include short scene creation, character development, and a long story. How fictional works are adapted to screenplays, and how each form uses elements of conflict, time, summary, and scene.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Levinthal Tutorial in Fiction
description: Undergraduate writers work individually with visiting Stegner Fellows in fiction. Students design their own curriculum; Stegner Fellows act as writing mentors and advisers. Students will meet once per week with the Stegner Fellow and also four times a quarter in discussions sections with other students and the Levinthal Program Coordinators. Times to be announced upon acceptance.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Screenwriting Intensive
description: The main requirement for this course is a full length film script. The course explores elements of screenwriting including beat structure, character creation, scene vs. montage, as well as description and dialogue. Students will read four to five screenplays during the first half of the course and then write a 90-page film script in the second half of the course. Students will additionally write synopses, treatments, character sketches, and beat sheets. Designed for any student who has always wanted to write a screenplay

subject: ENGLISH
title: Reading for Writers: Obsession as Muse
description: Taught by Jenny Tinghui Zhang, the Stein Visiting Writer. Being a writer means being in a constant state of obsession-what else could incite the passion and inquiry that makes a person want to create art? This class is interested in two things: one, how we, as writers, can identify and nurture our obsessions in order to deepen our creative practice and two, how we can mine our obsessions for our own writing and storytelling. For this class, I ask that you allow yourself to be obsessed, whether it be with a person, an animal, a concept, a pattern, or a corner of the world so niche that no one but you can call it home. Be prepared to go down rabbit holes, research in the field, and interact with your obsessions. Most of all, be prepared to write into your obsessions, letting them lead you out of narrative dead-ends and toward something greater, more divine. We will read across genres, including but not limited to novels, essays, short stories, plays, poetry, visual media, and more. Class will include take-home writing assignments and in-class writing exercises, as well as reading and workshopping each other's work with an eye toward constructive feedback, compassion, and collaboration.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Intermediate Creative Nonfiction
description: Continuation of ENGLISH 91. Reading a variety of creative essays, completing short writing exercises, and discussing narrative techniques in class. Students submit a short (2-5 page) and a longer (8-20 page) nonfictional work to be workshopped and revised.

subject: ENGLISH
title: DCI Intermediate Memoir Workshop
description: Open to DCI Fellows & Partners only. DCI Intermediate Memoir Workshop will take as its occasion for your creative development a continuing examination of memoir essays and memoir book excerpts. These texts broadly innovate within and outside of the formal traditions you studied in DCI Memoir workshop, to find new and exciting ways to represent personal experience. We will read authors including Kathryn Harrison, Brian Doyle, Jerald Walker, Patricia Hampl, MFK Fisher, Jo Ann Beard, and Tressie McMillan Cottom. This course will also serve as the continuing examination and practice of formal memoir writing. My goal for your learning in this class is that you walk out of our last session having done the following: 1) Written a next piece to follow in some way on your work in DCI Memoir: a new or next chapter, a related or new essay, an expansion into a larger piece, etc. 2) Looked at more sophisticated models for writing about your own life in a meaningful way, including hybrids of journalism and personal writing (e.g., The New Yorker), deep dives into personal subjects that twin with passions or areas of expertise, travel writing, and lyric forms of the essay. 3) Written two Short Essays based on more sophisticated writing prompts. 4) Participated in whole-class workshops for both Short Essays, and in a full-class workshop for your next piece. 5) Practiced giving and receiving helpful individual and workshop peer feedback. A variety of creative prompts, critical exercises, and assigned readings will foster your understanding and appreciation of creative nonfiction, as well as your growth as a creative writer. Energetic, committed participation is a must.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Levinthal Tutorial in Nonfiction
description: Undergraduate writers work individually with visiting Stegner Fellows in nonfiction. Students design their own curriculum; Stegner Fellows act as writing mentors and advisers. Students will meet once per week with the Stegner Fellow and also four times a quarter in discussions sections with other students and the Levinthal Program Coordinators. Times to be announced upon acceptance.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Techniques in Poetry: The Historic Hinge (AFRICAAM 114)
description: This course is designed to help the writer use historic iconography in their writing. We will explore both the methods of research and the craft of poetry. By the end of the quarter, you should understand not only what to include on the page from the research you've done but also of what informs the writing. You will post your research and original poems on a Substack and a podcast, for which you'll receive technical support before launching. The goal will be to find the proper structure and form to contain the historic material employed. You will also learn how to organize your research material for application to your own poetry. Don't worry: You will need neither prior experience writing poetry nor prior experience creating a podcast to do well this quarter.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Levinthal Tutorial in Poetry
description: Undergraduate writers work individually with visiting Stegner Fellows in poetry. Students design their own curriculum; Stegner Fellows act as writing mentors and advisers. Students will meet once per week with the Stegner Fellow and also four times a quarter in discussions sections with other students and the Levinthal Program Coordinators. Times to be announced upon acceptance.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Practice of Poetic Erasure
description: Choose a book - any book. Choose a song or film, choose a building, painting, or an epic. Now, imagine erasing most of the words (or images from that book, film, space) in order to create, or discover, a wholly new different story: your story, or another's story, some expression the original writer or artist themselves could not have conceived of when they created their text originally. This, crudely, is the definition of poetic erasure. Found poetry. If it sounds vile, it is. It can also be brilliant, emboldened, politically exacting, tender, historically revelatory, sublime, and thrilling. More often than not, it is also heartbreaking. Through weekly slide shows, readings, discussions, and workshops, we will explore the history of contemporary poetic erasure, placing emphasis on what might have been - and what could be - if we read a book from any myriad of directions other than ways the author intended. Indeed, one of the best unforeseen strengths (gifts?) of poetic erasure is that it makes us keenly aware of history's unspoken often unconscious intentions. What might have happened, for example, if Shakespeare were a woman, a woman who decided  to cut just a few more lines from her genius sonnets, choosing to create evocative early-modern avant-garde exploration instead? Or what might have taken place if a few of the English Romantics, in a communal renunciation of authorship, mashed all their poems into one much shorter, but anonymous, collective text? Who or what does the author become then? What if a Victorian writer had painted over the majority of her own novel, blocking out most of the words with opaque paint instead, dismissing altogether the habit of narrative cohesion? What does a "book" mean then? What is a "poem"? And what do these aesthetic gestures represent symbolically about our entwined cultures and histories? Perhaps most importantly, what occurs to our own linguistic indoctrination and unconscious historical intentions when we practice erasure ourselves? In this workshop, via a discussion of desire, war, expansionism, we will examine contemporary poetic erasures in order to focus on the means by which history - often unconsciously - saturates our literature and our own writing.  By repositioning erasure within the broader context of contemporary American poetry, this workshop will explore how poetic erasure offers writers a dynamic tool by which to push language, and perhaps most importantly, to be pushed by language. The goal of this workshop is to explore how an erasure practice can enable writers and artists to play more seriously, more openly and rigorously. Through weekly discussions, writing exercises, and workshops, participants will be encouraged to uncover - and utilize - the historical and aesthetic gestures at work, often unconsciously and ahistorically, within English itself.  Besides the usual requirements (astute participation, passionate engagement, regular attendance, a harmless and equally painless 10 minute oral report), in this workshop the main emphasis will be placed on students creating and workshopping their own original poetic erasures.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Honors Seminar: Critical Approaches to Literature
description: Overview of literary-critical methodologies, with a practical emphasis shaped by participants' current honors projects. Restricted to students in the English Honors Program.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Seniors Honors Essay
description: In two quarters.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Individual Work
description: Undergraduates who wish to study a subject or area not covered by regular courses may, with consent, enroll for individual work under the supervision of a member of the department. 198 may not be used to fulfill departmental area or elective requirements without consent. Group seminars are not appropriate for 198.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Capstone: Why Literature Matters (To Me)
description: This class will be a hybrid seminar and workshop. In the seminar, we will be pairing short literary texts with critical essays that respond to them. These will provide models for the work you will be pursuing in your capstone. Roughly one-half of the class meetings will be workshops. During the workshop, you will be actively revising a previously written essay, often expanding on the strengths of the earlier work, and cutting or rewriting entirely the weaker points. Additionally, all students are encouraged to meet with a professor who has expertise in your topic to discuss your topic and revisions at least twice during the quarter.Readings will be drawn from poetry, short stories, creative non-fiction, drama and journalism, and each of these will be paired with a critical response.  We will be looking at issues of narrative voice, as well as assessing what makes a great critical essay, noting especially protocols of scholarly research. Prior to the first class, each student must email me (pphelan@stanford.edu) a copy of the paper or project that will constitute the core of your capstone. This will assist me in selecting relevant readings.

subject: ENGLISH
title: I Bet You Think You're Funny: Humor Writing Workshop
description: Nothing is harder than being funny on purpose. We often associate humor with lightness, and sometimes that's appropriate, but humor is inextricably interlinked with pain and anger, and our funniest moments often spring from our deepest wounds. Humor can also allow us a platform for rage and indignation when other forms of rhetoric feel inadequate. This workshop will take students through the techniques and aesthetics of humor writing, in a variety of forms, and the main product of the quarter will be to submit for workshop a sustained piece of humor writing.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Book That Changed My Life
description: Can reading a  poem, story, novel, or essay help you figure out what you want to do with your life? The answer is a resounding yes for the Stanford faculty participating in this new one-credit class, "The Book that Changed My Life." Hear what some of Stanford's most popular and distinguished professors have to say on this topic - professors of African & African American Studies; Art & Art History; Bioengineering, genetics, medicine and biomedical data science;  History; Literature; Economics; Education, and Law. We will read short works (or excerpts from longer works) by James Baldwin, Charles Baudelaire, Wendell Berry,  Anton Chekhov, Sigmund Freud, Homer, James Joyce,  Nella Larssen, Norman, Maclean, Herman Melville, Grace Paley, Salman Rushdie, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Mark Twain, and Virginia Woolf. The class will meet Tuesdays 5:30-6:30.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Comics:  More than Words (DLCL 238, FILMEDIA 38)
description: This research unit looks at Comics from a transnational, cross-cultural, and interdisciplinary perspective. Each quarter we organize a series of lectures, reading sessions, and workshops around a main topic. This year we plan on exploring topics such as Manga, Manhwa, Manhua (Fall 2026) and Comics and Medicine (Winter 2027). In Fall and Winter, we will meet a total of 3 times at noon on the Thursdays of Weeks 3, 6, and 9. In the Spring quarter, we will have our first Stanford Comic-Con, a two-day event that will be held on Wednesday and Thursday of Week 4. To earn the unit during the Fall and Winter quarters, students must attend all events hosted, do the readings in advance of the meeting, and participate actively in the class discussions. To earn the unit during the Spring quarter, students must attend at least 4 of the 6 events at the Stanford Comic-Con. Some topics that we explored in past quarters are: Postcolonialism and Decoloniality, Feminism, Superheroes, Computer Science, Comic Theory, Environmentalism, and Early History of Comics.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Dickens Reading
description: Through the academic year, we will read one Dickens novel, one number a week for 19 weeks, as the Victorians would have done as they read the serialized novel over the course of 19 months.  The group gets together once a week for an hour and a half to discuss each number, to look carefully at the pattern that the author is weaving, to guess, as the Victorians would have done, what might be coming next, and to investigate the Victorian world Dickens presents.  We look carefully at themes, characters, metaphorical patterns, and scenes that form Dickens' literary world, and spend increasing time evaluating the critique that Dickens levels at Victorian life.   The weekly gatherings are casual; the discussion is lively and pointed.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Experiments in Making
description: This generative creative writing course is open to students across genres and is ideal for writers embarking on longform projects or integrating research into original texts. It is my hope that weekly, collective study of works by such thinkers as Kamau Brathwaite and Helene Cixous will agitate our imaginative practices in generative and needful ways. As a way of learning with assigned materials, class participants are expected to write and revise work in response to in-class prompts, give presentations on assigned topics in craft, and provide peers with thoughtfully considered feedback and observations of their work. The course will be reading and writing intensive. It will also be a kind of laboratory for trying and making. Among the artists whose work we will likely think with are Federico García Lorca, Helene Cixous, Kamau Brathwaite, Flying Lotus, Cristina Rivera Garza, Pina Bausch, Robin Coste Lewis, Bhanu Kapil, mangaliso buzani, Victoria Chang, Anne Boyer, and Ghassan Zaqtan.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Poetry: Wordsworth, Dickinson, Rilke
description: This class looks at three master poets, William Wordsworth, Emily Dickinson, and Rainer Maria Rilke, closely reading some of their most famous short lyrics, to think about the essence of poetic utterance, how words gain power when put in near-magical incantatory sequence, and what we contribute as readers and literary critics.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Lights, Cinema, and the Writer's Pencil! Vladimir Nabokov and Cinema (FILMEDIA 412A, SLAVIC 212)
description: An experimental and synesthetic author, Vladimir Nabokov (1899-1977) featured many references to films and actors in his novels - from Buster Keaton to Greta Garbo, and from Charlie Chaplin's "The Floorwalker" to Harold Lloyd's "Safety Last!" These references are not only thematic, but also stylistic, turning Nabokov into one of the first writers who tried and adapted cinematographic techniques to literary texts. In this way, Nabokov shapes a style that is able to tell stories through visual associations, to convey the dynamicity of our lives, and to express the human experiences of time and imagination. During the course, we will read Nabokov's writings (including "Lolita," "A Laughter in the Dark," "The Gift," and "Invitation to a Beheading") and contextualize him in his multi-cultural milieu - from pre-revolutionary Russia to the emigration in Europe and to his success in the US. We will see that Nabokov was a writer curious to explore human self-consciousness by responding to the cultural trends swirling around him. As we read his novels, we will watch early twentieth-century movies and discuss how Nabokov turned cinematographic techniques into literary devices. Together, we will reflect on how cinema has changed the way we tell stories and recount and visualize our experiences. Thanks to its interdisciplinary nature and to Nabokov being a multi-lingual author, the course is open to students of Slavic studies, English studies, comparative literatures, and cinema studies, as well as to students who are curious to explore the themes of experimentation and hybridization among the arts.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Victorian Poetry
description: Poetry in the British Victorian era was fraught with contradiction. Scientific progress contributed, on the one hand, to a reeling sense of doubt and disorientation within a universe that seemed to be becoming ever more complex and, on the other, to a deeper investment in domesticity and religious faith. Mourning and a sense of loss and melancholy became melodic, as poets sought for ideals and heroism within a self-interested, commercial society. Poets like Alfred, Lord Tennyson and the pre-Raphaelites (Dante Gabriel Rossetti, William Morris) turned to the chivalric adventures - knights, battles, and courtly ladies -  of Arthurian legend, while others like Robert Browning escaped into the Italian Renaissance for inspiration. The voice of women in poetry grew, expressing ambition and spiritual struggle, speaking out for classical female figures (Xantippe, Circe) in the form of the dramatic monologue, and addressing the plight of the 'fallen woman' and of the virtuous but inexperienced 'angel in the house.' In this course, we will read lyric, dramatic, and narrative poetry by Tennyson, Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning, D.G. and Christina Rossetti, Morris, Augusta Webster, Amy Levy, Matthew Arnold, Emily and Anne Brontë, Thomas Hardy, George Meredith, and Gerard Manley Hopkins.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Baroque Tragedy (ENGLISH 323A, FRENCH 223A, FRENCH 323A, ITALIAN 223A, ITALIAN 323A)
description: A study of major theories of the baroque by theorists such as Wolfflin, Croce, and Benjamin together with a close reading of baroque tragedies by Tasso, Milton, Shakespeare, Calderon, Racine, Joseph Simon, and others.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Don DeLillo and His Times, 1971-2026
description: Don DeLillo and His Times, 1971-2026

subject: ENGLISH
title: Fictions of Early Capitalism
description: Early modernity names the period of transition from feudalism to capitalism that included, among other changes, the dissolution of the monasteries, the enclosure of common lands, the formation of corporations, and the expansion of colonialism and trade. How did these transformations in the economy ramify in the literary production of the period? What is enabled and obscured by these grand narratives of historical change, and how have these useful fictions conditioned our perceptions of literary texts, genres, and forms? This seminar will take up these questions by examining travel narratives (Spenser, Raleigh), drama (Shakespeare, Massinger, Daborne), and early novels (Behn) alongside economic theory (Marx, Smith, et al.) and philosophies of history (Hegel, Nietzsche).

subject: ENGLISH
title: Literature Against the Law (CIVIC 135A, ENGLISH 135A)
description: The legal censorship of literature is on the rise again. But current efforts have their roots in a range of statutes from the last hundred and fifty years. In this course, we read politically significant literature that was subject to censorship alongside the various legal instruments used to censor them. These include more familiar statues like obscenity and sedition, as well as less likely suspects like libel law, customs agencies, and even blasphemy! If you enjoy fiction and are considering law school, this course is for you!

subject: ENGLISH
title: Before Novels
description: What is at stake when we identify ancient, medieval, or early modern works as proto-novelistic, especially when such texts encompass the wondrous, the mystical, the factual, and/or didactic? What do the "prosaic" dimensions of prose fiction disclose about our conceptions or history, truth, or reality? Readings for this course may include (in English translation where applicable) Lucian, A True History; Kempe, The Book of Margery Kempe; Cervantes, Don Quixote; Nashe, The Unfortunate Traveller; Hooke, Micrographia; Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year; Austen, Persuasion.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Gothic in Literature and Culture (COMPLIT 118, COMPLIT 238E, ENGLISH 138E)
description: This course introduces students to the major features of Gothic narrative, a form that emerges at the same time as the Enlightenment, and that retains its power into our present. Surveying Gothic novels, as well as novellas and short stories with Gothic elements, we will learn about the defining features of the form and investigate its meaning in the cultural imagination.  Gothic narratives, the course will suggest, examine the power of irrational forces in a secular age: forces that range from barbaric human practices, to supernatural activity, to the re-enchantment of modern existence.  We will also consider the importance for Gothic authors and readers of the relation among narrative. spectacle and the visual arts.  Primary works may include Ann Radcliffe's <e>The Italian, Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey, Victor Hugo's The Hunchback of Notre Dame, E.T.A. Hoffman's The Sandman, Mary Shelly's Frankenstein, and Edgar Allen Poe's The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym.  We may also do a section on vampires, including Bram Stoker's Dracula, and its remake in film by F.W. Murnau and Werner Herzog. Critical selections by Edmund Burke, Sigmund Freud, Walter Benjamin, Michel Foucault, and Terry Castle, among others.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Medieval Ecologies
description: How did medieval people interact with their broader environment? What can we learn from these interactions? In this course, we will explore how medieval literature and art situate human beings in relation to the nonhuman world, in ways that are simultaneously radically alien and resonant with our own modern perspective. Through a combination of creative and critical assignments, participants will reflect on how premodern modes of thought can illuminate our present, helping us envision new ways of interacting with our planet's many inhabitants.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Black Ecologies (AFRICAAM 140, AFRICAAM 240C, EARTHSYS 146J, EARTHSYS 246J, ENGLISH 146, ENGLISH 346A, FEMGEN 146B, FEMGEN 246B)
description: Black literature and media have long served as important sites of ecological thought and as blueprints for resistance to the combined matrices of imperialism, racialized dispossession, and extractivism. In exploring key works by Jamaica Kincaid, Derek Walcott, Zakiyyah Iman Jackson, adrienne maree brown, Julie Dash, and others, we will unpack and complicate the idea of the human, and prioritize intersectional approaches to thinking with the violence of climate catastrophe. In so doing, we will approach ecology as both subject and method, and investigate possibilities for radically other futures outside the entrapments of racial capitalism and environmental degradation. While our course texts index the disastrous effects of racial capitalism and accompanying ecocide, they also chart different modes of thinking-living-acting where "Black livingness" (McKittrick) is a central aspect of ecology.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Transpacific Literary Futures (ASNAMST 289)
description: Transpacific Literary Futures

subject: ENGLISH
title: Asian Myths, Modern Retellings (ASNAMST 128N)
description: This course focuses on Asian American literature that adapts traditional Asian myths and folktales into new American contexts. We will examine how Asian myths offer an ambivalent cultural inheritance for Asian Americans: on the one hand, serving as narrative tools for constructing identity amidst racism and assimilationist pressures; on the other, retaining burdensome roots of tradition that require reckoning within intergenerational Asian American communities. Whenever possible, we will examine original versions of an Asian myth first before exploring its English-language adaptations, identifying which narrative differences matter and analyzing why. Above all, students will get a sense of how to engage with myths as a literary genre acting in concert with the needs of specific historical and cultural moments. Familiarity with Asian languages and cultures is not required for this course but will be helpful for specific activities that we do in class.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Advanced Fiction Writing
description: Workshop critique of original short stories or novel.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Advanced Creative Nonfiction
description: English 291 takes as its occasion for your creative and critical development an examination of essays and book excerpts in various creative nonfiction subgenres. These essays and excerpts work within traditional and innovative forms to find new and exciting ways to represent personal experience. This course also serves as the continuing examination and practice of creative nonfiction in English 191. You will write, workshop, present to the class, and revise drafts of work. All workshops will serve as the springboard for larger class conversations about theme and craft. A variety of creative prompts, critical exercises, and assigned readings will foster your understanding and appreciation of creative nonfiction, as well as your growth as a creative writer. All prompts will move you toward a culminating project of realizing either an essay to submit for possible publication or a draft book-length synopsis and outline. This course is designed for students who have completed English 191. Students who have completed creative nonfiction writing course elsewhere or who have extensive other writing workshop experience may petition the instructor for enrollment. Energetic, committed participation is a must.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Advanced Poetry Writing
description: The focus of the course will be both on the generation of new work and on strategies to solve artistic problems through studies in poetic craft.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Literary Translation: Theory and Practice (COMPLIT 293, DLCL 293)
description: An overview of translation theories and practices over time. The aesthetic, ethical, and political questions raised by the act and art of translation and how these pertain to the translator's tasks. Discussion of translation challenges and the decision processes taken to address these issues. Coursework includes assigned theoretical readings, comparative translations, and the undertaking of an individual translation project. Enrollment limited. A core course for the Translation Studies Minor.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Reading Austen
description: An immersive seminar on Austen's fiction, for graduate and upper-level undergraduates. Our emphasis will be, as much as possible, on carefully reading the major novels and reflecting on the reading experience itself. We will also look at flashpoints in Austen criticism, including selections from three intensive, book-length studies by Claudia Johnson, Freya Johnston and D. A. Miller, as well as other critical essays. Here, too, a primary focus will be on the strategies of reading that are brought to bear in criticism. How is textual evidence deployed? How are particular passages selected and activated? How does criticism strive not merely to interpret but to recapitulate the experience of the novel?

subject: ENGLISH
title: Perceval and the Quest for the Holy Grail (COMPLIT 302G, GERMAN 302)
description: Beginning with Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Conte du Graal (ca. 1180), we examine the Grail story in its inaugural vernacular form - as a text defined by incompletion, formal ambiguity, and interpretive openness. We then turn to Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (ca. 1200-1210), which transforms Chretien's enigmatic conte into an architecturally intricate exploration of guilt, grace, kinship, and knightly becoming. The seminar will also attend to the story's remarkable afterlife in literary and artistic adaptation, with students presenting an adaptation of their choosing. Readings and discussion in English.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Queer Romance (COMPLIT 203R, FEMGEN 203F, FRENCH 203, FRENCH 303, ITALIAN 202)
description: "Sometimes I think I've found my hero, but it's a queer romance": these are Lorenz Hart's words, sung famously by Ella Fitzgerald, and they embody one of the central paradoxes of romance in both the medieval and the modern senses of the word: that heroism, like love, doesn't necessarily look the way we expect it to, and that some of the pleasure as well as the pathos of reading, and loving, lies in this misrecognition. This course explores the queerness of romance - its proliferation of bodies and desires, its flirting with and thwarting of the scripts for happy heteronormative couplehood, its erotic exuberance - by juxtaposing some of the classics of medieval continental literature with some particularly striking contemporary genre fiction. Expect to read Beroul's Tristan, Chretien de Troyes' Knight of the Cart, Marguerite Porete's Mirror of Simple Souls and Heldris of Cornwall's Silence alongside a handful of twenty-first century queer and trans romances. All texts will be read and discussed in English, although students are welcome to engage with Francophone material in the original if they so desire.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Character
description: How do loose bits of textual material transform into literary characters of heft and substance? How do we make sense of such characters beyond the most ordinary modes of identifying with or repudiating them? Before reflecting on the "rounded" characters familiar from the Victorian novel and more recent genres of writing, this course surveys ancient and early modern texts (with selections drawn from the Bible, Don Quixote, and the Shakespearean canon) for alternate models of the literary subject. We'll look at texts that deploy characters as embodiments of concepts or ideals before considering historical movements that have formed our taste for literary figures of flesh and blood. A focus on the implied people of texts requires an extended reckoning with social categories and ethical distinctions more generally. This course thus draws from the force of history as well as our day-to-day habits of deciphering the living characters around us. We'll direct this deep knowledge toward the searching - and, as participants should find, equally rigorous and exhilarating - experiments of textual interpretation.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Pitching and Publishing in Popular Media (DLCL 312, FEMGEN 312F)
description: FOR GRADUATE STUDENTS (undergraduates enroll in 119) Most of the time, writing a pitch for a popular outlet just means writing an email. So why be intimidated? This course will outline the procedure for pitching essays and articles to popular media: how to convince an editor, agent, or anyone else that your idea is compelling, relevant, and deliverable. We'll take a holistic approach to self-presentation that includes presenting yourself with confidence, optimizing your social media and web platform, networking effectively, writing excellent queries and pitches, avoiding the slush pile, and perhaps most importantly, persevering through the inevitable self-doubt and rejection.We will focus on distinguishing the language, topics and hooks of popular media writing from those of academic writing, learn how to target and query editors on shortform pieces (personal essays, news stories, etc.), and explore how humanists can effectively self-advocate and get paid for their work.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Late Seventeenth-Century Literature
description: A period in which public servants wrote experimental poetry, scientists practiced experimental philosophy, political activists dreamed of states of nature, and manual laborers wrote prose that wouldn't die. This moment of knowledge production - the alternate modernity in England also known as early modernity - will be approached holistically as well as in close textual range.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The World, The Globe, The Planet
description: This course will introduce graduate students to several competing concepts of world-circulating literatures and methodologies for studying them. As the title suggests, the course introduces students to more established ideas of "World Literature", concepts around "globalization" and its distinction from the World category, as well as ideas of Planetarity, including ecocritical approaches.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Love and Death
description: How do we put into words the ineffable emotions generated by love and grief? How have writers, across centuries and many different literary traditions, sung the praises of a beloved, or lamented the ache of loss? In this hybrid literature and creative writing course, we will alternate between the close-reading of model texts and generating original poetry and prose written under the influence of literary heroes.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Literature, Narrative, and the Self (COMPLIT 328, FRENCH 328, ITALIAN 328)
description: It is often said that "life is a narrative," or that "we live our lives in stories." But is this true? Do we always live our lives as narratives? Could we fail to live our lives as narratives? Could we choose not to live our lives as narratives? Even for those who do see their life as a story, will any old narrative do, or is there something special about the examples provided by the literary tradition? How does literary genre factor in? What is closure? And why are middles what they are? Readings from Appiah, Aristotle, Camus, Hume, Nietzsche, Simmel, G. Strawson, Velleman; Brooks, Woloch; Kahneman, Sacks; Shakespeare, Balzac, Sartre, Beckett, Calvino, Levi, Morrison. Films by Ephron, Kaufman, Polley. Taught in English.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Mental Traveler: Allegory, Symbol, Diagram from Dante to Blake
description: The long history of figural representation beyond the mimetic - allegorical, symbolic, diagrammatic - involves the human effort to limn the perceptible world with the divine. The Romantic poet and artist William Blake used allegorical narratives and symbolic artwork, diagrammatic imagery and designs to express his own complex idea of eternity and what it meant to travel, quite literally, through it. This course will explore the theory and methodology of figural technique, particularly as it emerges in the early Christian Era and becomes historicized and appropriated in the eighteenth century and beyond. We will focus on the central works in Blake's extensive canon devoted to the symbolic pilgrimage of the human through a cosmos that is larger than time. From The Mental Travller through The Four Zoas, from Chaucer's Canterbury Pilgrims through Jerusalem, Blake's poetry, illuminated artowork, and designs will provide the basis for a deeper plunge into allegory, symbol, and diagram. We will consider the origins of religious mythologies and the relation of quantum cosmology and differential topology to the captivating universe of an artist who considered himself a Traveller thro' Eternity.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Dark Aesthetics: The Decolonial Possibilities of Multifocal Novels
description: Over the past half century, multifocal narratives have emerged as a dominant literary mechanism for distributing narrative space across characters of different classes and ethno-racial communities. Such narratives seek to undo the pernicious epistemic effects of colonial histories while putting forward alternative ideas of subjectivity, community, and the logics by which people live together. By introducing readers to multiple worlds of sense - that is, to alternative domains of intelligibility inhabited by a variety of characters, each of which has its own sociality and set of values - multifocal narratives provincialize the so-called "universal" perspective and dismantle the Western idea of the autonomous individual. Employing a relational race studies approach to inquire into the historical emergence and ongoing articulations of race and ethnicity as powerful markers of human difference, we will multifocal novels by writers such as Tommy Orange, Bernardine Evaristo, Marlon James, Jennifer Egan, and Louise Erdrich, as well as read the scholarship of thinkers such as Walter Mignolo, Edouard Glissant, Audre Lorde, Frantz Fanon, Maria Lugones, and Gloria Anzaldua.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Ancients, Moderns, and Postmoderns
description: Many literary critics and art historians depend on stylized accounts of modernity, post-modernity, and antiquity.  We will ask what purpose such accounts serve, what historical conditions have given rise to them, and what dangers they may pose to critics today.  The primary purpose of this course is to equip graduate students to read critical arguments that turn on historical claims with greater sophistication and, just as important, to reflect on their own historical assumptions and methods.  A secondary purpose is to prepare students to write arguments that will speak not just to colleagues in their narrow historical period but to colleagues who work on periods remote from theirs.  One of the keys to succeeding as a critic is learning how to talk across period divisions.  In their final essays, students should feel free to write about any work of literature, art object, or historical event, provided they in some way employ or resist a historicist interpretation.  Essays on any of the theorists on the syllabus are also welcome.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Queer Theory: Literature, Performance, and Art (FEMGEN 335, TAPS 335T)
description: This is an interdisciplinary course introducing the primary contributions to the field of queer theory in the humanities. These readings will begin with Eve Sedgwick's work and responses to it from Heather Love, Jane Gallop, Jose Munoz, and Lauren Berlant. Then we will look at the work of Judith Butler and its impact on Performance Studies; readings here will include work by Phelan, Hart, and Halberstam. We will also consider queer theory's influence in Art History by reading texts by Norman Bryson, Jonathan Katz, Judith Bryan Wilson, and Richard Meyer (among others). We will also reflect on the critical discussion of why queer theory "failed." Readings will be by David Halperin and will also include President Trump's executive order mandating that the United States recognizes only two gender categories. In addition to reading and participating in all seminar meetings, students will be asked to give one short presentation of 20 minutes AND to serve as a respondent to the work of another student (10 minutes). These responses will serve to give students an opportunity to begin the difficult work of thinking across different fields. Final essays (15-20 pages) will engage with the material on the syllabus but they can be shaped in a way that best serves your overall interests and concerns.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Anguish and Desire in Premodern British Literature
description: This survey of premodern British literature will introduce graduate students to major premodern vernacular texts - their sources, genres, influence, and interpretative problems - through the related themes of anguish and desire. For what did early English writers and their personas long? How are the emotional pain and trauma of unfulfilled longing articulated and resolved? How useful might modern Trauma Theory, Affective Hermeneutics, and Phenomenology be in studying early literature? We will examine epic, lyric and wisdom poetry; Romance and mystical texts; hagiography, Chaucer's Wife of Bath, and Arthurian legend.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Premodern Aesthetics
description: What was premodern aesthetics? The question itself ensures raised eyebrows and accusations of anachronism. "Aesthetics" identifies a post-Enlightenment body of theory that subjects issues of beauty and taste to philosophical inquiry; following Kant's Third Critique, the "aesthetic judgment" is necessarily disinterested, and therefore at odds with the devotional, didactic, and political aims of much literature and visual art produced in the Middle Ages and the early Renaissance. In this seminar, we will discern the vocabulary and concepts with which premodern thinkers understood the category of beauty and its relationship to perception. To do so, we will examine an array of literary, theological, and philosophical works written from classical antiquity to the sixteenth century - among them, rhetorical treatises, biblical commentaries, and vernacular poetry and prose - that aim to describe, make sense of, and produce aesthetic experience. All assigned readings, except for those written in accessible Middle English, will be available in modern English translation. No prior knowledge of medieval literature is required.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Black Ecologies (AFRICAAM 140, AFRICAAM 240C, EARTHSYS 146J, EARTHSYS 246J, ENGLISH 146, ENGLISH 246, FEMGEN 146B, FEMGEN 246B)
description: Black literature and media have long served as important sites of ecological thought and as blueprints for resistance to the combined matrices of imperialism, racialized dispossession, and extractivism. In exploring key works by Jamaica Kincaid, Derek Walcott, Zakiyyah Iman Jackson, adrienne maree brown, Julie Dash, and others, we will unpack and complicate the idea of the human, and prioritize intersectional approaches to thinking with the violence of climate catastrophe. In so doing, we will approach ecology as both subject and method, and investigate possibilities for radically other futures outside the entrapments of racial capitalism and environmental degradation. While our course texts index the disastrous effects of racial capitalism and accompanying ecocide, they also chart different modes of thinking-living-acting where "Black livingness" (McKittrick) is a central aspect of ecology.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Cultural Studies and Cultural Criticism
description: The class will introduce graduate students to the fundamental methodologies of cultural studies and cultural critique, through foundational texts in these traditions as well as recent exemplary instances.  Traditions may include Frankfurt School, Birmingham School, and Chicago School sociology, as well as idiosyncratic US practitioners such from Susan Sontag and Leslie Fiedler to Andrea Long Chu.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Neo-Formalisms
description: Literary theory in the twenty-first century has been marked by a return to formalist modes of thinking about the text. Alternatively presented as a reaction to sociological or cultural modes of critical reading and a radical expansion of what "form" is, these so-called neo-formalist methods of interpretation have both returned us to an interest in close-reading, and surfaced alternative approaches to uncovering meaning in text. In this class, we will begin by revisiting formalist theories of the 20th century, including new criticism, structuralism, and linguistic theory before moving to interrogate recent formalist methods such as surface reading, distant reading, and cognitive scientific approaches to meaning in text.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Poems & Paintings
description: Do you love poetry, paintings, or perhaps both? Have you found that the more you attended to one of these forms, the more you understood about the other? This course begins with the assumption that the arts are in dialogue with each other. Our time in class will be rooted in group discussion and dialogue as well. Each week, we will look at several pairings of classic poems and enduring visual artworks. Sometimes these sets will include poems directly inspired by paintings or vice versa. Sometimes we will juxtapose paintings and poems that have no direct documentary connection but explore similar emotional and psychological terrains - love, grief, shame, joy, revelation, lostness, uncertainty, melodrama, secrets, the world of dreams.

subject: ENGLISH
title: History and Theory of the Novel: Foundations (COMPLIT 360B)
description: Can the novel, as genre, be conceptualized or critically synthesized? This course will approach such a daunting question from its two necessary starting-points: fiction and theory. On the one hand, we'll take up several of those major novels that have so often been viewed as aesthetically foundational: most likely Don Quixote, Emma, Madame Bovary and The Brothers Karamazov. On the other hand, we'll read the major theoretical statements of Lukacs (Theory of the Novel, Studies in European Realism, The Historical Novel) and Bakhtin (The Dialogical Imagination, Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics), as well as text-specific criticism. This small group of texts might be seen as both necessary and insufficient to the largest questions of the genre. Our focus will be on closely reading and engaging each text in its inviting and demanding singularity and in building an open, imaginative and wide-ranging dialogue between fictions and theories. (This course might be followed by a class the next year on History and Theory of the Novel: Experiments, extending these questions in a number of further formal, geographic and chronological directions).

subject: ENGLISH
title: History and Theory of the Novel I & II (COMPLIT 360C)
description: Can the novel, as genre, be conceptualized or critically synthesized? This course will approach such a daunting question from its two necessary starting-points: fiction and theory. On the one hand, we'll take up several of those major novels that have so often been viewed as aesthetically foundational: most likely Don Quixote, Emma, Madame Bovary and The Brothers Karamazov. On the other hand, we'll read the major theoretical statements of Lukacs (Theory of the Novel, Studies in European Realism, The Historical Novel) and Bakhtin (The Dialogical Imagination, Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics), as well as text-specific criticism. This small group of texts might be seen as both necessary and insufficient to the largest questions of the genre. Our focus will be on closely reading and engaging each text in its inviting and demanding singularity and in building an open, imaginative and wide-ranging dialogue between fictions and theories. (This course might be followed by a class the next year on History and Theory of the Novel: Experiments, extending these questions in a number of further formal, geographic and chronological directions).

subject: ENGLISH
title: Virginia Woolf: Modernist, Maker, Media
description: Survey of Woolf's major works, including novels, essays, reviews, and short fiction, including her role as self-publisher, and its impact on the recent turn in feminist book history and contemporary women's writing in new media.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Media Theory for Literary Studies
description: Introduction to media theory by way of some of its key texts and themes, with particular emphasis on how questions of medium, media, and mass media might be useful to literary studies in particular - that is, the study of predominantly textual artifacts. Works by Innis, McLuhan, Derrida, Adorno, Kittler, Hayles, Flusser and others.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Theatricality and Antitheatricality
description: The theater has never had a comfortable existence. Its detractors fall primarily into the Platonic camp, claiming that theater is mimesis, mimicry not reality, and by default is morally dangerous. Theater's supporters, on the other hand, follow Aristotle, and claim that theater is catharsis, a prompting of emotions to allow for release, a form of untruth that allows for truth to be uncovered. In this course, we will unpack the nuances of the anti-theatricality debates of late sixteenth and seventeenth century England, an era of constant threat to the theater. In addition to Plato, Aristotle, and Horace, we will be reading Philip Sidney, William Shakespeare, Thomas Heywood, William Prynne, John Milton, William Davenant, John Dryden, Thomas Rymer, and John Vanbrugh. We will focus on the theater's deep yet complex relationship to politics in this period, including the appropriation of theater for royal and imperial propaganda.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Contemporary Theory Lab (COMPLIT 367E, ILAC 367E)
description: This new graduate seminar examines the question of whether a new canon of theoretical monographs-as opposed to influential standalone essays or papers-has coalesced in recent years. We focus on a post-Foucaultian, post-1989 moment, understanding theory as an autonomous, interdisciplinary enterprise that is not subservient or reducible to philosophy or literary criticism but shares many of the core concerns of each discipline. The seminar provides students with a safe space to discuss cutting-edge ideas, arguing for, with, and against influential trends. We will study six to eight monographs in great detail, at least two of which will be determined by class vote. Of special interest are conceptual formations and methodologies that do not have an institutional home or pursue a narrow political agenda. Topics include anticolonial thinking, new materialism, affect studies, and the shadow of the linguistic turn. We may draw from a roster of thinkers such as Bruno Latour, Saidiya Hartman, Verónica Gago, Sianne Ngai, Rob Nixon, Sara Ahmed, Martin Hägglund, Arturo Escobar, Mark Fisher, Wendy Brown, and Fred Moten. Previous experience with theory is recommended. Assignments sequence short papers with revisions, short student presentations, and a final paper. Stanford faculty and outside guests will be a mainstay. Broader community engagement with theory, as well as student integration of the subject matter towards their independent research projects, will be central goals. Open to co-terms, masters, and PhD students in the humanities and social sciences.

subject: ENGLISH
title: 19th-Century American Literature Through the Short Story
description: A survey for graduate students of major topics in 19th-century American literature seen through the critical lens of the short story. According to the Russian formalist critic Boris Eikhenbaum, the short story was "the one fundamental and self-contained genre in American prose fiction," representing a parallel, self-contained, and developing tradition if anything more centrally located in the nation than the novel. The course aims to develop, as far as possible, ways to consider the short story as a distinct genre rather than a warm-up to the novel, and to explore the social and cultural forces that privileged the short story over other forms of prose fiction. We will focus on major short story collections from authors such as Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, Edgar Allan Poe, Sarah Orne Jewett, Kate Chopin, Charles Chesnutt, and Henry James. Topics germane to the short story include: attention and addiction; strangeness and the gimmick; ephemerality and liminality; scale and minorness; economy and work; networks and paratexts; detection and revelation; theory and metafiction.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Teaching, Ethics, and Literature in the Age of AI (COMPLIT 378)
description: The explosion of AI presents a critical, and unique, moment of crisis for education, and society in general. When artificial intelligence is promoted as not only more efficient, but also better, than human intelligence, when we defer to machines to do our reading and writing, the purpose and function of literary studies is destroyed. How and why then, do we proceed? This course is founded on the principle that only reading and speaking and writing together in a community of learning can we regain and invigorate literary studies and humanistic studies in general. We will read and discuss texts that have at their center questions of crisis and ethics and notions of collectivity - these texts in particular give us much to think on, and with.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Graduate Fiction Workshop
description: Open to Stegner Fellows in the Creative Writing Program only. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Comparative Studies of Race, Slavery, and Diaspora
description: This seminar examines the concept of race, processes of racialization, and theory and methods for the interdisciplinary and comparative study of race, slavery, and diaspora formation. Drawing on readings from across the humanities, but with a focus on literary studies, this course emphasizes comparison in three distinct ways: comparison of processes of racialization; comparison of academic disciplines in their approaches to race and enslavement; and comparison of racial formations across discrete historical periods and geographical areas. In its focus on theory and methods, this seminar encourages students to contemplate and formulate questions about knowledge production common to all academic disciplines.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Graduate Poetry Workshop
description: Open to Stegner Fellows in the Creative Writing Program only. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Independent Study
description: Preparation for first-year Ph.D. qualifying examination and third year Ph.D. oral exam.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Introduction to Graduate Study for Ph.D. Students
description: Required for first-year graduate students in English. The major historical, professional, and methodological approaches to the study of literature in English.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Pedagogy Seminar I
description: Required for first-year Ph.D students in English. Prerequisite for teaching required for Ph.D. students in English and Modern Thought and Literature. Preparation to enter professional educational practice as a Stanford TA in the department of English, including developing knowledge of how people learn, especially how college students learn, familiarity with the Stanford English Undergraduate curriculum and knowledge of English Literature curricular goals, and the fundamentals of teaching practice, including research-based practices for classroom management of discussion sections, for assessment, for teaching diverse learners, and for the ongoing analysis and improvement of one's own teaching. Emphasizes the development of pedagogical content knowledge in English and the development of a teaching philosophy as such.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Research Course
description: A special subject of investigation under supervision of a member of the department. Thesis work is not registered under this number.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Literary Lab (COMPLIT 398L)
description: Gathering and analyzing data, constructing hypotheses and designing experiments to test them, writing programs [if needed], preparing visuals and texts for articles or conferences. Requires a year-long participation in the activities of the Lab.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Revision and Development of a Paper
description: Students revise and develop a paper under the supervision of a faculty member with a view to possible publication.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Orals, Publication and Dissertation Workshop
description: For third- and fourth-year graduate students in English. Strategies for studying for and passing the oral examination, publishing articles, and for writing and researching dissertations and dissertation proposals. May be repeated for credit.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Thesis
description: For M.A. students only. Regular meetings with thesis advisors required. To enroll, make an appointment with English student services and provide confirmation of advisor consent.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Shakespearean Stage
description: The texts of Shakespeare's plays, as we now read them, are edited and concrete, stabilized in printed form. Yet, in their own moment, Elizabethan and Jacobean playtexts were anything but stable; they were messy, fluid, mutable, and subject to the capricious nature of the playhouse. To uncover the production process of early modern theater, we read a selection of primary source theatrical documents alongside plays that engage in metadrama, including Shakespeare's Hamlet, Twelfth Night, The Taming of the Shrew, and A Midsummer Night's Dream. We will then use this knowledge to adapt and perform Hamlet as a full-class production.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Earliest English Poetry
description: Earliest English Poetry

subject: ENGLISH
title: "Tell About the South": Cultural History of the American South (HISTORY 56S)
description: Americans feel compelled to "tell about the South," framing it as a provincial, backward region separate from the nation. Yet the region has consistently produced some of the most modern, emphatically American culture. This course investigates these tensions from the Old South to the New South, incorporating film nights, photography, music, and literature ranging from slave narratives to works by William Faulkner, Richard Wright, and Zora Neale Hurston. Together, we will ask: What is the South? What can the South explain about the United States? Students will learn the historical craft by asking how Southern history and culture were crafted.

subject: ENGLISH
title: From Page to Stage: Troilus and Cressida
description: The great city of Troy has been under siege for seven years. Both Greek and Trojan camps have lost the plot, if ever narrative coherence for their struggle did exist. The most irreverent of Shakespeare's "problem plays," Troilus and Cressida puts infighting warriors - and young love - to the test. The Trojan prince and fair Cressida circle each other at arm's length; so, too, do "insolent" Achilles and "blockish" Ajax. What forms can fidelity, authority, and desire's fulfillment take when partisan bloodshed is the order of the day? This course links the interpretative and performing arts in two phases. Participants first focus on the play-text and the creative openings afforded by Shakespeare's interlocutors past and present. They then draw these insights into a scaled-down performance to be held at the close of the quarter. Along the way, guest lecturers will lead workshops to enrich our sense of the possibilities of script adaptation, stage direction, and dramatic performance. Students will not be graded on their performance as actors. This remains a literature-forward course; no prior experience in the theater necessary. Students willing to contribute to the final production through non-acting roles (e.g. as publicists, musicians, costume designers, stagehands, extras) are very welcome. Participants should reserve time for FIVE additional rehearsal sessions to be held on Mondays at 7:30 pm.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Poems as Artificial Intelligence
description: In a column written soon after the public release of ChatGPT, Ezra Klein wrote that AI's "thinking," for lack of a better word, is utterly inhuman, but we have trained it to present as deeply human" (The New York Times, March 12, 2023). Implicit in Klein's thesis is the assumption that we do understand human thinking, or at least how to recognize it, and that AI confronts us with something radically different masquerading as the familiar. But perhaps the world has long been populated by different kinds of thinking entities. That appears to be the claim of a number of critics working on poetry today: these scholars argue that poems are their own species of thinking machine, with the ability to represent a speaker's thinking, to facilitate a reader's thinking, to articulate structures of thinking, or even to think for themselves. In this course, we'll examine such claims by close reading poems from a range of writers while also engaging works of criticism that grapple with these questions from formalist, phenomenological, and philosophical perspectives. We'll ask what it might mean to say that poems think and whether they can help us think critically about thinking in general, about the ways AI is represented and understood as thinking, and about the cognitive dynamics of our increasingly AI-inflected economy and culture.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Surveillance and the Realist Novel
description: Over the past few decades, surveillance has become an inescapable presence in our day-to-day lives. From our phones listening to us, to facial recognition through in-store surveillance monitoring, to the geographical data we surrender every time we upload a run to Strava nothing is private. Much like the relationship between rising surveillance and the rapid technological advancement of today, the nineteenth-century saw an increase in surveillance and the apparatuses available to exercise it, shaping surveillance into a central preoccupation of the nineteenth century's most rapidly-evolving literary form: the realist novel. This course examines how discourses of surveillance shape the novel form in the nineteenth century and today- from a period heavily associated with both the rise of the novel and the rise of regulatory infrastructures to our own contemporary context. We will explore surveillance as the subject of novelistic representation in its depictions of capitalism and social class, law, policing, and sexuality, while also considering how novels (and more broadly, form itself) react to and against the surveillance of reading. Our primary text selection will begin by focusing on nineteenth-century novels (Balzac's Pere Goriot and Charles Dickens' Great Expectations), where we'll locate how surveillance operated in the epoch's newly industrialized cities and influenced the modes of narration, character development, and plot structures associated with literary realism. We will then consider how the confluence of new surveillance culture and globalization impact the contemporary realist novel in Mohsin Hamid's The Reluctant Fundamentalist. Secondary readings from key works in critical theory, postcolonial criticism, and queer theory, as well as theories of the novel, will give us a robust conceptual framework to supplement our primary texts.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Tragicomedy
description: What is tragicomedy? From the amphitheatres of ancient Greece and Rome to twenty-first-century television screens, this hybrid dramatic genre has undergone numerous metamorphoses, combining its constituent parts, tragedy and comedy, in new and surprising ways. Is tragicomedy best defined by its mixing of high and low characters and subject matters? Or does it primarily indicate aspects of structure and plot? Could tragicomedy be best understood through its juxtaposition of emotions and affective responses? Or might it even index a basic existential reality: the tragicomic nature of human experience? In this class we will explore these questions through a transhistorical selection of drama, including works by Euripides, Shakespeare, Kleist, Beckett, and Pinter. Alongside these dramatic works, we will engage a wide selection of critical, theoretical, and philosophical texts.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Knights in Shining Armor: Gender and Chivalry from Chaucer to Chappell Roan
description: The image of the knight in shining armor permeates popular culture - from the court of King Arthur and Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, through the Pre-Raphaelites and Romantics, to the Met Gala red carpet. Why is this an aesthetic that lasts? What is it about the chivalric knight that serves as a useful mechanism for artists throughout the ages? In this course, we will examine the knightly figure through theoretical lenses including gender and class to better understand the interplay between identity and aesthetic. 'Texts' will span literature, film, fashion, and more, including works by Chretien de Troyes, Chaucer, Keats, Tennyson, Judith Butler, Chappell Roan, and Zendaya by Law Roach.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Media, Technology, Narrative
description: Media and technology characterize modern life; do they also limit our cultural imagination? In this class, we explore the imaginative and narrative dimensions of technology and media in four modes: communication, science, travel, and environment. The course traces the field of media theory, starting from Marshall McLuhan's groundbreaking Understanding Media and broadening out into the recent turn towards the natural world with "elemental" media studies. Course materials include works by Henry James, Benjamin Labatut, Octavia Butler, and Virginia Woolf, as well as screenings of Oppenheimer (2023), The White Lotus (2025), and No Reservations (2008). Together, we'll consider: what kinds of stories are told about technology, today and historically? How does a medium determine the content of a story? Are some media better suited to narrative than others, and why? This is a writing intensive course with a final critical paper. All writing assignments in the class will scaffold towards this paper, modeling the sustained inquiry required to produce scholarly work. Students are encouraged to write on topics and texts of interest to them in consultation with the instructor.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Jane Austen's Fiction
description: Austen's finely wrought novels were unlike any previous fiction, offering an intensely realized example of literary originality. This class focuses on Austen's major writing, all published in a remarkable ten year period. These novels - including Pride and Prejudice, Emma, Mansfield Park and Persuasion - have had a profound impact on the development and understanding of the novel as an art form.  We'll take the measure of Austen's inventiveness and her subtle, engrossing experiments in narrative voice, fictional character, representation and literary form. Our two goals will be to closely engage each novel (looking at the major interpretative and aesthetic questions that are generated) and to track the rich dialogue that takes place between her different texts when they are read together.

subject: ENGLISH
title: 'A Model Island': Britain in Historical and Cultural Perspective
description: What's `culture'? There is no such thing as `British culture' as a coherent singular phenomenon, but `culture' can be a useful lens to think about a place, its entanglement with the past and the rest of the world. In this class we can understand how the ideas and social relations that constitute the common-sense fiction of British culture and the very notions of `Britishness', `Englishness', etc. came about historically and are sustained in contemporary contexts. As well as learn how to use `culture' as a heuristic-critical tool to make sense of a particular place's entanglement in history, politics, and cultural production.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Mark Twain and American Culture (AMSTUD 68N)
description: Preference to freshmen. Mark Twain defined the rhythms of our prose and the contours of our moral map. He recognized our extravagant promise and stunning failures, our comic foibles and tragic flaws. He is viewed as the most American of American authors--and as one of the most universal. How does his work illuminate his society's (and our society's) responses to such issues as race, gender, technology, heredity vs. environment, religion, education, art, imperialism, animal welfare, and what it means to be "American"?

subject: ENGLISH
title: Shakespeare's Rivalries
description: Before Shakespeare sat at the center of the literary canon, his reputation was rivaled by the likes of Christopher Marlowe, Ben Jonson, Thomas Kyd, and others. This seminar pairs Shakespeare's works with his competitors to investigate the literary scene that produced the most famous writer in English. Topics include the aesthetics of revenge, the performance of racial difference, and the drama of the soul.

subject: ENGLISH
title: After the Apocalypse
description: What happens after the world, as we know it, has ended? Or rather, what do literary representations of religious, economic, and climatological end-times reveal about how humans confront the intractable societal contradictions and challenges they face? In this course, we read a variety of apocalyptic and post-apocalyptic narratives to examine the resources such narratives offer for coping with real and imagined existential terror. In the process, we pose several related questions: Where does the idea of the apocalypse originate? Who is the apocalyptic narrator and for what purposes does he or she tell the tale? Does apocalypse have a temporality? Is it always in the future, or might it already have occurred? Using the tools of close reading and historical criticism, the course builds an archive of knowledge about the narrative, visual, and aural features of the literary apocalypse, and the strategies humans imagine for coping with the aftermath of devastation.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Philosophy and Literature (CLASSICS 42, COMPLIT 181, FRENCH 181, GERMAN 181, ILAC 181, ITALIAN 181, PHIL 81, SLAVIC 181)
description: Can novels make us better people? Can movies challenge our assumptions? Can poems help us become who we are? We'll think about these and other questions with the help of writers like Toni Morrison, Marcel Proust, Bong Joon-ho, Charlie Kaufman, Emily Dickinson, William Shakespeare, and Samuel Beckett, plus thinkers like Montaigne, Nehamas, Nietzsche, Nussbaum, Plato, and Sartre. We'll also ask whether a disenchanted world can be re-enchanted; when, if ever, the truth stops being the most important thing; why we sometimes choose to read sad stories; whether we ever love someone for who they are; who could possibly want to live their same life over and over again; what it takes to make ourselves fully moral; whether it's ever good to be conflicted; how we can pull ourselves together; and how we can take ourselves apart. (This is the required gateway course for the Philosophy and Literature major tracks. Majors should register in their home department.)

subject: ENGLISH
title: Asian American Pop Culture: Representation, Aesthetics, Reception (ASNAMST 85)
description: While conversations around Asian representation in US media have historically centered on exclusion from the mainstream, the 21st century has seen the global rise and popularity of various forms of Asian and Asian American pop culture. Asian media, music, memes, fashion, beauty, games, and celebrities have become household names, no longer consigned to the realm of obsessive otaku or cringeworthy Koreaboos. We will explore how Asian American popular culture has been created, consumed, discussed and debated in an era of what Lori Kido Lopez has called "Asian American media abundance." This course has three units: representation, aesthetics, and reception. In the first unit, we discuss what it means - or would it mean - for Asian Americans to be represented "properly" in media. How do we assess successful representation? What is the relationship between racial representation and race/racism in American society more broadly? In the second unit, we investigate the aesthetic properties that we have come to associate with Asian and Asian American pop culture, such as cuteness. What does it mean for a text to look, sound, or "feel" Asian American? In the third unit, we explore how audiences have understood, assessed, and responded to Asian American representation in media. Historically and in the present, how have Asian Americans developed media institutions, distribution networks, and fan communities?

subject: ENGLISH
title: American Hauntings
description: Exploration of the cultural, psychological, social, and political dynamics of haunting in American literature, ranging from the early national period to the late twentieth century, looking at ghost stories as well as other instances of supernatural, emotional, or mental intervention.  Authors include Charles Brockden Brown, Washington Irving, Edgar Allan Poe, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Charles Chesnutt, Henry James, Edith Wharton, Toni Morrison, Stephen King.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Poetry and Magic
description: Poetry and Magic investigates the interplay between poetic form and magic practice. Reading poems that assume a supernatural presence in the world - and the ability of the poet to interact with that presence - we'll discuss how magic poems work, why magic still holds appeal for readers and writers, and how an understanding of magic can function as a way of thinking about many kinds of poetry.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Autofiction: Transforming the Story of the Self
description: The rise of autofiction is the most significant reconfiguration of the relationship between reader, writer, and text in the past 20 years. Autofiction's negotiations between aesthetics and intimacy strike powerful chords with contemporary readers, transforming "plotless" books by Rachel Cusk, Karl Ove Knausgaard, and Nobel laureate Annie Ernaux into bestselling international literary sensations. In this Creative Critical course, students will engage autofiction and autotheory as both creative writers and scholars. We will seek to grasp the genre's scope, power, questions, and potential.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Science Fiction: Time (Travel) in Narrative
description: In this course, we'll explore how time functions as a core element in narrative, shaping character as well as plot, as we read examples from the genres of time travel, the multiverse, and generation ships. We'll consider how representations of time are interwoven with depictions of space, and we'll discover that science fiction can allow for both social critique and the imagination of alternative worlds, all while telling an engaging story.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Climate Lit: Survival, Activism, and Writing 'The Natural World'
description: This seminar will ask you to consider stories not just entertainment or moral instruction, but as models of survival, joy, and personhood in a complex future. Frameworks of Ecocriticism, political activism, and narrative technique will inform our central texts - Marilynne Robinson's Housekeeping, Octavia Butler's Parable of the Sower, and Richard Powers's Overstory. The questions of our texts will be the questions of our course: in a fraying world, how might we imagine new ways of living, being, and thriving?

subject: ENGLISH
title: Autobiographical Writing
description: The stories we tell about ourselves are as diverse and rich as the people who tell them. Yet, the ways we tell those stories often follow familiar patterns. Why is that? And how can we innovate beyond these conventions to energize both the reader and the storyteller? This creative-critical seminar invites undergraduates to explore narrative identity theory through the study and practice of storytelling. Our focus will be on how lyric and narrative strategies can bring new vitality to personal "life stories." We will engage with three remarkable works that challenge traditional forms and offer fresh possibilities.
