subject: FILMEDIA
title: History of World Cinema I: Silent Cinema and Modern Life (FILMEDIA 300A)
description: Film's first decades were among its most exciting, as filmmakers explored the possibilities of this new medium. Modern life had exploded with technologies of production, communication, & transportation, and writers and filmmakers alike pondered the implications of this new mode of experiencing a new, modern world. From one-shot "actualities" to the development of storytelling techniques, to experiments in visual, rhythmic, and polemical form, and feature films in opulent picture palaces, 1895 to 1930 presented a blizzard of exploration and achievement that set the stage for what followed, but which remains, today, absolutely thrilling in its own right.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: History of World Cinema III: Queer Cinemas Around the World (ARTHIST 164, ARTHIST 364, CSRE 102C, CSRE 302C, FEMGEN 100C, FEMGEN 300C, FILMEDIA 300C, GLOBAL 193, GLOBAL 390, TAPS 100C, TAPS 300C)
description: This course provides an overview of cinema from around the world since 1960, highlighting the cultural, political, and economic forces that have shaped various film movements over the last six decades. Specific topics may vary by term/year/instructor. This term's topic, Queer Cinemas around the World, engages with a range of queer cinematic forms and queer spectatorial practices in different parts of the world, as well as BIPOC media from North America. Through film and video from Kenya, Malaysia, India, The Dominican Republic, China, Brazil, Palestine, Japan, Morocco, the US etc., we will examine varied narratives about trans experience, same-sex desire, LGBTQI2S+ rights, censorship, precarity, and hopefulness. This course will attune us to regional cultural specificities in queer expression and representation, prompting us to move away from hegemonic and homogenizing understandings of queer life and media. Notes: Screenings will be held on Fridays at 1:30PM in Oshman Hall. Screening times will vary slightly from week to week.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Close Cinematic Analysis: Poetic Cinema (ARTHIST 199, ASNAMST 108, FEMGEN 104, FILMEDIA 301, TAPS 101F)
description: "What is poetic cinema?" This course begins with theoretical attempts at a definition by such thinkers as Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky, writer and filmmaker Pier Paolo Pasolini, and film scholars Tom Gunning and P. Adams Sitney - along with some of their examples such as Dziga Vertov's documentary A Sixth Part of the World (1926), Michelangelo Antonioni's Red Desert (1964), and the early films of Maya Deren.  We will continue to consider these definitions of the poetic mode in relation to specific elements of film such as sound, and films historically proclaimed as "poetic," including Surrealist films, films of the American avant-garde, and the "Poetic School" of Soviet cinema.  Other potential sites of poetic cinema we may consider include the Griot poetry system in Nollywood films, song lyrics in Hindi films, and adaptations of long poems such as The Shahnameh. The course has three main goals:  to chart and familiarize ourselves with the history of poetic cinema; to recognize and analyze the qualities and elements that tip a film - or part of a film - into the category of film poetry; and, more broadly, to hone our skills of close attention and analysis.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Theories of the Moving Image: The Technologically Mediated Image (FILMEDIA 302)
description: This course examines influential theories of film and media from the early twentieth century to the present. Prerequisites: FILMEDIA 4.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: How French Women (Re)invented Cinema (FEMGEN 192, FRENCH 192, FRENCH 392)
description: Film as a technology was invented by the Lumiere brothers in Paris in 1895. But it was a French woman, Alice Guy, who transformed cinema into an art form. She directed the first narrative fiction film, La Fee aux Choux (The Fairy of the Cabbages, 1896) - a whimsical debunking of maternal myths and gender stereotypes. She was also the first female film producer, pioneered innovative special effects, and was the first to cast an all-Black production, in 1912. Yet, until recently, she has been erased from history books. This course tells another history of cinema: one written entirely by women, and often in Paris. From Alice Guy to Agnes Varda, Claire Denis, and the bold post-#metoo innovators Celine Sciamma, Julia Ducourneau or Mona Achache, women have revolutionized the seventh art, its techniques, its imaginary, and challenged the male gaze from within. Along with female screenwriters, actresses, directors of cinematography and producers, they have transformed cinema into a poetic and political tool to explore new forms of subjectivity, love, womanhood, and reshape French culture. In the wake of #metoo - which started in the film industry - and amid a series of high-profile sexual violence scandals (Depardieu, Polanski, Benoit Jacquot), France is undergoing profound cultural shifts around gender equality, power, violence, and the representation of women. As both an art form and an industry that capitalizes on images of pleasurable bodies, cinema stands at the heart of these debates. The guests for this course will address this conjuncture from their lived professional experience.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Around the World in Ten Films (FILMEDIA 335, GLOBAL 135)
description: This is an introductory-level course about the cinema as a global language. We will undertake a comparative study of select historical and contemporary aspects of international cinema, and explore a range of themes pertaining to the social, cultural, and political diversity of the world. A cross-regional thematic emphasis and inter-textual methods of narrative and aesthetic analysis, will ground our discussion of films from Italy, Japan, United States, India, China, France, Brazil, Nigeria, Russia, Iran, Mexico, and a number of other countries. Particular emphasis will be placed on the multi-cultural character and the regional specificities of the cinema as a "universal language" and an inclusive "relational network."There are no prerequisites for this class. It is open to all students; non-majors welcome.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: An Architectural Imagination (ARTHIST 140)
description:
What is architecture? What questions and needs does it respond to? What kind of an imagination does it provoke? What is it about our relationship to architecture that has led to so many forms of cultural expression to draw from its theoretical and practical frameworks? Drawing from the work of thinkers and practitioners from across a wide variety of mediums, including film, fashion, performance, and visual art, this course will examine these questions in an effort to unpack how this modality of imagination shapes our knowledge of ourselves, others (human and non-human), and the cosmos. 
This course introduces students to the histories and theories of architecture as one of the earliest forms of interdisciplinary thought. Students without a background in art or architecture are encouraged to enroll.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Moon Shots: Lunar Images in Modern and Contemporary America (AMSTUD 145X)
description: The Moon is simultaneously familiar and alien, near at hand and yet largely beyond our reach. As such, it has been the object of close, careful, scientific observation and a site for fantasy and dreams. This course examines the history of American representations of the Moon from the mid-19th century through the present, with particular attention to the interplay between the real and the fantastic in imaginings of the Moon. It brings into conversation art, photography, literature, film, and the history of science. Topics include the social and historical context of lunar images; media and methods for representing the Moon; hoaxes, skepticism, and critiques of lunar images and exploration; and Moon and its role in American national identity, politics, and culture. Also considered: plans for future lunar travel and settlement.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: The Hollywood Musical (FILMEDIA 367)
description: The course will emphasize the sense of liberation that arises in the film musical--a liberation that is both reality and illusion, and which can be physical, emotional, aesthetic, and social, all at once. Performance, not narrative, is central to the genre. Topics will include the dynamic interplay of song, stage, screen, and body; the relation of narrative and non-narrative elements; the staging of identity (whether individual, racial, gendered, or ethnic); the centrality of Black and Jewish culture to the genre; issues of queer reception and interpretation; as well as the utopian possibilities offered up by many a musical.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: AI Art, Performance, and Aesthetics (ARTSTUDI 192, ARTSTUDI 392, FILMEDIA 392, TAPS 192A, TAPS 392A)
description: Co-taught by a media theorist and a theater historian, this seminar introduces students to key theories and debates around AI, art, and performance. Students will learn about artists who use machine learning and related algorithmic processes to create their work, as well as theorists, historians, and critics seeking to understand this fast-moving technology. Throughout the course, we will situate AI within a broader history of technical and aesthetic developments, including cybernetics, generative art, and aleatoric processes. AI art and performance is a complex and urgent subject that demands consideration of technological, artistic, social, political, and philosophical concerns. Together, we will discuss artists such as Refik Anadol and Stephanie Dinkins and theorists such as N. Katherine Hayles and Hito Steyerl, while also making field trips to Bay Area exhibitions as appropriate.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Iberian Cinema From the 1950s to the 2000s (ILAC 210)
description: The course is an overview of select Spanish, Basque, Portuguese and Catalan films from the 1950s to the 21st century. We will consider the filmmakers' strategies to bypass censorship, the difficulty of recollection after trauma, how cinematic images can invoke the past through the exploration of subjectivity, and the representation of problems such as violence against women, the ravages of politically correct condemnation, or the drama of rural communities under globalization. Films by José Luis Garcia Berlanga, Luis Bunuel, Víctor Erice, Carlos Saura, Pedro Almodovar, Alejandro Amenabar, Miguel Gomes, Julio Medem, Ventura Pons, Bigas Luna, Iciar Bolain, Agusti Villaronga and Carla Simo.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Documentary Perspectives I (FILMEDIA 410)
description: This class traces the development and evolution of observational cinema, setting out to define and explore observational filmmaking as a strategy to prize the experiential and immerse the viewer in the present tense. We start with the early Cinema Verite and Direct Cinema films from France, Canada and the U.S. and expand the possibilities of the observational form into the experimental films of the 1970s and beyond. The films selected for this course represent classics of the genre and of modern documentary film in general, but also allow for films that blur lines between experimental, documentary and fiction forms.  Lectures and readings will focus on providing a clear cinematic context for observational techniques, raising aesthetic, technical and ethical questions for the class to consider. This course is a collective inquiry into documentary filmmaking practice, and as such requires a deep engagement with screenings, readings and our in-class discussions.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: The Films of Richard Linklater (AMSTUD 226, FILMEDIA 426)
description: Richard Linklater has been a powerful force in American independent cinema from his low budget Austin comedy, Slacker to his elegant, Oscar-nominated Blue Moon (2025). He merits study as a filmmaker in that he is at once comparable to an Hollywood studio director like Howard Hawks (the range of genres, the cohort of steady collaborators, the emphasis on the interplay among actors), and to a tradition of recent, more contemplative and phenomenologically-concerned American filmmakers, including Terence Malick and Chloe Zhao, who are explicitly attuned to spatiotemporal experience and the wonders of the  everyday world. His filmography encompasses drama, comedy, non-fiction, science fiction, animation, and a musical (in progress). Films include the "Before" trilogy in collaboration with Ethan Hawke and Julie Delpy, such commercial hits as School of Rock and Hit Man, animated films including a philosophical exploration "The Waking Life" and A Scanner Darkly, the best adaptation of Philip K. Dick; and movies about movies, such as Me and Orson Welles and the recent Nouvelle Vague. Linklater's engagingly narrative films, humanist and empathetic, are equally interesting as investigations of the lived experience of real locations and passing time. Before Sunrise takes place in real time, while Boyhood, a coming-of-age movie, was made across twelve summers, with the cast aging visibly as the story unfolds.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: The Russian and Soviet Avant-Garde (ARTHIST 275, ARTHIST 475A, FILMEDIA 475, REES 275A)
description: This course approaches the Russian and Soviet avant-gardes through three central themes:  things, forms, and thinking. 'Things' speaks to such key concepts as dialectical materialism, nonobjective art, and faktura.  'Forms' encompasses the intricate paths of Russian Formalism as well as Constructivist design. 'Thinking' threads through things and forms as they were understood to shape subjectivities.  We will consider many arts:  literature and poetry, visual arts, fashion, architecture and film, placing the greatest emphasis on film.  Our reading will be wide-ranging in terms of time and discipline.  It will include, among others, avant-garde artists such as Kazimir Malevich and Sergei Eisenstein and their contemporaries Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Eikhenbaum. We will also read more contemporary art historians such as Christina Lodder, Yves-Alain Bois, John Bowlt, T. J. Clark, Christina Kaier, and Aglaya Glebova; film and literary scholars such as Jessica Merrill, Nariman Skakov, and Emma Widdis; and Russian historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick, Terry Martin, and Yuri Slezkine.  Films range from melodrama (Olga Preobrazhenskaya's 1927 The Peasant Women of Ryazan) to Dziga Vertov's documentaries and Eisenstein's Ivan the Terrible (1945 and 1958).  We will also make time to look at archival materials in Special Collections.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Movies and Methods: The Films of Howard Hawks (FILMEDIA 490)
description: In the 1950s, Truffaut proposed that the best cinema expressed the sensibility of the director. He, and critics who followed, even found "auteurs" (authors) in films from the "factory" of the Hollywood studios; including Howard Hawks. Critic Robin Wood and filmmaker Quentin Tarantino each cited Rio Bravo as the best film ever made, and Mulvey exempted him from the "male gaze." He marked westerns, comedies, gangster films, musicals, and scifi, specializing in groups under pressure, people defined by their jobs: the recurring issue is whether they're "good enough" to be part of the group, or the couple, or the world.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Architecture and Space in Twentieth-Century Iranian Cinema (COMPLIT 190)
description: This course examines architecture in its broadest sense - urban and rural, interior and exterior - as represented in twentieth-century Iranian cinema, with a particular focus on the pre-1979 period. Through close readings of films by Ebrahim Golestan, Bahram Beyzaie, Nasser Taghvai, Abbas Kiarostami, Forough Farrokhzad, Shahla Riahi, and others, students trace how confinement, exposure, and the boundary between private and public shift across directors, and what these differences reveal about each filmmaker's stance toward modernity. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze cinematic space as argument, showing how architectural choices encode ideological commitments that dialogue, character, or plot alone cannot carry. Comparing directors' divergent treatments of confinement, threshold, and exposure, students will develop a critical framework for understanding cinema as a medium in which ideology is built, quite literally, into space.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Films & Media Studies Internship
description: Professional experience in a field related to the cinematic arts (film, television, media) for six to ten weeks. Internships may include work for production companies, producers, studios, networks, films, television series, directors, screenwriters, non-profit organizations, academic publications and related workplaces. Students arrange the internship, provide a confirmation letter from the hosting institution, and must receive consent from the faculty coordinator to enroll in units. Students submit weekly self-assessments, and evaluations from the student and the supervisor are submitted at the end of the internship. Summer internships may be credited in fall quarter. Restricted to declared majors and minors. May be repeated for credit.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Honors Thesis Writing
description: May be repeated for credit.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Independent Study: Film and Media Studies
description: Prerequisite: student must have taken a course with the instructor and/or completed relevant introductory course(s). Instructor consent and completion of the Independent Study Form are required prior to enrollment.  All necessary forms and payment are required by the end of Week 2 of each quarter. Please contact the Undergraduate Coordinator in McMurtry 108 for more information. May be repeated for credit.

title: Theories of the Moving Image: The Technologically Mediated Image (FILMEDIA 102)
description: This course examines influential theories of film and media from the early twentieth century to the present. Prerequisites: FILMEDIA 4.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Media and Mediums (FILMEDIA 6)
description: What is a medium? This course starts from the assumption that the answer to this question is not as obvious as it might at first appear. Clearly, we know some media when we see them: radio, film, and television are in many ways paradigmatic media of the twentieth century. But what about the computational, networked media of the twenty-first century? Are these still media in the same sense, or has the nature of media changed with the emergence of digital technologies? And what, for that matter, about pre-technical media? Is painting a medium in the same sense that oil or acrylic are media, or in the sense that we speak of mixed media? Is language a medium? Are numbers? Is the body? As we shall see, the question of what a medium is raises a number of other questions of a theoretical or even philosophical nature. How is our experience of the world affected or shaped by media? Are knowledge and perception possible apart from media, or are they always mediated by the apparatuses, instruments, or assemblages of media? What is the relation between the forms and the contents of media, and how does this relation bear on questions of aesthetics, science, technology, or politics? The lecture-based course addresses these and other questions and seeks in this way to introduce a way of thinking about media that goes beyond taken-for-granted ideas and assumptions, and that has a potentially transformative effect on a wide range of theoretical and practical interests.Film & Media Studies majors and minors must enroll for 5 units.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Comics:  More than Words (DLCL 238, ENGLISH 1C)
description: This research unit looks at Comics from a transnational, cross-cultural, and interdisciplinary perspective. Each quarter we organize a series of lectures, reading sessions, and workshops around a main topic. This year we plan on exploring topics such as Manga, Manhwa, Manhua (Fall 2026) and Comics and Medicine (Winter 2027). In Fall and Winter, we will meet a total of 3 times at noon on the Thursdays of Weeks 3, 6, and 9. In the Spring quarter, we will have our first Stanford Comic-Con, a two-day event that will be held on Wednesday and Thursday of Week 4. To earn the unit during the Fall and Winter quarters, students must attend all events hosted, do the readings in advance of the meeting, and participate actively in the class discussions. To earn the unit during the Spring quarter, students must attend at least 4 of the 6 events at the Stanford Comic-Con. Some topics that we explored in past quarters are: Postcolonialism and Decoloniality, Feminism, Superheroes, Computer Science, Comic Theory, Environmentalism, and Early History of Comics.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Introduction to Film Study (CSRE 5)
description: Introduction to Film Study introduces you to film as art, as entertainment, a field of study, and an everyday cultural practice. This course enables you to analyze films in terms of their formal elements, themes, and narrative structures. You learn to 'read' details of cinematic 'language' such as the arrangement of shots (editing), the composition and framing of a shot (cinematography), the overall look of a film (mise-en-scene), and its sound environment. We not only identify such cinematic details, but also consider how they contribute to the overall meaning of a film. Thinking about film and writing about film are intricately linked and inform each other deeply. Learning to write about film with sophistication requires a grasp of the mechanics of writing, familiarity with film terminology, and an understanding of film theory and history. This course helps you develop skills in critical viewing, reading, and writing. We explore basic concepts that have been important to the study of film, such as genre, authorship, and stardom to comprehend how films make meaning within their social, political, cultural, and historical contexts.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Lights, Cinema, and the Writer's Pencil! Vladimir Nabokov and Cinema (ENGLISH 212A, SLAVIC 212)
description: An experimental and synesthetic author, Vladimir Nabokov (1899-1977) featured many references to films and actors in his novels - from Buster Keaton to Greta Garbo, and from Charlie Chaplin's "The Floorwalker" to Harold Lloyd's "Safety Last!" These references are not only thematic, but also stylistic, turning Nabokov into one of the first writers who tried and adapted cinematographic techniques to literary texts. In this way, Nabokov shapes a style that is able to tell stories through visual associations, to convey the dynamicity of our lives, and to express the human experiences of time and imagination. During the course, we will read Nabokov's writings (including "Lolita," "A Laughter in the Dark," "The Gift," and "Invitation to a Beheading") and contextualize him in his multi-cultural milieu - from pre-revolutionary Russia to the emigration in Europe and to his success in the US. We will see that Nabokov was a writer curious to explore human self-consciousness by responding to the cultural trends swirling around him. As we read his novels, we will watch early twentieth-century movies and discuss how Nabokov turned cinematographic techniques into literary devices. Together, we will reflect on how cinema has changed the way we tell stories and recount and visualize our experiences. Thanks to its interdisciplinary nature and to Nabokov being a multi-lingual author, the course is open to students of Slavic studies, English studies, comparative literatures, and cinema studies, as well as to students who are curious to explore the themes of experimentation and hybridization among the arts.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Films of Stanley Kubrick (FILMEDIA 224)
description: This graduate seminar will explore the cinema of Stanley Kubrick, a widely acclaimed film auteur known for works such as 2001: A Space Odyssey, A Clockwork Orange, and Barry Lyndon. The seminar will focus on close analysis of practically all of Kubrick's films, from a variety of methodological perspectives: authorship, formal/stylistic analysis, book-to-screen adaptation, and more.

Linklater's engagingly narrative films, humanist and empathetic, are equally interesting as investigations of the lived experience of real locations and passing time. Before Sunrise takes place in real time, while Boyhood, a coming-of-age movie, was made across twelve summers, with the cast aging visibly as the story unfolds.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: The Russian and Soviet Avant-Garde (ARTHIST 275, ARTHIST 475A, FILMEDIA 275, REES 275A)
description: This course approaches the Russian and Soviet avant-gardes through three central themes:  things, forms, and thinking. 'Things' speaks to such key concepts as dialectical materialism, nonobjective art, and faktura.  'Forms' encompasses the intricate paths of Russian Formalism as well as Constructivist design. 'Thinking' threads through things and forms as they were understood to shape subjectivities.  We will consider many arts:  literature and poetry, visual arts, fashion, architecture and film, placing the greatest emphasis on film.  Our reading will be wide-ranging in terms of time and discipline.  It will include, among others, avant-garde artists such as Kazimir Malevich and Sergei Eisenstein and their contemporaries Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Eikhenbaum. We will also read more contemporary art historians such as Christina Lodder, Yves-Alain Bois, John Bowlt, T. J. Clark, Christina Kaier, and Aglaya Glebova; film and literary scholars such as Jessica Merrill, Nariman Skakov, and Emma Widdis; and Russian historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick, Terry Martin, and Yuri Slezkine.  Films range from melodrama (Olga Preobrazhenskaya's 1927 The Peasant Women of Ryazan) to Dziga Vertov's documentaries and Eisenstein's Ivan the Terrible (1945 and 1958).  We will also make time to look at archival materials in Special Collections.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Movies and Methods: The Films of Howard Hawks (FILMEDIA 290)
description: In the 1950s, Truffaut proposed that the best cinema expressed the sensibility of the director. He, and critics who followed, even found "auteurs" (authors) in films from the "factory" of the Hollywood studios; including Howard Hawks. Critic Robin Wood and filmmaker Quentin Tarantino each cited Rio Bravo as the best film ever made, and Mulvey exempted him from the "male gaze." He marked westerns, comedies, gangster films, musicals, and scifi, specializing in groups under pressure, people defined by their jobs: the recurring issue is whether they're "good enough" to be part of the group, or the couple, or the world.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: The Video Essay: Writing with Video about Media and Culture
description: In this seminar, we explore what it means to 'write with video,' and we learn to make effective and engaging video essays. Specifically, we examine strategies for communicating through video, and we conduct hands-on exercises using digital video editing software to construct arguments, analyses, and interpretations of film, television, video games, online media, art, and culture. Compared with traditional text-based arguments, the video essay offers a remarkably direct mode of communicating critical and analytical ideas. Video essayists can simply show their viewers what they want them to see. This does not mean, however, that it is any easier than an essay composed with ink and paper. Like the written essay, the new technology introduces its own challenges and choices, including decisions about organization of space and time, audiovisual materials, onscreen text, voiceover commentary, and visual effects. By taking a hands-on approach, we develop our skills with editing software such as Adobe Premiere Pro and Apple's Final Cut Pro while also cultivating our awareness of the formal and narrative techniques employed in cinema and other moving-image media. Through weekly assignments and group critique sessions, we learn to express ourselves more effectively and creatively in audiovisual media. As a culmination of our efforts, we assemble a group exhibition of our best video essays for public display on campus.No previous experience is required, but a willingness to learn new technologies (in particular, video editing software) is important.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Media and Mediums (FILMEDIA 306)
description: What is a medium? This course starts from the assumption that the answer to this question is not as obvious as it might at first appear. Clearly, we know some media when we see them: radio, film, and television are in many ways paradigmatic media of the twentieth century. But what about the computational, networked media of the twenty-first century? Are these still media in the same sense, or has the nature of media changed with the emergence of digital technologies? And what, for that matter, about pre-technical media? Is painting a medium in the same sense that oil or acrylic are media, or in the sense that we speak of mixed media? Is language a medium? Are numbers? Is the body? As we shall see, the question of what a medium is raises a number of other questions of a theoretical or even philosophical nature. How is our experience of the world affected or shaped by media? Are knowledge and perception possible apart from media, or are they always mediated by the apparatuses, instruments, or assemblages of media? What is the relation between the forms and the contents of media, and how does this relation bear on questions of aesthetics, science, technology, or politics? The lecture-based course addresses these and other questions and seeks in this way to introduce a way of thinking about media that goes beyond taken-for-granted ideas and assumptions, and that has a potentially transformative effect on a wide range of theoretical and practical interests.Film & Media Studies majors and minors must enroll for 5 units.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Qualifying Examination Preparation
description: For Art History Ph.D. candidates. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Independent Study
description: For graduate students only. Approved independent research projects with individual faculty members.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Extended Seminar
description: May be repeated for credit. (Staff)

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Curricular Practical Training
description: CPT course required for international students completing degree.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: The New Wave: How The French Reinvented Cinema (FRENCH 87N)
description: When the French New Wave burst onto the stage in 1959, it changed forever the way films are made and the ways we think about cinema. Shooting on location with small crews, light cameras, unknown actors and improvised scripts, a group of young film critics turned filmmakers circumvented the big studios to craft low-budget films that felt fresh, irreverent and utterly modern. In just a few years, the Nouvelle Vague delivered such landmark works as Truffaut's 400 Blows, Godard's Breathless or Resnais' Hiroshima mon amour. Together with Agnes Varda, Eric Rohmer and Claude Chabrol, they redefined the essence of cinema as an art form as complex and multi-layered as literature. Yet, after having been hailed as revolutionary, the Nouvelle Vague was soon dismissed as 'rather vague and not all that new. 'Why did these films look so radically fresh? What is their common aesthetics, when each 'auteur' claimed an utterly personal style for him or herself? And what did their immediate success and early fall from grace tell us about France in the early 60s?  This survey course will explore a unique moment in French culture and the history of cinema, when radical politics, youth culture, and jazzy aesthetics coalesced into dazzling experiments on the screen that continue to influence world cinema to this day. Focus is on cultural history, aesthetic analysis, and interpretation of narrative, sound and visual forms. Satisfies Ways AII (Aesthetic and Interpretative Inquiry). Films in French with Subtitles. Taught in English.

subject: FILMEDIA
title: Introduction to Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity (ARTHIST 98, CSRE 100, EDUC 166C, ENGLISH 172D, PSYCH 155, SOC 146, TAPS 165)
description: This course covers foundational concepts in the creation and application of racial and ethnic categories and identities, the perception of racialized others, and the systematic institutionalization of racialized hierarchies. We take a transdisciplinary approach to interrogating how socially constructed differences are realized and how they may be transformed. Key topics include: ideology, identity, intersectionality, discrimination, hierarchy, solidarity, resistance, reproduction, and transformation.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Science/Fiction: Screenwriting about Science
description: The bounds of human knowledge are pushed and reshaped by scientific research, but transforming those discoveries into cinematic material isn't simple. Without slipping into cartoonish Sci-Fi, how can creative people imagine science, technology, engineering, and math as source material for entertainment? How can climate science stories avoid "preachy" polemics? Or nanotech affect us at human scale? Or medical innovations be realized realistically? In this writing workshop, students will discover the screenwriting medium along with case studies in science-based cinema and visits from Stanford researchers to create original science-based scripts, treatments, and pitch decks.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Writing the Television Pilot (FILMPROD 301T)
description: A writing workshop in which students are introduced to the basic structures and genre of television pilots and to writing within the screenwriting/television writing form. Students will develop, outline, and workshop their own original pilot episode and series bible. Serves as a prerequisite for FP104 Intermediate Screenwriting. Enrollment by decision of instructor. Limited to 16 students. Priority will be given to film studies majors and minors, then seniors, with extra preference for students who have tried unsuccessfully to take the class in the past. You must attend the first meeting; the class list will be finalized after that first session.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Screenwriting II: Intermediate Screenwriting (FILMPROD 304)
description: Priority to Film and Media Studies majors and minors, and seniors. Craft, form, and approaches to writing for the screen. Students will write, workshop and rewrite the first act of a feature screenplay and create rough outline material for the rest of the film. Prerequisites: FP101, FP101T or ENGL190F and consent of the instructor.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Crafting Story for Film and Television (FILMPROD 305C)
description: Was there a time when a movie or TV episode affected you, made you jump, cry, or simply floored you? In those moments you were likely manipulated by dozens of narrative mechanisms -- invisible to an unaware audience -- that are the core tools of screenwriting. Learn the craft of generating cinematic material and organizing it for effect through case study screenings of popular film and television, followed by creative exercises in concept, protagonist, act structure, dramatic tension, and more. Explore the different structural underpinnings of film and television and generate original material of your own in this lecture course.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Introduction to Film and Video Production
description: Hands-on. Techniques of film and video making including conceptualization, visualization, story structure, cinematography, sound recording, and editing. Enrollment limited to 12 students. Priority to junior/senior Film & Media Studies majors. Admission determined on the first day of class.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Filmmaking: Ethno-fictions and Shared Anthropologies
description: Ethnographic documentary film, just like ethnography itself, began as a colonial practice. It has relied on unacknowledged biases and personal experiences of the filmmakers to create portraits of cultures and communities around the world. To study documentary film today requires recognizing and acknowledging this lens of otherization; it requires grappling with questions around representation. In this course we look at works that turn the lens inward and offer a self-examination of one's own culture or the land that the makers belong to. This inversion of gaze is the fulcrum of this course. We work through the convergence of thinking and practice as filmmaking process, with an emphasis on how to work with sound to create portraits. For final projects, students work in groups to make 3-5 minute video portraits of individuals or communities of their choice, exploring in the work itself the place of the personal and the place they are looking from.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Elements of Filmmaking: Sound Design (FILMPROD 410)
description: This course offers students an understanding of contemporary practices in editing and sound design as they relate to documentary film production. Through critical analysis of how films are constructed in the edit room and how sound and image work in relation to one another, as well as a series of practical assignments in (re-)editing footage and designing sound for film, the students will gain a foundation of craft they can apply to their filmmaking.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Elements of Filmmaking: Cinematography (FILMPROD 411)
description: This course offers students an understanding of contemporary practices in cinematography as they relate to documentary film production. Through close analysis of a variety of examples and a series of practical assignments with cameras, lighting and working with color, the students will gain a foundation of craft they can apply to their filmmaking.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Crafting Story for Film and Television (FILMPROD 105C)
description: Was there a time when a movie or TV episode affected you, made you jump, cry, or simply floored you? In those moments you were likely manipulated by dozens of narrative mechanisms -- invisible to an unaware audience -- that are the core tools of screenwriting. Learn the craft of generating cinematic material and organizing it for effect through case study screenings of popular film and television, followed by creative exercises in concept, protagonist, act structure, dramatic tension, and more. Explore the different structural underpinnings of film and television and generate original material of your own in this lecture course.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Non-Fiction Narratives
description: Restricted to M.F.A. Documentary Film students. This course will introduce students to the conceptual framework of filmmaking and the skills required in researching and planning documentary films. You will develop key directing and producing expertise through the preproduction and production of your projects, which will complement class discussions and individual meetings. Special emphasis will be given to the relationship between the sound and the image.

subject: FILMPROD
title: The 16mm Film
description: Restricted to M.F.A. Documentary Film students. This course will introduce each student to the fundamentals of 16mm documentary filmmaking. You will acquire hands-on experience in cinematography, sound recording, lighting, and editing. During the quarter, you will direct, shoot, and edit a "process exercise" and a final project. You will also perform various crew roles for other students as assigned. Critiques of creative work will emphasize the conceptual, aesthetic, and technical aspects of film production. Each student will show their final Fall Film at the end-of-quarter public screening.

subject: FILMPROD
title: The Spring Film I
description: Restricted to M.F.A. Documentary Film students. Through this course, students will research, develop, and embark on the production of their final first-year M.F.A. documentary film. We will focus on the relationship between form and content, as students learn to articulate their ideas in preparation for production.  Development and production of the films will be spread throughout the quarter, with students bringing materials to class to inform the discussion of their films.

subject: FILMPROD
title: The Spring Film II
description: Restricted to M.F.A. Documentary Film students. This course will guide the students through the post-production of their final.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Documentary M.F.A. Thesis Seminar: Intention
description: Restricted to M.F.A. documentary students. During this course we develop and define the intention of the M.F.A. Thesis Film. Through rigorous research and critical thinking we aim to determine the language of the film and the filmmaking approach. Aside from developing our own artistic practice we will continue to deepen our inquiry about the documentary genre.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Documentary M.F.A. Thesis Seminar: Encounters
description: Restricted to M.F.A. documentary students. This course will guide each student through the production and early post-production of the M.F.A. thesis project. Emphasis will be placed on shooting strategies, aesthetic choices, ethical challenges and practical production issues.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Documentary M.F.A. Thesis Seminar: Forms
description: Restricted to M.F.A. documentary students. This course will guide each student through the post-production of the M.F.A. thesis project. Emphasis will be placed on structure, narration, visual and sound design of the film, as well as a range of legal issues. Additionally, the students will reconsider their artistic and professional practices ahead of completing their M.F.A. degrees. The course will result in the public screening of the thesis films and a Q&A with the filmmakers.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Elements of Filmmaking: Sound Design (FILMPROD 210)
description: This course offers students an understanding of contemporary practices in editing and sound design as they relate to documentary film production. Through critical analysis of how films are constructed in the edit room and how sound and image work in relation to one another, as well as a series of practical assignments in (re-)editing footage and designing sound for film, the students will gain a foundation of craft they can apply to their filmmaking.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Elements of Filmmaking: Cinematography (FILMPROD 211)
description: This course offers students an understanding of contemporary practices in cinematography as they relate to documentary film production. Through close analysis of a variety of examples and a series of practical assignments with cameras, lighting and working with color, the students will gain a foundation of craft they can apply to their filmmaking.

subject: FILMPROD
title: Filmmaking Practices
description: Restricted to M.F.A. Documentary Film students. This course provides an opportunity to each student to explore and craft their own filmmaking practice, both as a series of creative acts and as a set of professional values and heuristics. Through a variety of examples and assignments, students will explore the tension between an artistic practice and its presentation through product, and learn ways of navigating that tension in their own work.

subject: FINANCE
title: Finance
description: This course covers the foundations of finance. While we emphasize applications that are vital for corporate managers, we cover topics that are of great importance to all investors making investment decisions. Essential in these decisions is the process of valuation, which will be a central theme throughout the course. Topics include criteria for making investment decisions, valuation of financial assets and liabilities, portfolio risk and return, and financing and capital structure choices. This course is designed to provide students who have had little prior exposure to finance with the tools necessary to estimate the value of a business enterprise or a financial investment decision.

subject: FINANCE
title: Accelerated Managerial Finance
description: This course covers the foundations of finance with an emphasis on applications that are vital for corporate managers. We will discuss many of the major financial decisions made by corporate managers, both within the firm and in their interactions with investors. Essential in most of these decisions is the process of valuation, which will be an important emphasis of the course. Topics include criteria for making investment decisions, valuation of financial assets and liabilities, relationships between risk and return, capital structure choice, payout policy, the use and valuation of derivative securities, and risk management. This course is targeted to those students who are new to finance and for those with little quantitative background. No previous background in finance is required or expected for this course. Content will be comparable to F201, but the majority of course lecture material will be delivered online, with in-class sessions devoted to applications of key concepts. This 'flipped classroom' version of the course is intended for self-motivated students with an interest in applications. Prerequisite material for the course will be posted online in the fall.

subject: FINANCE
title: Corporations, Finance, and Governance in the Global Economy
description: As executives, entrepreneurs, global leaders, and change agents tasked with developing transformative solutions of tomorrow, you will need certain skills and tools to interact with and navigate the complex and ever-changing financial landscape. This course focuses on the development of these skills and tools through the analysis of concise real-world financial situations around the globe. Topics include valuation of cash flows and control; the capital structure, payout policy and governance of both mature and entrepreneurial firms; restructuring and managing financial distress; the use of public markets to obtain liquidity and multiple share classes to retain control; financing and governance in venture capital and private equity; the rise of activism; and social responsibility and debates about the objectives of the firms of the present and future.

subject: FINANCE
title: Corporate Finance: Applications, Techniques, and Models
description: This course will develop and apply the basic tools and models of corporate finance to real-world corporate decisions. This course is designed to be the second course in the standard finance sequence; that is, it is designed to be the natural follow-up to the Fall Finance course. This course will develop and extend standard tools and techniques of financial analysis, valuation, and model-building, and apply these methods to a wide range of cases. Case topics will include mergers and acquisitions, private equity, corporate governance, capital structure, agency conflicts, and corporate restructuring. For all of these applications, this course will emphasize the central importance of financial analysis, valuation, and modeling to guiding optimal decision making.

subject: FINANCE
title: MSx: Finance
description: This course covers the foundations of finance with an emphasis on applications that are vital for corporate managers. We will consider many important financial decisions made by corporate managers, both within the firm and in their interactions with investors. Essential to most of these decisions are financial valuations, which will be an important emphasis of the course. Topics include criteria for making investment decisions, valuation of financial assets and liabilities, relationships between risk and return, and capital structure choice.

subject: FINANCE
title: Capital Markets and Institutional Investing
description: This course takes a look at institutional investing from the asset owner or limited partner's perspective (sovereign wealth funds, endowments, pension funds, life insurance companies, etc.) The course is co-taught by Ana Marshall, the CIO of the Hewlett Foundation, and Hanno Lustig, who was on the Allocation Advisory Board of the NBIM. We cover the tools of modern asset allocation and manager selection with a special focus on the challenges posed by alternative asset classes (hedge funds and private equity). To provide additional context, Ana Marshall will lecture on best practices in asset allocation and manager selection.. The course material is founded on insights from modern finance and the economics of delegated asset management, complemented by industry perspectives. The target audience for this course includes all students who are interested in careers or already have careers in asset management. The course objective is to help you develop an understanding of the main challenges in the asset allocation and manager selection process, and hand you the tools to navigate these challenges.

subject: FINANCE
title: International Finance and Macroeconomics
description: An introduction to the global economy. We will cover a number of important topics for firms, investors, and policymakers: global capital flows, international financial markets, the role of the US and US dollar in the international monetary system, the history and future of global reserve currencies (stablecoins?), exchange rates (floating, fixed, and monetary unions), financial crises, international financial policy (capital controls, bank regulation, FX intervention), currency wars, tax havens and global wealth dynamics, global trade, and trade wars. Emphasis will be on data-driven approaches. No prior knowledge is assumed. An MBA class designed for those looking to understand today's global economic issues.

subject: FINANCE
title: Investment Management and Entrepreneurial Finance
description: The Investments course comprises an intensive overview of the craft of fundamental investing in both the public and private equity markets. The pedagogy of F321 is three-fold: - Each of our 20 class sessions is taught by a great GSB alumni investor. These sessions are a mix of cases forcing you to come to judgments on potential investments, and talks around an investor's Investment Philosophy and underwriting approach. All of our speakers are fundamental investors (those who look to business fundamentals to determine future value) we do not bring in speculative traders, macro hedge funds, crypto pioneers, etc. - In addition to the class sessions, there is a significant amount of out-of-class reading. Two of the most influential investing books ever written -  The Intelligent Investor by Benjamin Graham and Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits and Other Writings by Philip Fisher - are required reading. These texts are augmented with a series of 10 Teaching Notes that we have developed to translate the principles and wisdom of Graham and Fisher, along with those of Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Seth Klarman and other investment greats, into a concrete investment methodology that you can apply in practice. These Teaching Notes begin with a discussion of broad-based fundamental investing topics - risk-taking, modelling, valuation and capital structure fundamentals - and then outline the approach of a persona we have developed to reflect the views of Graham, Fisher, et al -  the Conservative Fundamental Investor. - The class culminates in two final projects designed to put the learnings from the class into practice: (1) an Investment Memo on a public company, outlining a company overview, an investment thesis, a valuation assessment and ultimately your judgment of whether or not to make an investment in the stock of the company, and (2) a paper detailing your personal Investment Philosophy that you will develop based on perspectives you will be exposed to in the class. This paper is your opportunity to explore your own views on how you plan to invest going forward. This class is relevant for students who intend to pursue careers in private or public equity investing, as well as those who want to better understand investing from the perspective of an entrepreneur, senior executive or individual. It is not, however, an entry-level finance class. It is expected that all students come into F321 with basic corporate finance, statistics, modelling and strategy tool kits. In establishing the elements of the investing craft that we will cover in this course, we will go back to First Principles and reground new concepts in these core underlying skills. But our aim for the quarter is to layer on to this foundation the intellectual, interpersonal and, as importantly, the intrapersonal (self-awareness, humility, mental discipline, patience and equanimity are critical elements of the craft!) framework for how to apply these skills to become a great investor. This is a lot to cover in one quarter and means we will not have the bandwidth to address the foundational skills sets, on top of which this course is built, in any meaningful capacity. Established and taught for 50 years by the legendary Professor Jack McDonald, the Investments course will be taught again in 2026 by Erik Ragatz `01, former Partner of Hellman & Friedman and member of their investment team for over 20 years, and Professor Steve Grenadier.

subject: FINANCE
title: Financial Restructuring
description: Most GSB students will encounter distressed situations at various points during their careers, in their capacity as executives, business owners, investors, advisors, lenders, customers, suppliers, or competitors. Knowing how to navigate these situations is a critical skill in business. Financial restructuring is the process by which distressed companies, and their key stakeholders, use in-court and out-of-court tools and methods to renegotiate their key contracts for the purpose of rehabilitation. In contrast with operational restructuring, financial restructuring focuses on resolving problems on the 'right-hand side' of a company's balance sheet - its debt and non-debt liabilities. This course provides an intensive overview of financial restructuring techniques and processes from the perspectives of distressed firms and their key stakeholders. It is intended for those who plan careers in general management, private equity, entrepreneurship, credit and special situations investing, commercial and investment banking, turnaround management, or financial advisory services. While it is primarily a finance course, it incorporates interdisciplinary elements including negotiations, game theory, strategy, and business law. It is an advanced course, and enrolling students should be reasonably comfortable with financial analysis, valuation techniques, and basic financial modeling.

subject: FINANCE
title: Economics of the Private Equity Industry
description: This course covers the in depth the private equity (PE) industry, including venture funds, buyouts, funds of funds, and other investments vehicles investing in private assets. Our viewpoint is that of an investor, whether a general partner of a management firm partnership or the limited partner investing in these funds. We concentrate on the financial and economic aspects and will take a practical yet rigorous view. Examples of issues that we will cover: How to select fund managers? How are PE funds raised? Can we predict returns of PE asset class? Is there a persistence in returns? What are the most important provisions of a limited partnership agreement? How to negotiate fund terms? What is the lifetime income of general partners? What are optimal investment strategies for PE asset allocation? How to value PE assets and funds? The course is very applied, with a lot of real-life and live cases. The course features guest speakers: VC, buyout fund, fund of funds managers, limited partners. No prior knowledge of the PE industry is needed.

subject: FINANCE
title: Energy Finance
description: This course covers the principles and practice of energy finance. The energy industry has undergone a transformation in recent decades, as new technologies promise cleaner and more efficient energy for residential, commercial, industrial, and transportation purposes. The transition to a new energy economy is drawing large amounts of new financing from both older traditional sources such as banks and public markets, as well as newer entrants including private equity and institutional investors such as sovereign wealth funds and pension funds. The course covers financing and valuation considerations in both traditional and emerging energy sectors, including conventional power, renewables, storage, LNG, nuclear, and digital energy platforms. Students will develop knowledge and skills in energy finance through case studies and interactions with practitioners. Format: 20% lecture, 80% case study. Cases will be short mini-cases designed for use in this course, with guest speakers as appropriate.

subject: FINANCE
title: Advanced Corporate Valuation
description: This intensive course provides an advanced understanding of modern corporate finance, emphasizing the connection between financial theory and real-world practice. Students will master analytical frameworks for sophisticated financial analysis and explore how corporations make critical decisions affecting firm value. Upon completion, students will have the theoretical foundations necessary for advanced finance electives. Students should have a background in finance fundamentals and an interest in understanding the theoretical underpinnings of advanced financial concepts and their practical application. The course begins with a comprehensive review of essential concepts, followed by two interconnected modules. The first module examines the determination of optimal capital structure, starting with the Modigliani-Miller Theorem, which establishes the conditions under which project choice and financing can be separated. We then explore why these conditions rarely hold in practice: financing decisions convey information to capital markets, shape managerial incentives, and have tax implications. The module concludes with two valuation methodologies linking financing and valuation: WACC and APV approaches. The second module introduces optionality and its applications to financial and real assets. Students learn to identify and value embedded options in corporate decisions. The course concludes by demonstrating that corporate hedging policies are integral components of capital structure strategy, not independent considerations. The course employs lectures supplemented by case studies that illustrate theoretical concepts in complex, real-world contexts, ensuring students develop both conceptual understanding and practical analytical skills.

subject: FINANCE
title: Corporate Financial Modeling
description: This course teaches the fundamentals, best practices, and advanced techniques of corporate financial modeling. We begin with operating models and integrated financial statements, then build transaction-focused analyses for major corporate events, including venture capital funding, mergers and acquisitions, and leveraged buyouts. Throughout, we connect modeling choices to ideas from the MBA core - especially accounting and finance - and take a hands-on approach to see how theory is applied in real decisions. The course emphasizes critical modeling skills, disciplined best practices, and the ability to identify common pitfalls. Students will complete a series of cases and develop tools for forecasting earnings and pro-forma financial statements, valuation, assessing financing needs, merger analysis, and LBO evaluation. Students will also practice presenting their work and critically evaluating others' models. By the end of the course, students will be able to construct, present, and critique complex models that inform corporate financial decision-making.

subject: FINANCE
title: Advanced Corporate Financial Modeling
description: Students will engage in the development of corporate financial modeling cases and solutions. Students will also develop materials to aid others in building financial models, and serve as case leaders during lab workshops. Extensive background in financial modeling and experience with Excel is required.

subject: FINANCE
title: Financial Trading Strategies
description: The purpose of this course is to familiarize students with the different types of trading strategies employed by hedge funds. Throughout the sessions, students will be challenged to understand and explore the application and implementation of these different strategies. Trading simulations employed on the Rotman Interactive Trader will be used extensively in this course as a way to learn and test different strategies. All classes will be held in the Real-time Analytics and Investment Lab (RAIL), located on the third floor of the Bass Building (B312). Students are expected to attend all sessions. Grades are based on in-class simulation results, class participation, and two written assignments.

subject: FINANCE
title: The Chinese Economy and Financial Markets
description: Since the early 1990s, China's financial markets have been growing at an astonishing speed, along with its unprecedented economic growth in the past three decades. Beijing has been pushing forward China's liberalization process and integration with the rest of the world, especially on the frontier of financial markets, though since 2018 it seems that China has reached the crossroad, facing significant geopolitical risks and domestic economic growth pressure. This course aims to provide an in-depth coverage of China's financial markets and their reform processes post 1990's, including but not restricted to -SOE reform and growth model in early years; -Banking system; -Financial markets include stock market and bond market; -Housing and real estate market; -International trade status and exchange rate policy; -China's new growth engine, if any; -U.S.-China relations and recent policy shift. The course coverage will be through lectures, reading of research, including primary source documents and secondary (journalistic and analyst) commentary. There will be a range of subject-matter-expert speakers, and active class participation is expected. Evaluations will be based on case presentations and term papers on the most recent events. Only graduate students and undergraduate senior students are allowed.

subject: FINANCE
title: Private Equity Investing Fundamentals
description: Excellent investing is a craft that combines both science and art. This course offers a practitioner's introduction to the fundamentals of private equity investing, focusing on long-term, private, illiquid, and leveraged investments. It is designed for students with little or no prior experience in private equity or investing. The first half of the course builds the investor's toolkit: industry analysis, company evaluation, valuation methodologies, capital structure construction, and disciplined investment decision-making. It then puts students in the seat. Through a single in-depth case study, students follow one real company from its 2015 buyout through the COVID-19 pandemic to its IPO and eventual exit. Midway through the course, student deal teams present a buyout proposal to an investment committee that includes the company's actual lead private equity investors, then study the decision those investors made and how it played out. The second half applies the same frameworks well beyond a single buyout, covering the history and future of private equity, the macroeconomic and market backdrop, public market investing and spotting winners and losers, sports franchises as an emerging asset class, and investing in the era of AI. World-class investors and industry experts join nearly every session, including founders and CEOs, senior partners of the largest private equity firms, economists, and public market investors. On the last day of class, students receive a real Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM) and write an individual investment memo in class, using all the tools developed during the quarter. By the end of the course, students will have practical frameworks to evaluate and execute private investments with confidence, and will begin to think like an investor. Advanced finance is not required, but students should be comfortable with basic accounting, financial statements, and net present value (NPV) concepts.

subject: FINANCE
title: Angel and Venture Capital Financing for Entrepreneurs and Investors
description: This course covers all the stages of funding for early stage high-growth companies, from seed funding to venture capital rounds to a successful exit. We will concentrate on how entrepreneurs and investors make and should make important decisions. Examples of issues that we will cover are: How can entrepreneurs raise funding successfully? What are typical mistakes entrepreneurs make in raising capital and negotiating with investors? How to choose your investor? How to pitch to an investor? How do angels and VCs generate and process their deal flow and select companies? How are VCs involved in business decisions such as recruiting talent and replacing CEOs? What are the important provisions of financial contracts between VCs and founders? How to value early-stage companies? The course is very applied and mostly case-based. We will discuss a lot of nitty-gritty details that is a must for founders and investors. Case protagonists, founders, angels, and VCs will be among guest speakers. No prior knowledge of the VC industry is needed.

subject: FINANCE
title: Exploring Fintech Innovations
description: This MBA elective explores how financial technology is reshaping the landscape of traditional financial services and driving innovation across banking, payments, lending, insurance, and wealth management. The course examines a broad range of topics, including the evolution of payment systems, blockchain and digital assets, open banking and data portability, AI-driven asset and wealth management, and the rapidly growing field of regulatory technology. A central theme of the course is understanding why traditional financial institutions have been slow to address key frictions - such as high transaction costs, limited access, and information asymmetries - and how Fintech entrants have stepped in to fill these gaps. The course also explores the regulatory considerations and policy trade-offs that shape the adoption and governance of new financial technologies across different jurisdictions. Class sessions integrate assigned readings, case studies, and students' own professional experiences to deepen understanding of Fintech innovations in both developed and emerging markets. Guest speakers from leading Fintech companies and established financial institutions will offer firsthand industry perspectives on the opportunities and challenges of technological disruption in finance.

subject: FINANCE
title: Private Wealth Management and Personal Investing
description: The Private Wealth Management and Personal Investing course will address issues that relate to the management of personal assets as opposed to institutional investing. Many investment courses at the GSB emphasize large institutional portfolios but this course is about portfolio decisions for individuals. It will cover the origins and growth of private wealth management as an industry, investment planning, risk management, inter-generational transfers of wealth, choice of wealth advisors and philanthropy. Special emphasis is on understanding how wealth managers may be evaluated, including potential conflicts of interest, and performance measurement. Classes will focus on case studies and various readings. Each class will include visits from professionals in the wealth management and personal investing business. Active class participation and a group project are required.

subject: FINANCE
title: Private Equity - An Overview of the Industry
description: The primary goal of this 2-unit course is to introduce students to the private equity industry and to the buyout business, the largest segment of the PE market and where the industry got its start. The course will examine some of the industry's history and development, and why and how investors allocate capital to private equity. We will consider how PE firms make investments, from identifying a good deal, to valuing it, and winning it in a competitive process. We will discuss the sources of buyout returns, how PE firms add value to their portfolio companies, and some of the common mistakes firms make. Finally, we'll talk about how private equity has grown through innovation and what the future might hold for the industry. We will meet for nine sessions, each for a duration of 90 minutes. Most classes will also include a distinguished visitor who works in the industry and will offer insights into their private equity firm and their career. Written work will focus on a group presentation at the end of the course. The presentation assignment is to pick a hypothetical buyout investment of the group's choosing and describe the investment from beginning to end in a 12-page PowerPoint.

subject: FINANCE
title: Financial Markets I
description: This course is an introductory PhD level course in financial economics. We begin with individual choice under uncertainty, then move on to equilibrium models, the stochastic discount factor methodology, and no-arbitrage pricing. We will also address some empirical puzzles relating to asset markets, and explore the models that have been developed to try to explain them.

subject: FINANCE
title: Dynamic Asset Pricing Theory
description: This course is an introduction to multiperiod models in finance, mainly pertaining to optimal portfolio choice and asset pricing. The course begins with discrete-time models for portfolio choice and security prices, and then moves to a continuous-time setting. The topics then covered include advanced derivative pricing models, models of the term structure of interest rates, the valuation of corporate securities, portfolio choice in continuous-time settings, and finally market design. Students should have had some previous doctoral-level exposure to general equilibrium theory and some basic courses in investments. Strong backgrounds in calculus, linear algebra, and probability theory are recommended. Problem assignments are frequent and, for most students, demanding. Prerequisite: F620 and MGTECON600 (or equivalent), or permission of instructor.

subject: FINANCE
title: Corporate Finance Theory
description: This course considers a wide range of topics in theoretical corporate finance (broadly interpreted). Topics include capital structure decisions, agency conflicts in the firm, dividend policy, security design, optimal financial contracting, the theory of the firm, the market for corporate control, and banking and financial intermediation, among others. The primary focus is on how asymmetric information, agency conflicts, strategic interactions, and incomplete contracting affect corporate financial decision-making. The course aims both to familiarize students with influential papers and current research, and to promote new research ideas in the area.

subject: FINANCE
title: Advanced Corporate Finance
description: This is a PhD-level course on advanced topics in corporate finance, mainly covering theoretical issues with empirical implications. With technical tools in continuous-time models, we will examine issues in dynamic optimal contracting and capital structure, capital market frictions and implications on corporate finance, financing and investment with macroeconomic implications, and recent development in banking and financial crisis. A requirement for this course is that students complete one project (either theoretical or empirical).

subject: FINANCE
title: Empirical Corporate Finance
description: This course provides an introduction to empirical research in corporate finance, with an emphasis on the application of cross-sectional and panel data econometric techniques for causal inference. The course assumes knowledge of econometrics at the level of MGTECON 603.

subject: FINANCE
title: International Finance and Macroeconomics
description: This is an advanced graduate-level course in international finance and macroeconomics. The course focuses on empirical methods, stylized facts, new advances in large-scale empirical work, and applied theory. This course is targeted to advanced second year PhD students. The course assumes familiarity with the basics of graduate-level macroeconomics and finance. Students without the necessary familiarity with these techniques are welcome to take the course, but should expect to have to fill the gaps on their own (and with the help of their classmates!). Given the target audience above, the course has three main objectives. 1. To introduce and investigate both classic and new economic issues at the frontier of current research in international finance and macroeconomics. The purely pedagogical part of the course aims to make students familiar with the questions, the current state of research, and the empirical tools currently being used. 2. To create a mental framework and intuitive understanding of important and active questions. What makes a question interesting? What makes a paper a good paper? How to develop a reasoned view of new (and perhaps yet un-studied) issues in international finance and macroeconomics? This objective is less direct and less formal, but aims to transition the students into full-time researchers. 3. To kick-start students on independent research. For those interested in applied work the course makes you familiar and tries to connect you with existing data at the frontier of the field, both public and proprietary. For those interested in theoretical work the course staff acts as a sounding board for early research ideas.

subject: FINANCE
title: Advanced Empirical Corporate, Banking and Household Finance
description: This course discusses empirical aspects of major topics in corporate finance, banking, financial regulation, and household finance. The course is designed for students doing their PhD in finance, economics and accounting. The class is very interactive.

subject: FINANCE
title: Finance Faculty Research Workshop
description: In this course, the finance faculty will present their recent research in financial economics. The course will focus not only on the research itself but also on the process. How did this research project get started? How did this research project evolve? The course is designed to help Ph.D. students understand the research process.

subject: FINANCE
title: Macroeconomics and Financial Markets
description: This PhD course will cover research topics at the boundary between macroeconomics and finance. Topics will include the study of macroeconomic models with financial frictions, the term structure of interest rates, conventional and unconventional monetary policy, sovereign debt crises, search frictions and segmentation in housing markets, (over)leveraging by households, heterogeneous expectations, excess volatility, financial bubbles and crises. Student presentations and course paper requirement. Designed for second year PhD students in economics or finance.

subject: FINANCE
title: PhD Directed Reading (ACCT 691, GSBGEN 691, HRMGT 691, MGTECON 691, MKTG 691, OB 691, OIT 691, POLECON 691, STRAMGT 691)
description: This course is offered for students requiring specialized training in an area not covered by existing courses. To register, a student must obtain permission from the faculty member who is willing to supervise the reading.

subject: FINANCE
title: PhD Dissertation Research (ACCT 692, GSBGEN 692, HRMGT 692, MGTECON 692, MKTG 692, OB 692, OIT 692, POLECON 692, STRAMGT 692)
description: This course is elected as soon as a student is ready to begin research for the dissertation, usually shortly after admission to candidacy. To register, a student must obtain permission from the faculty member who is willing to supervise the research.

subject: FINANCE
title: Doctoral Practicum in Teaching
description: Doctoral Practicum in Teaching

subject: FINANCE
title: Doctoral Practicum in Research
description: Doctoral Practicum in Research

subject: FINANCE
title: TGR Dissertation (ACCT 802, GSBGEN 802, HRMGT 802, MGTECON 802, MKTG 802, OB 802, OIT 802, POLECON 802, STRAMGT 802)

subject: FRENCH
title: Lyric Returns: Craft and Creative Translation (ITALIAN 113)
description: This course features the study of premodern texts (poetry, romance, novellas) and students' creative translations as an informed critical engagement with those texts. As a WIM course each week will feature two sessions: a critical engagement with the primary text, and a study of a modern translation; and the writing of a creative translation. The critical sessions will be devoted to students learning about the historical and cultural context of premodern texts, along with their conventions of poetic form, genre and rhetoric. Texts will be in English but students can consult them in the original language (and in some cases versions in manuscripts or as song). In this course we will study how premodern writers foreground their craft of writing and how they devise poetic and narrative strategies for their treatment of desire, memory, or an unattainable beloved object. We will also discuss how modern translators devise methods for returning to the past in new ways and how and why they find contemporary relevance in the premodern.

subject: FRENCH
title: Literature and the Brain (COMPLIT 138, COMPLIT 238, ENGLISH 118, ENGLISH 218, FRENCH 218, PSYC 126, PSYCH 118F)
description: How does fiction make us better at reading minds? Why do some TV shows get us to believe two contradictory things at once? And can cognitive biases be a writer's best friend? We'll think about these and other questions in the light of contemporary neuroscience and experimental psychology, with the help of Song of Solomon (Toni Morrison), Madame Bovary (Gustave Flaubert), season 1 of Westworld (Lisa Joy / Jonathan Nolan), and short readings from writers like Louise Glück, Jorge Luis Borges, Virginia Woolf, and Marcel Proust. We'll also ask what we see when we read; whether the language we speak affects the way we think; and why different people react differently to the same book. Plus: is free will a fiction, or were you just forced to say that?

subject: FRENCH
title: Introduction to the Medical Humanities (ANTHRO 120H, DLCL 120, ITALIAN 120)
description: Medical Humanities is a humanistic and interdisciplinary approach to the topic of medicine. It explores the experience of health and illness as captured through the expressive arts (painting, music and literature), across historical periods and in different cultures, and as interpreted by humanistic scholars in the humanities and social sciences as well as in medicine and policy. Its goal is to give students and scholars an opportunity to explore a more holistic and meaning- centered perspective on medical issues. It draws attention not only to diagnosis, but to the meaning and experience of illness and healing, to the way that medicine is an art form as well as a science, and to the way institutions and culture shape illness.

subject: FRENCH
title: Literature, Revolutions, and Changes in 19th- and 20th-Century France (FRENCH 332B)
description: This course explores central texts of 19th- and 20th-Century French literature, following the evolution of important literary movements during those centuries of cultural and social transformation.
