subject: GERMAN
title: Technology and the Meaning of Life (HISTORY 105G)
description: What does it mean to be human if thinking and reasoning can be done by a machine? The advent and proliferation of generative AI tools raises a host of profound and unsettling questions. While some herald the AI revolution and its promise to liberate us from mental drudgery, others prophecy doom and oppression. While the technology might be new, the anxiety and ambivalence are not. From Socrates, who worried that the technology of writing would "implant forgetfulness in the learners' soul," to Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer who quipped, "machinery mutilates people today, even if it also feeds them," writers and thinkers across place and time have looked on with horror and awe, hope and despair, as technology has transformed the way we live, work, and gain knowledge of our world. In this intellectual history seminar, we will read classic texts that have engaged with questions related to technological innovation and taken stock of both its promise and peril. Readings include work by Plato, Martin Heidegger, Karl Marx, Max Weber, Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer, Walter Benjamin, Hannah Arendt, Rachel Carson, Herbert Marcuse, Michel Foucault, Alan Turing, and Donna Haraway. Alongside these texts we will consider some of the historical developments and themes that motivated these authors: industrialization, the mechanization of warfare, nuclear destruction, the space age, the rise of consumer culture, environmental degradation, the spread of surveillance technologies, and reproductive freedom. Through reading, discussing, and working out complex ideas together, this class will give us a deeper vocabulary and conceptual framework for thinking through the current moment.

subject: GERMAN
title: Writing About Germany: New Topics, New Genres
description: Writing about various topics in German Studies. Topics based on student interests: current politics, economics, European affairs, start-ups in Germany. Intensive focus on writing. Students may write on their experience at Stanford in Berlin or their internship. Fulfills the WIM requirement for German Studies majors. Taught in English and German. We meet as a group once a week; meeting times are arranged with the professor.

subject: GERMAN
title: Fairy Tales
description: This course examines fairy tales as narratives of identity formation. Fairy tales teach us how to behave, desire, fear, and belong. We will look at the original tales by the Grimm Brothers (The Frog Prince, Rapunzel, Sleeping Beauty, etc.), later versions of their famous stories, as well as contemporary fairy tales, including film (e.g., Pan's Labyrinth, Maleficent, Wicked) to expose the enduring relevance of this genre. As the creative assignment in this class, students will have the opportunity to create their own fairy tales, using various media. Students who are German minors or majors may participate in a separate section in German and enroll in four units. All other students should enroll in three units.

subject: GERMAN
title: Thomas Mann's Der Tod in Venedig
description: Thomas Mann was one of the most prominent German-language authors of the first half of the twentieth-century.  His novella, Der Tod in Venedig (Death in Venice), published in 1912, is  a seminal example of  modernist literature as well as an indicator of the culture currents in Europe on the eve of the First World War. It recounts the story of a famous author facing a psychological crisis that he hopes to resolve with a vacation in Venice, where however he encounters a city gripped by cholera. Against that backdrop, Mann explores philosophical questions concerning the nature of art and education, the legacy of the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, the eruption of suppressed desires, and the rumblings of nationalism. This course offers an opportunity for a close reading of the German-language text and its philosophical context.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Conversation (GERMAN 235)
description: This small, individualized course will offer students the chance to work on their spoken expression and critical thinking, in German. Topics will change each quarter but will span contemporary politics and culture, film, literature, and visual arts. The focus will be on speaking German in small groups, as opposed to formal presentations or written assignments. Students will have the opportunity to pursue topics of personal interest, as well as work collaboratively and individually on projects intended to foster advanced communicative skills. Students interested in enrolling in this course should email Department of German Studies Director, Professor Lea Pao.

subject: GERMAN
title: Monsters and Mermaids (COMPLIT 244G, GERMAN 243)
description: Monsters are all around us. We encounter them in stories, movies, and sometimes even in our dreams. In their diversity, they show that our imagination is limitless, but they also pick up on the fears and desires of our cultures and histories as well as how we have been depicting others and defining ourselves. In this course, we will "read monsters" as reflections of specific cultural and historical moments from the Middle Ages to today. Want to find out more about the mermaid depicted on your Starbucks cup? Or learn what causes shapeshifting? Add a little bit of magic to your life with this course about dragons and witches, while exploring the real-world consequences of these fantastical ideas.

subject: GERMAN
title: Heroes and Heroines (COMPLIT 151G, COMPLIT 251G, GERMAN 251)
description: What makes a hero (and, indeed, a heroine!) and why do we need them? This course explores the many faces and functions of heroines and heroes throughout ancient and medieval storytelling up until today. We will look at famous warriors such as Alexander the Great, the Amazons, and King Arthur as well as heroic animals and saints, outlaws, tricksters, and fools in European (German) epics as well as the Arabian nights or the Persian Book of Kings, tracing their representation up until today e.g. in DC and Marvel Universe. On this ground, we will explore the literary, historical, cultural, and gender dynamics in the construction and reimagination of heroes and heroines throughout time and space, while also disrupting and questioning the grand heroic narratives through our own analytical and creative takes on 'the hero'. All texts and class discussions will be in English.

subject: GERMAN
title: CAPITALS: How Cities Shape Cultures, States, and People (COMPLIT 100, DLCL 100, FRENCH 175, HISTORY 106E, ILAC 175, ITALIAN 175, URBANST 153)
description: This course takes students on a trip to major capital cities at different moments in time, including Renaissance Florence, Golden Age Madrid, colonial Mexico City, imperial Beijing, Enlightenment and romantic Paris, existential and revolutionary St. Petersburg, roaring Berlin, modernist Vienna, and transnational Dakar. While exploring each place in a particular historical moment, we will also consider the relations between culture, power, and social life. How does the cultural life of a country intersect with the political activity of a capital? How do large cities shape our everyday experience, our aesthetic preferences, and our sense of history? Why do some cities become cultural capitals? Primary materials for this course will consist of literary, visual, sociological, and historical documents (in translation). No prerequisites. Attendance to lecture required.

subject: GERMAN
title: Philosophy and Literature (CLASSICS 42, COMPLIT 181, ENGLISH 81, FRENCH 181, ILAC 181, ITALIAN 181, PHIL 81, SLAVIC 181)
description: Can novels make us better people? Can movies challenge our assumptions? Can poems help us become who we are? We'll think about these and other questions with the help of writers like Toni Morrison, Marcel Proust, Bong Joon-ho, Charlie Kaufman, Emily Dickinson, William Shakespeare, and Samuel Beckett, plus thinkers like Montaigne, Nehamas, Nietzsche, Nussbaum, Plato, and Sartre. We'll also ask whether a disenchanted world can be re-enchanted; when, if ever, the truth stops being the most important thing; why we sometimes choose to read sad stories; whether we ever love someone for who they are; who could possibly want to live their same life over and over again; what it takes to make ourselves fully moral; whether it's ever good to be conflicted; how we can pull ourselves together; and how we can take ourselves apart. (This is the required gateway course for the Philosophy and Literature major tracks. Majors should register in their home department.)

subject: GERMAN
title: German Capstone Project
description: Each student participates in a capstone interview and discussion with a panel of the German Studies faculty on topics related to German cultural and literary analysis. In prepration for the interview/discussion, students submit written answers to a set of questions based on several authentic cultural texts in German. The written answers, normally in English, should be well-formed and coherent. Within the interview/discussion, students must demonstrate a further understanding of the topic(s) posed, through cogent argument.

subject: GERMAN
title: Individual Work
description: Repeatable for Credit.  Instructor Consent Required

subject: GERMAN
title: Denazification (COMPLIT 202G)
description: The process of denazification played a pivotal role in the culture and politics of the early Federal Republic of Germany. What it accomplished, could have accomplished and was intended to accomplish is subject to debates to the present day. This course combines an in-depth look at denazification processes, a history of cultural reflections on denazification, and political debates about denazification from the 1940s until today. Course readings and discussion in English.

subject: GERMAN
title: Cabinets of Wonder (COMPLIT 211G)
description: Humans have long been fascinated with marvelous and curious things. It is well known that in the 16th century, a dedicated practice of collecting existed as a way to grasp the world.  Emperors, noblemen and scholars all across Europe established spaces for holding and exhibiting all sorts of objects they deemed worth possessing. These cabinets of wonder, also known as cabinets of curiosities, soon became both scientific tools to study the natural world and aesthetic symbols designed to entertain and to manifest one's socioeconomic status. Frequently included were: fossils, narwhale horns, and precious stones; sculptures, paintings and porcelain; astrolabes, clocks, and automatons, and much more. In this course, we will delve into the history of cabinets of wonder and ask what has made them so fascinating for so many centuries. We will explore their history, which began in antiquity, and has lasted well into our contemporary era. We will also look more closely into Stanford's own related history and the objects located in the Cantor Museum, where Jane and Leland Stanford established a collection to commemorate their son. This local installation by Mark Dion, one of the best known contemporary artists working within the tradition of cabinets of wonder, is dedicated to Leland Stanford Jr. and his love of collecting. It will serve as a starting point for our exploration as we examine the associated feelings of power, melancholy and mourning: https://museum.stanford.edu/exhibitions/melancholy-museum-love-death-and-mourning-stanford.

subject: GERMAN
title: Theodor W. Adorno: History, Society, Aesthetics (COMPLIT 218)
description: This course introduces students to the philosophy of Theodor W. Adorno (1903-1969) -- including his influential theories of authoritarianism, aesthetics, music and society. Readings and discussion in English.

subject: GERMAN
title: Drive, Instinct, and Will in Philosophy and Literature (COMPLIT 227)
description: What drives us? Why do we do what we do, or want what we want? This seminar offers an introduction to the history of a powerful idea: namely, that humans are driven not only by rational thought and conscious intention, but also by unconscious, instinctual forces. Across a wide historical range but with emphasis on the German tradition, we will examine how philosophy, literature, and psychoanalysis have conceived of such forces and the many names they have invented for them. As part of our exploration, we will encounter and call into question a series of familiar oppositions - between the somatic and the mental, between the mechanical and the organic, and between scientific and imaginative modes of writing. Readings may be drawn from authors such as: Plato, Augustine, Leibniz, Georg Buchner, Heinrich von Kleist, E.T.A. Hoffmann, Edgar Allan Poe, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Bergson, and Freud.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Literature (800-1700) (GERMAN 330)
description: This course surveys different genres and of premodern German literature, including mysticism, Romance, heroic epic, lyric poetry, and the early novel.  All texts available in English and German.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Literature (1700-1900) (GERMAN 331)
description: Want to learn about Germany's (in)famous fairytales, political plays, sentimental accounts, and horror stories? This course offers an introduction to the variety of German literature from 1700-1900 in the midst of major historical events such as the Enlightenment, the French revolution, and the invention and struggles of nation states. From Goethe to Heine, the Brothers Grimm to Fontane, Mereau to Kleist - we will meet them all and explore the historical and cultural connections of these turbulent texts that have shaped storytelling in Europe up until today. Knowledge of German will be helpful, but all texts will also be provided in English translation.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Literature 3: Museum of Modern Poetry (GERMAN 332)
description: This course is about theory, practice, and making of modern German poetry. We will use, as our guide through the poetic history of the 20th century, Hans Magnus Enzensberger's groundbreaking anthology Museum of Modern Poetry, first published in 1960. The Museum was a collection of 351 poems, each printed in its original language and in German translation and organized into 10 categories (places, oceans, graves, laments, figures, etc.). Among the poets and translators were Wallace Stevens, Emily Dickinson, Vladimir Mayakovsky, Octavio Paz, Langston Hughes, Nazim Hikmet, Aimé Césaire, Fernando Pessoa, Giuseppe Ungaretti, Rainer Maria Rilke, and Léopold Sédar Senghor; Ingeborg Bachmann, Paul Celan, Nella Sachs, and Marie Luise Kaschnitz. Enzensberger aimed to document the history of modernist poetry and manifest its ongoing influence as part of artistic and readerly practice. The museum is thus a paradox: like all guides to the future it is composed entirely of ideas from the past, which is why Enzensberger recommended, in his preface, thinking of the book as an "annex to the artist's workshop." We will read a small selection of German poems and: 1) explore the difference between a poem as an object of history and a process of meaning-making, and historicize the idea that there might be a difference; 2) translate the poems we'll read into different languages (and/or dialects; we can discuss what we want "language" to mean), using translation as a museum practice and as a mode of reading. As part of the course, we will produce our own museum of modern poetry. Paradoxically, no knowledge of German is required.

subject: GERMAN
title: Monsters and Mermaids (COMPLIT 244G, GERMAN 143)
description: Monsters are all around us. We encounter them in stories, movies, and sometimes even in our dreams. In their diversity, they show that our imagination is limitless, but they also pick up on the fears and desires of our cultures and histories as well as how we have been depicting others and defining ourselves. In this course, we will "read monsters" as reflections of specific cultural and historical moments from the Middle Ages to today. Want to find out more about the mermaid depicted on your Starbucks cup? Or learn what causes shapeshifting? Add a little bit of magic to your life with this course about dragons and witches, while exploring the real-world consequences of these fantastical ideas.

subject: GERMAN
title: Heroes and Heroines (COMPLIT 151G, COMPLIT 251G, GERMAN 151)
description: What makes a hero (and, indeed, a heroine!) and why do we need them? This course explores the many faces and functions of heroines and heroes throughout ancient and medieval storytelling up until today. We will look at famous warriors such as Alexander the Great, the Amazons, and King Arthur as well as heroic animals and saints, outlaws, tricksters, and fools in European (German) epics as well as the Arabian nights or the Persian Book of Kings, tracing their representation up until today e.g. in DC and Marvel Universe. On this ground, we will explore the literary, historical, cultural, and gender dynamics in the construction and reimagination of heroes and heroines throughout time and space, while also disrupting and questioning the grand heroic narratives through our own analytical and creative takes on 'the hero'. All texts and class discussions will be in English.

subject: GERMAN
title: The Sacred at Hand (COMPLIT 260, COMPLIT 360, TAPS 260E)
description: This seminar explores the phenomenology of the sacred as it emerges within ordinary lived experience, drawing primarily from modern German arts and letters. We read poets of attentiveness (such as Holderlin, Rilke, Lasker-Schuler, and Celan) alongside thinkers who theorize the conditions of meaningful encounter (such as Rosenzweig, Buber, Weil, Heidegger, Hartmut Rosa, and Byung-Chul Han) and practitioners of duration and presence in contemporary art (such as Pina Bausch, Gerhard Richter, and Marina Abramovic). Emerson and Marilynne Robinson offer counterpoints from the American tradition. We ask how artistic form might not merely represent but actually structure the conditions under which such experiences can appear. The course extends beyond the seminar room. We visit sites such as Goldsworthy's Stone River and the Windhover Contemplative Center, where art and architecture discipline perception. Circumstances permitting, we may attend local performances and exhibitions. Assignments include analytical essays, seminar discussion, and exercises in phenomenological description. Taught in English; all readings in translation.

subject: GERMAN
title: Prospects for Transatlantic Relations: What Holds the West Together? (GERMAN 367)
description: International relations between the United States and Europe, especially Germany, have been particularly important on both sides of the Atlantic. However new and old problems are generating considerable tension. This short course will focus on resilience as a response to geopolitical and geoeconomic changes with regard to three topics: 1) The Global Economy Without a Benevolent Hegemon: Unpredictable Uncertainty; (2) Old Lessons from Economics: John M. Keynes's "National Self-Sufficiency" (1933) and Albert O. Hirschman's "National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade" (1945); (3) Policy for National Resilience: Innovation, Immigration, Investment. Meeting times: This block seminar meets from 9:00am to 11:00am in room 260-252 on Monday, November 2, Wednesday, November 4, and Friday, November 6 2026, as well as other occasional meetings TBD. Taught in English with readings in German and English (German reading knowledge not required).

subject: GERMAN
title: Directed Reading: Comprehension Research in Second-language Contexts
description: This course reviews the research literature on comprehension with a particular emphasis on reading comprehension.

subject: GERMAN
title: Perceval and the Quest for the Holy Grail (COMPLIT 302G, ENGLISH 302G)
description: Beginning with Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Conte du Graal (ca. 1180), we examine the Grail story in its inaugural vernacular form - as a text defined by incompletion, formal ambiguity, and interpretive openness. We then turn to Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (ca. 1200-1210), which transforms Chretien's enigmatic conte into an architecturally intricate exploration of guilt, grace, kinship, and knightly becoming. The seminar will also attend to the story's remarkable afterlife in literary and artistic adaptation, with students presenting an adaptation of their choosing. Readings and discussion in English.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Literature (800-1700) (GERMAN 230)
description: This course surveys different genres and of premodern German literature, including mysticism, Romance, heroic epic, lyric poetry, and the early novel.  All texts available in English and German.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Literature (1700-1900) (GERMAN 231)
description: Want to learn about Germany's (in)famous fairytales, political plays, sentimental accounts, and horror stories? This course offers an introduction to the variety of German literature from 1700-1900 in the midst of major historical events such as the Enlightenment, the French revolution, and the invention and struggles of nation states. From Goethe to Heine, the Brothers Grimm to Fontane, Mereau to Kleist - we will meet them all and explore the historical and cultural connections of these turbulent texts that have shaped storytelling in Europe up until today. Knowledge of German will be helpful, but all texts will also be provided in English translation.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Literature 3: Museum of Modern Poetry (GERMAN 232)
description: This course is about theory, practice, and making of modern German poetry. We will use, as our guide through the poetic history of the 20th century, Hans Magnus Enzensberger's groundbreaking anthology Museum of Modern Poetry, first published in 1960. The Museum was a collection of 351 poems, each printed in its original language and in German translation and organized into 10 categories (places, oceans, graves, laments, figures, etc.). Among the poets and translators were Wallace Stevens, Emily Dickinson, Vladimir Mayakovsky, Octavio Paz, Langston Hughes, Nazim Hikmet, Aimé Césaire, Fernando Pessoa, Giuseppe Ungaretti, Rainer Maria Rilke, and Léopold Sédar Senghor; Ingeborg Bachmann, Paul Celan, Nella Sachs, and Marie Luise Kaschnitz. Enzensberger aimed to document the history of modernist poetry and manifest its ongoing influence as part of artistic and readerly practice. The museum is thus a paradox: like all guides to the future it is composed entirely of ideas from the past, which is why Enzensberger recommended, in his preface, thinking of the book as an "annex to the artist's workshop." We will read a small selection of German poems and: 1) explore the difference between a poem as an object of history and a process of meaning-making, and historicize the idea that there might be a difference; 2) translate the poems we'll read into different languages (and/or dialects; we can discuss what we want "language" to mean), using translation as a museum practice and as a mode of reading. As part of the course, we will produce our own museum of modern poetry. Paradoxically, no knowledge of German is required.

subject: GERMAN
title: Prospects for Transatlantic Relations: What Holds the West Together? (GERMAN 267)
description: International relations between the United States and Europe, especially Germany, have been particularly important on both sides of the Atlantic. However new and old problems are generating considerable tension. This short course will focus on resilience as a response to geopolitical and geoeconomic changes with regard to three topics: 1) The Global Economy Without a Benevolent Hegemon: Unpredictable Uncertainty; (2) Old Lessons from Economics: John M. Keynes's "National Self-Sufficiency" (1933) and Albert O. Hirschman's "National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade" (1945); (3) Policy for National Resilience: Innovation, Immigration, Investment. Taught in English with readings in German and English (German reading knowledge not required).

subject: GERMAN
title: Introduction to the Profession of Literary Studies (COMPLIT 369, DLCL 369, FRENCH 369, ILAC 369G, ITALIAN 369, SLAVIC 369G)
description: A survey of how literary theory and other methods have been made institutional since the nineteenth century. The readings and conversation are designed for entering Ph.D. students in the national literature departments and comparative literature.

subject: GERMAN
title: German Studies Lecture Series
description: What's happening in German Studies today? The GSLS invites 3 speakers per quarter to present on their work and research in German literature, culture, politics, and history, offering students an insight into the current field of German Studies and an engagement with topics ranging from medieval fabrics to the refugee crisis. Luncheons are scheduled every first Tuesday of the month. To earn the unit for this course, students will attend the lecture, read 1-2 articles or book chapters written by the speaker of the week, and complete one short 2-page writing assignment (this could be a reflection, a review, a creative assignment, a poetic adaptation of a talk - we'll discuss). Taught in German and English.  Enroll for Credit/No Credit

subject: GERMAN
title: Graduate Studies Colloquium
description: Colloquium for graduate students in German Studies. Taught in English. May be repeated for credit.

subject: GERMAN
title: Dissertation Prospectus Colloquium
description: Repeatable for Credit

subject: GERMAN
title: Individual Work
description: Repeatable for Credit.  Instructor Consent Required.

subject: GERMAN
title: Nietzsche and the Search for Meaning
description: Many of us have heard his declarations of the death of God, the arrival of the Superman, and the need to live beyond good and evil.  But what, beyond such sound bites, did Nietzsche actually teach?  How can his writings be understood in the context of their own time?  And what significance might they hold for us today? Taught in English.

subject: GERMAN
title: TGR Dissertation
description: Doctoral students who have been admitted to candidacy, completed all required courses and degree requirements other than the University oral exam and dissertation, completed 135 units or 10.5 quarters of residency (if under the old residency policy), and submitted a Doctoral Dissertation Reading Committee form, may request Terminal Graduate Registration status to complete their dissertations.

subject: GERMAN
title: 10 Poems That Will Change Your Life
description: This course is for anyone who has ever been afraid of poetry, anyone who has ever thought that poems are too difficult to understand, a course for anyone who has fallen in love with poetry before, and for anyone who has used a poem to make a difference in someone's life. You will learn how to read, understand, and if you don't already like poetry. We will read poems from different centuries, different kinds of writers, and different media (paper, computer screens, and even DNA); they will be about loss and love and war and loyalty and bacteria. Some of them will be about you. You will develop interpretive skills that come with this range of poetic forms and structures and will learn how to think about what it means for something to be poetic, whether it is a poem, a Leonard Cohen song, a last minute field goal, or a toilet. Can the poems in this class really change your life? (What would that even mean? We'll discuss.) Maybe; maybe not. But they're certainly going to try. Taught in English

subject: GLOBAL
title: Iranian Cuisine
description: Course offers an introductory look at Iranian cooking and cuisine. Through weekly themes and the preparation of dishes, students will learn about the history of Iranian cuisine, essential ingredients, and general cooking techniques. Guest chefs will lead cooking sessions. Class begins the second week of the quarter and meets for eight consecutive weeks. Application information will be provided in the preceding quarter. Selected students will receive an enrollment code. Enrollment priority will be given to Global Studies UG minors with the Iranian Studies specialization. This class will be held in an R&DE Training Kitchen to be announced. Enrolled students will received further direction regarding the location.

subject: GLOBAL
title: South Asia at Stanford
description: This course provides an introduction to the many disciplines and scholars at Stanford focusing on South Asia. Over the quarter we will learn about the literatures, histories, languages, arts, religions, politics, and economies of this diverse region. Examples are Queer South Asia via cinema, Hindu Epics, past and present, and How Nonviolence Works: Lessons from India's Independence Struggle

subject: GLOBAL
title: The Local Worlds of Early Modern Iran (HISTORY 281L)
description: This course explores the history of early modern Iran through the lens of local and regional history. Organized as a province-by-province journey across the Iranian world, it examines the histories of Iran's regions under four successive dynasties - the Safavids, Afsharids, Zands, and Qajars. Over the course of the quarter, students will investigate the political, social, economic, and cultural development of different provinces from the beginning of the sixteenth century to the Constitutional Revolution of 1906. Particular emphasis will be on the primary sources available for reconstructing the history of these regions and on the methodological challenges of writing local history in early modern Iran.

subject: GLOBAL
title: Around the World in Ten Films (FILMEDIA 135, FILMEDIA 335)
description: This is an introductory-level course about the cinema as a global language. We will undertake a comparative study of select historical and contemporary aspects of international cinema, and explore a range of themes pertaining to the social, cultural, and political diversity of the world. A cross-regional thematic emphasis and inter-textual methods of narrative and aesthetic analysis, will ground our discussion of films from Italy, Japan, United States, India, China, France, Brazil, Nigeria, Russia, Iran, Mexico, and a number of other countries. Particular emphasis will be placed on the multi-cultural character and the regional specificities of the cinema as a "universal language" and an inclusive "relational network."There are no prerequisites for this class. It is open to all students; non-majors welcome.

subject: GLOBAL
title: Iranian Visionary: On 'Abdu'l-Baha's Modernism
description: Among the handful of occasions when Stanford's President has required all students and faculty to attend a public lecture, two names are widely remembered: Martin Luther King Jr. and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. Less well known is that in 1912, Stanford's founding President David Starr Jordan - himself one of the original trustees of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace - extended that same rare invitation to 'Abdu'l-Baha Abbas, a Persian thinker and social reformer who had spent decades as a prisoner of the Ottoman Empire before his release in 1908. During his 1912 North American tour, Abdu'l-Baha Abbas spoke before an audience of approximately 2,000 Stanford faculty and students on the themes that defined his public mission: the abolition of war, the oneness of humanity, the dangers of unchecked technological progress, the adoption of a universal auxiliary language, the advancement of women's education and equality, and the question of racism and racial justice in America. His presence at Stanford was not incidental - it reflected a serious intellectual engagement with the modern world at a moment of profound global transformation. This course asks: what kind of modernism did 'Abdu'l-Baha Abbas's vision represent? We will examine the philosophical and historical roots of his thought, tracing how an Iranian prisoner of conscience became one of the early twentieth century's most compelling voices on global order and human advancement. Our primary texts will be The Secret of Divine Civilization (1875), a foundational political treatise advocating constitutional governance, rational administration, and cultural reform in the Muslim world, and A Traveller's Narrative (1886), a historical account of the Babi and Baha'i movements that raises essential questions about religion, modernity, and political authority from the perspective of a fictional traveler to the East. The course will also study key text by Baha'u'llah, the founder of the Baha'i Faith, that include The Kitab-i- Aqdas: The Most Holy Book (ca. 1873) as well as Baha'u'lah's letters to the world's rulers, to understand the foundation of 'Abdu'l-Baha Abbas's modern vision.

subject: GLOBAL
title: Undergraduate Directed Reading
description: Independent studies for undergraduate students under the direction of a faculty member for which academic credit may properly be allowed. May be repeated for credit.

subject: GLOBAL
title: History of World Cinema III: Queer Cinemas Around the World (ARTHIST 164, ARTHIST 364, CSRE 102C, CSRE 302C, FEMGEN 100C, FEMGEN 300C, FILMEDIA 100C, FILMEDIA 300C, GLOBAL 390, TAPS 100C, TAPS 300C)
description: This course provides an overview of cinema from around the world since 1960, highlighting the cultural, political, and economic forces that have shaped various film movements over the last six decades. Specific topics may vary by term/year/instructor. This term's topic, Queer Cinemas around the World, engages with a range of queer cinematic forms and queer spectatorial practices in different parts of the world, as well as BIPOC media from North America. Through film and video from Kenya, Malaysia, India, The Dominican Republic, China, Brazil, Palestine, Japan, Morocco, the US etc., we will examine varied narratives about trans experience, same-sex desire, LGBTQI2S+ rights, censorship, precarity, and hopefulness. This course will attune us to regional cultural specificities in queer expression and representation, prompting us to move away from hegemonic and homogenizing understandings of queer life and media. Notes: Screenings will be held on Fridays at 1:30PM in Oshman Hall. Screening times will vary slightly from week to week.

subject: GLOBAL
title: Capstone Project: Global Studies Minor
description: Students completing a capstone project for the Global Studies Minor must enroll in this course for units (1-5) with their capstone advisor selected as the instructor. The course may be repeated for credit, with advisor approval. Students are expected to participate in regular advising meetings with the instructor.

subject: GLOBAL
title: The World Wars: A Global History, 1914-1945 (HISTORY 207G, HISTORY 307G)
description: This course explores the First and Second World Wars, the defining conflicts of the twentieth century, as global events that reshaped societies, empires, international politics, and the very notion of humanity. Spanning from the causes of the First World War to the legacies of dropping atomic weapons on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, this course explores the political, moral, and ideological forces that gave rise to total war and examines how these conflicts transformed human lives in Europe, Japan, the Pacific, and the United States. We will investigate the wars within the context of imperial rivalry, nationalism, and industrial militarization. But throughout we will also be attuned to their unprecedented human toll, including genocide, and their lasting destabilizing impact. We will conclude by exploring the legal processes and commemorative efforts that aimed at promoting reconciliation, lasting peace, and global political order in the postwar period.

subject: GLOBAL
title: Culture and Revolution in Africa (AFRICAAM 213, COMPLIT 213, FRENCH 213E, HISTORY 243E)
description: This course investigates the relationship between culture, revolutionary decolonization, and post-colonial trajectories. It probes the multilayered development of 20th and 21st-century African literature amid decolonization and Cold War cultural diplomacy initiatives and the debates they generated about African literary aesthetics, African languages, the production of history, and the role of the intellectual. We will journey through national cultural movements, international congresses, and pan-African festivals to explore the following questions: What role did writers and artists play in shaping the discourse of revolutionary decolonization throughout the continent and in the diaspora? How have literary texts, films, and works of African cultural thought shaped and engaged with concepts such as "African unity" and "African cultural renaissance"? How have these notions influenced the imaginaries of post-independence nations, engendered new subjectivities, and impacted gender and generational dynamics? How did the ways of knowing and modes of writing promoted and developed in these contexts shape African futures?

subject: GLOBAL
title: History of World Cinema III: Queer Cinemas Around the World (ARTHIST 164, ARTHIST 364, CSRE 102C, CSRE 302C, FEMGEN 100C, FEMGEN 300C, FILMEDIA 100C, FILMEDIA 300C, GLOBAL 193, TAPS 100C, TAPS 300C)
