It focuses on basic social institutions and cultural norms in traditional Chinese society and their modern transformations.  The readings, drawn mainly from the disciplines of history and anthropology, cover topics of family, kinship, marriage, popular religions, ethnicity, community institutions, imperial state power, and rural and urban political economies.  The course draws particular attention to China's constant modernizing efforts in the past century, especially during the socialist revolution and post-Mao reforms, as well as their bearings upon contemporary Chinese social practices and cultural patterns.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Basic Presentation Skills and Daily Situations I - Putonghua
description: An upper elementary listening and speaking course in Putonghua and the continuation of CLCP1123. Students will explore more language scenarios based on daily situations and learn how to present basic ideas orally in real-life settings. Accuracy in pronunciation, grammar, and usage is emphasised.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Oral Skills Practice II - Putonghua
description: An intermediate listening and speaking course in Putonghua, focusing on completing linguistic tasks through oral communication. Students will be trained to use Putonghua in daily situations and semi-formal situations. Accuracy in pronunciation, grammar, and usage is emphasised.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: The Study of Music
description: This course explores music as a fundamental human practice, and introduces the study of music as central to broader humanistic inquiry. By engaging with styles and performance practices from various regions and historical eras, students will develop an understanding of the diverse ways in which music intersects with human experience, culture, and history. To this end, the course employs an issue-based approach. The first several class sessions deal with fundamental questions about music, such as: What is music? How do musical sounds communicate meaning? What are the relationships between musical sounds, contexts, listening habits, and human behavior? How and why do scholars study music? The remainder of the semester is devoted to particular case studies that explore music's relationship to other realms including politics, religion, identity, and globalization. The class is structured around interactive lectures, demonstrations, discussion, and in-class group activities. No prior musical background or training is required.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Special Topics in International Asian Studies I
description: This course investigates various discourses of Hong Kong ranging from the British colonial perspective to the post-1997 handover Beijing-government perspectives, to the nuances between migrants and expats. Throughout a variety of themes, students will learn to listen to and articulate different discourses and the connections between them. The major course objective is to understand these various discourses of the city, and to investigate their ideological implications and effects on its everyday life. By looking at marginalised groups and spaces that are often overlooked in official narratives of economic prosperity and cultural hybridity, this course engages with alternative stories in the city through readings, screenings, and fieldtrips. The course approaches less talked about dimensions of the city from various film, spatial and food productions. Students will be able to visit vibrant and precarious cityscapes of Nepali ethnic minorities, the less talked about New Territories, and engage with other local marginalized communities.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Special Topics in Chinese Studies: History of Gender and Sexuality in Modern China
description: This course offers qualified students an opportunity to explore at an advanced level a topic determined by the course teacher with respect to student interest or timely relevance, as well as its distinctiveness from current course offerings. The course involves intensive reading and essay writing. Students are expected to meet the course teacher regularly to discuss the readings and formulate critical synthesis of different readings. The teacher will give students feedbacks on each writing assignment to help student improve English academic writing. The topic to be covered in 2026 Fall is "History of Gender and Sexuality in Modern China."

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Meanings of Life
description: In societies across the world, people have different culturally-shaped senses of what their lives mean: people may live for money, love, honour or fame; for family, company, country or religion. This course examines the processes through which meanings of life are formulated and maintained in day-to-day life in societies past and present; it also explores life meaning as a way of comprehending the evolution of human societies. The course uses the concept of "meanings of life" as a window into the anthropological understanding of cultural difference and cultural evolution.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Application of Vocabulary and Grammar I - Cantonese
description: An elementary course designed to familiarise students with the use of romanization, basic vocabulary and sentence structure. Vocabulary introduced is based on everyday conversations and daily usage. The focus will be on appropriateness in language use.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Sound Culture in Modern China
description: This course introduces students to the key concepts and research methodologies of sound studies by examining how music, soundscapes, and auditory culture intersect with society, history, politics, and cultural identities in contemporary China. It will first explore key concepts such as soundscape, sonic culture, hearing and listening, and research methodologies of sounds studies in the field of Chinese studies. Afterwards, it will look at how sound was designed, created, shaped, practiced, listened to, and perceived in multiple mediums including musical performance, radio and audio dramas, as well as film, animation, and television in contemporary China. Students will be exposed to a variety of multimedia products that foreground the richness of sound culture. Through these works from the Chinese Mainland, Hong Kong, China and Taiwan, China, sound's function as a medium for expressing and constructing cultural identity and socio-political connotations will be explored.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Advanced Communication Skills and Culture I - Putonghua
description: An advanced course designed for students who have completed CLCP3353 or CPTH3353. The course is designed to enhance students' language skills in communication, as well as to increase their understanding of Chinese social customs and culture through a series of training, including listening comprehension, special report, group discussion, etc.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Media Representations of Minorities in Hong Kong
description: How do we understand the notion of "minority"? And how does "minority", look like, in cinema? This course examines the rich tradition of critical film theory and provides students with an understanding of its main concerns and debates, concerning "minority" identities and subalternity. Addressing key discussions about media representations of "minority", the course will look at the politics of representation and its impacts, both on- and off-screen. We will be looking at how media works to construct "the Other" in different contexts, and delve into important work which have inspired minority cinema, subaltern cinema, avant-garde cinema, local cinema, and independent cinema among other counter-movements, as well as recent re-conceptualizations and exploration of representations marginalized identities, positions, and experiences, local and abroad. Across different systems of representation, from fine art to mainstream cinema to advertising, different groups, especially marginalized ones with little access to the mechanisms of production, have been constructed and existed as spectacle or passive object "to-be-looked-at," in critical film theorist Laura Mulvey's now often quoted words. Lacking representations both behind the camera and in front of it, how are the lives of different social "minorities" affected by biased media representations? How are stereotypes and biases created, disseminated, perpetuated, and reproduced through media, and to what consequences? Mulvey's groundbreaking analysis of gendered looking relations in classical Hollywood cinema has since generated numerous analyses of the standings of different socially and culturally marginalized groups, such as ethnic minorities, queer communities, and people with disabilities, etc., as spectacle or passive object "in films cut to the measure of desire" of the dominant social groups. What happens when "minority" artists, audiences, and theorists look back, and seek to rebel against such cinematic traditions by experimenting with alternative visual languages and narrative tools? Critics showed how different marginalized groups around the world attempt to take control of their positioning through viewing or using texts in their own ways, and by creating their own. Minority cinemas and independent creators have been actively carving out space to tell their own unique stories of lives at the margin in dramatically different cultural contexts, and these images are further complicated by engagements with them through the intersecting lens including ethnicity, class, gender, sexuality, ability, queerness, and more. In the course, we will look at how socially marginalized groups, such as gay and lesbians, transgender persons, ethnic minorities, women in different stages of their lives, people with mental illness, teenagers, the elderlyand many others are portrayed, and seek to expand their on-screen existence in Hong Kong media. In the exploration, we will engage with key questions in critical film studies, including spectatorship, authorship, popular culture, character stereotypes in genre films, self-representation, systems of media production, pro-sumer culture, (g)local cinema, alternative cinema, and new media. Students would be introduced to trailblazing works by "minority" filmmakers and media creators worldwide, and important cinematic and media movements that challenge the status-quo. Special focus will be placed onto important works in Hong Kong and Asia for critical examination and comparative studies. Through critical exercise and reflection on notions such as power, diversity, equality, and freedom, the course aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Advanced Topical Conversation II - Social Life (Putonghua)
description: An advanced course designed for students who have completed CLCP4433 or CPTH4433. The course is designed to enhance students' language skills in communication, as well as to increase their understanding of life in China through a series of training, including reading and listening comprehension, special report, group discussion, etc.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Urban Sociology
description: Sociology has always had an intimate relationship with cities. Urbanization - the increase of the share of the population living in cities - was one of the developments that early sociologists sought to study and explain. Since then, the global urban population has only continued to increase. Today, over half of humanity lives in cities and towns, making urban society as essential to understand now as it was in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Urban sociology has many sides, but in this course, students will learn about four main topics: 1) Early theories and classic statements on urban life, 2) the distinctive social character of the "urban experience," 3) understanding urban space through the political economy approach, and 4) examining urban spatial processes within and beyond Hong Kong, including affordable housing, gentrification, the creative class, and minorities in the city.

subject: OSPHONGK
title: Computational Education
description: This course answers the question: 'What is education's digital future?' Then students start building solutions. It invites students to rethink how AI will impact the future of education. It brings together technical challenges such as: how can we build an AI system to understand students as they learn, and social ones: what sort of learning experiences do we want for future students? In 2026 (and beyond), AI algorithms will impact learning around the world, and as such is a great conversation to have while abroad. This course covers cutting-edge education algorithms used to model students, assess learning, and design widely deployable tools for open access education.

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: Third-Year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication, First Quarter
description: Goal is to express thoughts and opinions in paragraph length in spoken and written forms. Materials include current Japanese media and literature for native speakers of Japanese. Cultural and social topics related to Japan and its people. Prerequisite: Placement Tests, JAPANLNG 23. See http://japanese.stanford.edu/?page_id=39.

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: Zazen: A Practicum in Zen Meditation
description: Zen teaching through practice and experience. Condensed practicum course where students receive zazen training and experience monastic life in Myoshinji, the largest Zen complex in Japan, under the guidance of Rev. Daiko Matsuyama, Deputy Head Priest of Taizo-in temple. Over one week, regular early morning zazen training sessions on site in Taizo-in temple plus visit to World Cultural Heritage site Ryoanji with a private viewing and workshop. Other aspects of monastic life such as temple cleaning, and learning how to rake and care for the dry gardens at Taizo-in. Course culminates in an overnight zazen training session in Myoshinji's magnificent Hatto Dharma Hall. Enrollment limited.

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: Second-Year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication, First Quarter
description: (Formerly OSPKYOTO 17K.) Goal is to further develop and enhance spoken and written Japanese in order to handle advanced concepts such as comparison and contrast of the two cultures, descriptions of incidents, and social issues. 800 kanji, 1,400 new words, and higher-level grammatical constructions. Readings include authentic materials such as newspaper articles, and essays. Prerequisite: JAPANLNG 3 if taken 2012-13 or later (JAPANLNG 7 if taken 2011-12 or earlier)

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: Structure and Shape: From the Middle Ages to the Present
description: In any trip to historical locations, it is impossible not to wonder how the magnificent and monumental buildings of the middle age were constructed without the availability of the omnipresent cranes and construction elevators of nowadays. More perplexing yet, is how the architects of yesteryear managed to design them without the understanding of structural mechanics we have today. The course will explore some of the considerations behind these designs, and how they affected the shape of the buildings, moving through locations, from Europe to Asia, as well as through the ages, up to today's structures. In the process, we will introduce basic ideas on strength of materials and structural mechanics. We will also touch upon similar observations on the relation between shape and function in some biological structures. Classes will consist of lectures, hands-on designs, discussions, and visits to some landmark structures.

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: First-Year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication, Second Quarter
description: Continuation of JAPANLNG 1. First-year sequence enables students to converse, write, and read essays on topics such as personal history, experiences, familiar people. Prerequisite: JAPANLNG 1 if taken 2012-13 of later (JAPANLNG 7 if taken 2011-12 or earlier)

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: Capturing Concepts: A Photographic Exploration of the Origins of Kanji
description: Under guidance of official photographer for KYOTOGRAPHIE International Photography Festival, photograph scenes from everyday life in Kyoto to portray contemporary versions of the ancient forms and original meanings of ten different kanji. Develop observational, interpretive and creative abilities as well as improve technical skills (including picture composition and image editing). Enrollment limited.

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: First-Year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication, Third Quarter
description: (Formerly OSPKYOTO 9K). Continuation of 2K. First-year sequence enables students to converse, write, and read essays on topics such as personal history, experiences, familiar people. Fulfills University Foreign Language Requirement. Prerequisite: JAPANLNG 2 or OSPKYOTO 2K if taken 2012-13 or later (JAPANLNG 8 if taken 2011-13 or earlier)

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: Grassroots Environmentalism in Japan
description: Exploration of the history, impact, structures and successes of local environmental movements in Japan.

subject: OSPKYOTO
title: A Journey into the Buddhist Visual Arts of Japan
description: Impact of Buddhism on the arts and culture of Japan as seen in the ancient capital of Kyoto. Image production, iconography, representational strategies, as well as the ritual and visual functions of Buddhist sculpture and painting with a focus on selected historical temples and their icons. Also examination of architectural and landscape elements of temple layouts, within which iconographic programs are framed, images are enlivened, and practices centered on these devotional and ritual art.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Composition and Writing Workshop for Students in Madrid
description: Advanced. Writing as craft and process, emphasizing brainstorming, planning, outlining, drafting, revising, style, diction, and editing. Students choose topics related to their studies.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Accelerated Second-Year Spanish I
description: Part I of an intensive sequence in Madrid integrating language, culture, and geo/sociopolitics of Spain. Emphasis is on achieving advanced proficiency in oral and written discourse, including formal and informal situations, presentational language and appropriate forms in academic and professional contexts. Prerequisite: Completion of 11 or 21B more than two quarters (six months) prior to arriving in Madrid.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Accelerated Second-Year Spanish II
description: Intensive sequence integrating language, culture, and geo/sociopolitics of Spain. Emphasis is on achieving advanced proficiency in oral and written discourse, including formal and informal situations, presentational language, and appropriate forms in academic and professional contexts. Prerequisite: 11 or 21B within two quarters (six months) of arriving in Madrid or 12 or 22B, or equivalent placement.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Understanding Spain: Insights Through Study Abroad
description: Required for all Madrid students, this course gives structure to the 10-week experience through a number of lectures and activities intended to cover a wide selection of culturally and academically significant topics to understand Spain as well as its international context. Both the Orientation and the weekend Study Trip form part of this course. Compliance with the language pledge is one of the requirements to pass this course.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Flamenco Dance
description: Practical instruction. The rhythms and styles of flamenco and the expression of feelings proper to this art form which synthesizes song, music, and dance. "Zapateado" (footwork), "braceo" (arm positions and movement technique), and choreographies, including Rumba flamenca and Sevillanas..  Enrollment is limited.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Directed Reading on Catalan, Galizian, or Basque Languages
description: For students interested in studying one of the languages spoken in Spain other than Spanish. A Directed Reading Proposal must be submitted to the Overseas Studies Office and to the Program Director at least two months prior to the quarter of intended study. This directed reading may be taken only in addition to twelve units of regular coursework offered directly by the Center.

description: Humanities or Arts course at a local Spanish university. Students enrolled in the Madrid Program will receive an email from Madrid Program Director with information about these course opportunities at local partner institutions, including the action to take for applying. title: Madrid University: Health & Medical Studies
description: Health or Medical Studies course at a local Spanish university. Students enrolled in the Madrid Program will receive an email from Madrid Program Director with information about these course opportunities at local partner institutions, including the action to take for applying.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Canarian Night Skies
description: Exploration of night skies in Spain's Canary Islands as well as those seen from California. Science for non-majors. Constellations, Solar System, Galactic and Extragalactic objects. Unique characteristics of the Canary Islands as astronomical reserve studied prior to field trip to the Canary Islands. Comparison of naked-eye Canarian and Californian night skies. Study and exploration of relevant astronomical instrumentation as well as representative celestial objects. Astrophotography-related activities. Enrollment is limited.  Enrollment using permission number, please contact Claudia Sanchez, Madrid Academic Coordinator at cesanchez@stanford.edu.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: New Political Dynamics in Contemporary Spain
description: Current Spanish politics, historical background followed by focus on contemporary political events, actors and institutions. Special attention to the most dynamic aspects such as the appearance of new parties and the adjustments of the old ones; the demands of social movements, with a special emphasis on feminism; current debates about how to deal with the past (historical memory policies); or the evolution of the territorial conflict, with a special focus on Catalonia. Experiential approach with opportunities to engage in dialogue on the different issues, both with Spanish citizens and with political actors.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: The Jacobean Star Way and Europe: Society, Politics and Culture
description: The Saint James' Way as a tool to understand historic dynamics from a global perspective. Its effect on the structures that form a political and institutional system, and its society, economy, and ideology. Enrollment limited.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Bing Study Excursion
description: This 1-unit course offers students an immersive exploration of Spain's rich cultural and historical diversity through one or two preparatory sessions followed by a three-day Bing study excursion. Each trip is organized around one or more themes that, while rooted in a specific region, address broader dynamics relevant to understanding Spain's multifaceted heritage. By visiting historical landmarks, engaging with cultural traditions, and experiencing regional cuisine firsthand, students gain valuable insights into the interplay between local identities and larger cultural, historical, and social contexts.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Women in Art: Case Study in the Madrid Museums
description: Viewing the collections at the Prado Museum through study and analysis of the representations of women. Contemporary literary texts and images that situate paintings in the historical, social, and political conditions that produced the works. Limited enrollment.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Drawing with Four Spanish Masters: Goya, Velazquez, Picasso and Dali
description: In this studio and art course, we shall investigate a variety of approaches, techniques, and processes in drawing. In addition, we shall take advantage of Madrid's first rate museums and their rich collections of paintings and drawings by Goya, Velázquez, Picasso, and Dalí in order to explore further the experience of drawing. We shall explore subject matter such as the figure, still life, interiors, landscape, and non-representational drawing. As we shall visit and explore a different Spanish master approximately every two and a half weeks, with each type of subject matter, we will also investigate different readings, media, and concepts. The class will be conducted as a workshop with the first few minutes devoted to discussion of work students have brought in and the remainder of the class left for drawing. Museum visits will focus on the work of one of the four artists with tie to study and explore the work and learn approaches and attitudes that could possibly influence your own work. The course is designed for students interested in Spanish art and in drawing, either with or without previous experience.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Migration and Multiculturality in Spain
description: This course analyzes current migration flows and their implication, one of the most pressing issues in Spain and the European Union today.  Students will be provided with the theoretical and conceptual framework needed to critically analyze both the diversity and complexity of migration and its effects on society and culture.  The focus will be primarily on the city of Madrid and the course will provide students with field experience to understand how the city has become a place of coexistence for different ethnic and cultural groups, as well as the challenges this multiculturalism implies.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Latin Americans in Spain: Cultural Identities, Social Practices, and Migratory Experience
description: Shift  in recent decades from Spain being a country of emigration to one attractive for immigration, especially for people coming from Latin America. Transnational processes of interculturality, integration and assimilation as illustrated by the different ways that immigrant Spaniards relate to Spanish society in Spain.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Health Care: A Contrastive Analysis between Spain and the U.S.
description: History of health care and evolution of the concept of universal health care based on need not wealth. Contrast with system in U.S. Is there a right to health care and if so, what does it encompass? The Spanish health care system; its major successes and shortcomings. Issues and challenges from an interdisciplinary perspective combining scientific facts with moral, political, and legal philosophy.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Internship Seminar: Experiential Learning through Service and Professional Opportunities
description: This class is designed to offer real time engagement in the professional life of Madrid. Service work, including volunteering with NGOs and nonprofits, and professional opportunities at companies and institutions ranging from architecture, to publishing, sustainability and to business, serves as the foundation for an experiential learning approach to optimize self-awareness and intercultural competency development. A student-centered approach helps to connect concrete experience with abstract concepts chosen from the students' individual and collective interest areas. Possibilities may include learning about the Spanish educational, social services, migration, entrepreneurship, and business systems. Students develop goals, meet challenges, develop language skills, and acquire a global perspective on today's issues. The course is structured around lecture-workshops, participant observation reflection through field-notes, and individual debriefing meetings with the professor. Requirements include an oral presentation and a final paper based on field experiences and academic research. Prerequisite: completion of SPANLANG 11 or 21B within two quarters (six months) of arriving in Madrid or completion of 12 or 22B, or equivalent placement. Limited enrollment

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Flamenco and Jazz: An Appraisal of the Creative Encounters between two Improvised Genres
description: Jazz and Flamenco are music genres that originated and evolved in subaltern groups. They are both artistic practices that sufficiently resemble one another, thus inviting a comparative study. This course is multi-disciplinary in scope, and consciously emphasizes the links between history, politics, and expressive culture employing readings and theoretical frameworks from the areas of ethnomusicology, jazz studies. Jazz criticism, anthropology, flamencology, and folklore.  Note: This course must be taken for a minimum of 3 units and a letter grade to be eligible for Ways credit.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Dissimilar Early Modern Bodies: the visual representation of the "Other".
description: Dissimilar Early Modern Bodies: the visual representation of the "Other".    Enrollment is Limited.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Sefarad: The Jewish Community in Spain
description: The legacy of Sefarad, the Jewish community in Spain. Historical evolution of the Sephardic community, under both Muslim and Christian rule, including the culmination of Anti-Semitism in 1492 with the expulsion of the Jews. Cultural contribution of the Hebrew communities in their condition as a social minority, both in al-Andalus, the peninsular Islamic State, and in the peninsular Christian kingdoms.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Spain Through its Gastronomy: A Cooking Workshop
description: A travel through the rich diversity of Spanish contemporary cuisine. Limited enrollment.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Madrid Through My Eyes: A Theoreticl/Practical Documentary Film Workshop
description: Theoretical and practical view of Spanish language documentary cinema; potential of this type of film making as a form of personal expression. Tools for understanding and analyzing this type of cinema. Creative and analytical reflection on student 's Madrid experience; develop individual visual discourse to portray life in the city by filming a short documentary.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Cities and Creativity: Cultural and Architectural Interpretations of Madrid
description: Most of the world population lives in urban environments, and this trend is set to continue on the increase in coming decades. What is more, the vast majority of human beings carry out their daily activities of residence, work, education, sport and leisure in built, architectural settings. Architecture and its projection at the macro scale (the city) therefore construct the stage upon which human life is essentially enacted. This course is intended to encourage students to acquire a more in-depth awareness of Architecture and the city, with a focus on recent currents in the progress of both, such as sustainability, environmentalism and the relationship with nature. These topics are underpinned by a discussion of theory and illustrated by a study of the city of Madrid: an example of a hybrid architectural/planning experiential environment that looks to the future with an ambition for modernization. Limited Enrollment.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Fashion and Design: Spanish and European Culture through Attire
description: This course addresses aspects of Spanish and European culture, based on the multidisciplinary study of attire and fashion from the perspectives of sociology, history, and art. This pluralistic viewpoint will serve as the framework from which to reflect on the social dynamics associated with clothing: the imitation or differentiation of the individual in social groups, economic inequalities and luxury, the construction of dress as it relates to social characteristics linked to gender, or the new paradigm of sustainable fashion. Limited enrollment.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Appreciating Spanish Music
description: Unique aspects of Spanish art music. Participation in concert outings and field trips for live performances of studied repertoire. No previous knowledge of music required. Enrollment limited.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Revolutions: The Power of An Idea
description: Course description: This humanities course will examine the concept and development of revolutions and globalization. We will focus in situations of status quo, chance of reforms and "change through revolutions", including alternatives not taken. We will have a general approach to the narratives and tools of global revolutions and human management of change, including technologies provided and environment, providing multidisciplinary methods of inquiry. We will analyse cases connected with cultural landscapes and institutions -museums, academies- from Madrid and Spain, giving the students a unique individual experience of material culture: texts, paintings, buildings, or sounds. The program will explore the so-called "Atlantic revolutions", from the 1770s to the 1820s, including those in the USA, France, Haiti, Spanish or Portuguese America, and other representations of "political modernity". Then we will study revolutions in Economy and production in the 1800s, from iron and coal to steel and petrol, Technoscience, the 1950s, Cold War, China and other Asian and African models. Last but not least, we will study cultural revolutions in the Sixties, from food to music, fashion, consumerism, politics and the last global age, including digital impacts.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: (Re)Framing Disability Intersections with Race, National Origin, & Culture in Spain and the U.S.
description: The course examines the notion of difference and its colonial roots to understand how it has historically permeated views of disability and its intersections with other categories of difference, including race, national origin, and culture in the U.S. and Spain. We will examine how research communities have been complicit in using the idea of difference to portray these groups in deficient ways. The course is designed to disrupt individual centered conceptions of disability and to challenge deterministic and static visions of culture. Moreover, we will unpack disability intersectionalities with explicit attention to history and power in these national contexts. The course is organized around interdisciplinary themes that include the construction of identities, the study of interactional ecologies through attention to talk and narratives, analysis of professional authority in professional encounters, institutional practices (e.g., diagnosis, classification) and spatial considerations. Students will participate in field trips to educational institutions in Madrid to observe and interview actors working with individuals that embody the categories covered in the course. These trips will enrich the review of the course materials and inform students' completion of assignments.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Clinical Internship
description: In this academic internship, pre-med students shadow a doctor in a leading private hospital network. All medical and surgical specialties are available. In addition to the 50 practicum hours, students will have 5 different thematic sessions with a local physician and faculty member to reflect and build upon their experiences. Students enrolled in the Madrid Program will receive an email from the Director with information about this clinical internship opportunity, including the application process. Enrollment limited. Prerequisite: Completion of SPANLANG 11 or 21B within two quarters (six months) of arriving in Madrid or completion of 12 or 22B, or equivalent placement. This course will have limited enrollment.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: The Psychology of Study Abroad: Identity, Learning, and Transformation
description: Have you ever wondered what happens to your mind when you are fully immersed in a foreign environment? How does navigating an unfamiliar city change the way your brain processes information, or what happens to your sense of self when you begin to express your identity in a new language? This course invites you to look beyond the surface of your time in Spain and treat Madrid as a living laboratory for psychological analysis. Rather than simply experiencing the city, you will use research-based frameworks to examine how cultural immersion reshapes the way you think, learn, and relate to others. The course explores the science of neuroplasticity in unfamiliar settings and why the "cognitive disequilibrium" of culture shock can be a necessary step for meaningful growth. Over the semester, you will move from sightseeing toward deep immersion by examining the psychological dynamics of belonging and solitude, identity development across cultures, and the ways privilege and positionality shape engagement in global spaces. You will use accessible analytical tools - experiential learning, reflection on how you learn, and strategies for transferring learning across contexts - to make sense of real-world situations. Assignments are analytically structured and research-informed, building skills you can apply in Madrid and beyond. Open to students from all disciplines; no prerequisites. While reflective, the course centers on academic analysis and theory-driven inquiry.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: The Literatures and Cultures of the Hemispheric Americas and Spain
description: This seminar explores some of the Chilean Roberto Bolanos's writings he composed in Chile, Mexico City, and Spain. We will not only analyze Bolano's Nocturno de Chile , a novel about Pinochet's dictatorship, but also follow Bolano from Chile to his exile in Mexico City and Spain where he wrote his infrarealist poetry and short stories. In addition to Bolanos' work, we will also examine the Mexican writers, Yuri Herrera's novel, Senales que precederan al fin del Mundo, a novel about migration and the US-Mexico borderlands, and Sara Uribe's Antigona Gonzalez, an experimental narrative about the 'disappeared' killed by the Gulf Cartels in Tamaulipas, Mexico. Calling attention to fresh innovations in literary form, voice, multi-lingual perspective, and representation, this course also affirms the lead role of Chilean, Mexican, Latinx, and Spanish writers and artists in reshaping hemispheric Americas and global literatures and cultures. The last third of the course will explore Diego Velazquez's iconic painting "Las Meninas" and the Los Angeles artist Jay Lynn Gomez's tribute to Velazquez in her painting "Las Meninas, Beverly Hills." Here, we will explore what both Las Meninas "paintings" by Velazquez and Gomez tell us about Spain and the Greater borderlands of Los Angeles, California. We will visit both the Prado and Sofia museums in Madrid, where Velazquez's and Gomez's painting are housed. Finally, we will conclude the course by examining some of Spain's pop star, Rosalia's videos dedicated to flamenco and prison reform. We will explore Rosalia's video and song entitled "Juro Que" and see how this contemporary Spanish artist innovates flamenco's long tradition of denouncing the violence of incarceration, particularly as it relates to Gitano, or Spanish Roma, communities. By analyzing the ethno-racial and gendered dimensions of the construction of the poetic speaker/singer in "Juro Que," we will explore how Rosalia continues flamenco's tradition of decrying anti-Gitano carceral violence and revises the boundaries of this sonic tradition. In its opposition to Spanish law, as well as the ethno-racial stereotypes produced by the good Gypsy/bad Gypsy dichotomy, Rosalia's "Juro Que" comments dramatically on the historical function of the Gypsy paradigm in Spain.

subject: OSPMADRD
title: Mythic Madrid: Greek and Roman Tales in The City
description: Mythic Madrid will anchor the study of Classical narratives in the "reception history" of traditional tales, primarily through the unmatched artistic and cultural resources in the city's superb museums. Each week, the class will meet one day at a relevant site-- the Prado, the  Museo Arqueologico Nacional, the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, the Cerralbo Museum or the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, for example. We will examine together paintings, graphic arts, sculptures, or video installations that explicitly feature one or more Classical myth. During the other 90-minute class session each week, intellectual backgrounds to the narratives will be analyzed in illustrated lectures and class discussions. Reading material will comprise primary ancient sources in translation; several accessible scholarly analyses of the given tales; and a selection focused on the reception of myth (for instance, operatic renditions of the Orpheus story; dramas built around the Trojan saga; iconic modern dances centered on Medea, etc). Evaluation by two short papers and final oral exam.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Victorian Gothic, Sensation, and Detective Fiction
description: In this course we will study and discuss examples of the gothic, sensation, and detective fiction that flooded the literary market during the Victorian period. Like their eighteenth-century gothic predecessors, many of these texts lacked literary respectability, though they achieved best seller status. Far beyond simply providing a jaded reading public with scandalous and suspenseful narratives loaded with sex, crime, mystery and even the supernatural, these texts attempted to expose not only the secrets of their protagonists, but also the seamy underbelly of outwardly respectable Victorian society, epitomized by the family with its angel of the house. Topics for discussion will include the literary and moral value of these sub-genres of the novel and what they reveal about Victorian society's anxiety over transgressive - and therefore prohibited - elements in the domestic and public sphere.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Oxford Tutorial
description: OSPOXFRD 195A - Oxford Tutorial

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Directed Reading A
description: Course may be repeated for credit.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Dealing with Data
description: Dealing with data is a fundamental skill for the modern world.  In this course, we will learn two broad dominant paradigms for how to deal with data.  The first way deals with extracting causal relationships from data.  The second way focuses on summarizing and describing patterns in data.  Building from first principles, we will explain the basic ideas and concepts behind each of these approaches, and explore how they relate to each other.  Throughout the course, we will incorporate data from the US and the UK, and we will see plenty of examples from across computer science, engineering and economics. There are no prerequisites for this course: We will adapt the level to meet student needs, including having open-ended assignments to allow students to engage with the material at their current level.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Magic in the Medieval West
description: Medieval people practised magic. To think about the history of medieval magic is to think about a wide swathe of human activities and anxieties, from the prevention of illness to the pursuit of wealth, from the hunt for military glory to ensuring personal safety during travel. Magical practices were everywhere. and practised at every level of society. Medieval people also, worried about magic. The line between scholarship and heresy, the miracles of saints, and the practices of witches and necromancers was fine and contested. For some medieval thinkers, religion and magic were as obviously opposed as scientific method and magical thinking are in the twenty-first century. For others, magic was a respectable branch of learning, supported by authority and tradition, new learning from the Muslim world, and precedent from Christian teaching. Magic in the Medieval West explores this important area of medieval life. It presents the challenges and the opportunities of discovering what practices were actually followed by medieval people, what they thought others were up to, and how these related to their wider understanding of the world they inhabited. It takes advantage of the unique manuscript resources available in Oxford, the expanding body of primary sources now available in translation, and the increasingly rich scholarship on this important area of medieval social and cultural history.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Comparative Politics and Institutions: Contemporary Debates
description: This course's main objective is to present and discuss contemporary issues and challenges to democratic governance and political institutions. In particular, it seeks to identify and assess these challenges by comparing different political systems and observing the differences/similarities among them. The comparative nature of this course will examine: (i) the structure and dynamics of different political systems; (ii) some of the challenges that modern democracies face; and (iii) the benefits and limitations of comparative analysis.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Nationhood: Theory and History
description: What is nationhood and how should we think its history? This course pivots around a paradox in scholarship. On the one hand, 'modernism' that frames nationhood as a modern phenomenon that was non-existent or unimportant before the eighteenth century has become the dominant paradigm in ethnicity and nationalism studies since the 1980s. On the other hand, the same period has seen the publication of literally thousands of books and articles on ethnicity and national identity in the Middle Ages. How can we make sense of the parallel existence of these two paradigms and what can we learn from thinking across this chronological rift? The goal of this course is to interrogate the conceptual and empirical arguments and limitations of both paradigms and explore - through a combination of historiographical critique and thematic case-studies - the possibility of articulating a critical theory and history of nationhood that is not defined by the 'modern'/'pre-modern' divide.

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Practical Ethics for Artificial Intelligence
description: AI has attracted significant attention in the last year, initially due to the release of ChatGPT, followed by backlash and efforts at creating effective regulation. Questions of ethics underlie every aspect of AI, beginning with the question of whether it is even coherent to speak of an intelligence other than humans. This course presents current ethical issues in the development and application of artificial intelligence through a series of recent case studies. We will spend the first part of the course studying major ethical frameworks (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics) and closely-linked research areas within AI and machine learning. In the second part of the course, we will apply these principles to case studies from major areas of debate in AI, with a focus on the translation of ethical principles into practical decisions.The first examples from AI we will cover are existential risks in the context of utilitarianism, the "hidden" labour force of AI in the context of deontology, and the problem of replacing humans in the context of virtue ethics. For the case studies, we will first study fairness and bias in the training and deployment of machine learning models. We will ask what it means for an AI system to be "fair", and how to regulate models which are not interpretable. This is followed by the problems of copyright and large scale training datasets for generative AI models, where we will ask what constitutes unfair use of existing material when it is only being used to train. We continue in a more hypothetical lens with a discussion of whether or not an AI system could be a moral agent or patient, and what rights a non-human intelligence might have. Finally, we conclude with the alignment problem, where we focus on the practical challenges of value alignment and the plausibility of finding a set of values which could be universally accepted. In the last week of the course, students apply their learnings with group presentations on published academic research, unpacking the ethical questions underlying technical developments

subject: OSPOXFRD
title: Collecting the World
description: The art, science, and culture of the creation, transmission and collection of valuable, useful and informative objects and texts before the twentieth century, and the associated theories, purposes, and methods for collecting `worldly' goods and other valuables. Means by which local academic practices engaged with global developments in the arts and sciences through examination of primarily early modern material and intellectual culture in and around Oxfordshire. Assessments of quality, meaning, usage, cultural significance and the reception of material 'treasures' in the storage rooms, vaults, and on display in museums, galleries, and libraries.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: French Lecture Series 1
description: Students explore Paris  on their own,  by constructing a personal series of lectures, guided visits or talks that the city has to offer. Students must choose at least six lectures. They must be in French (autumn and spring). Lectures can be in English for STEM students in winter who have had their French prerequisite waived. Additionally, students will be expected to write a journal of approximately two pages at the end of the series, which reflects on what they have learned from these various lectures.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Internship
description: Internships represent an excellent framework to develop academic study and to understand the underpinnings of a foreign culture. Internships involve on-site activity, observation or research positions offered by institutions affiliated with the Stanford program. Internships in Paris include French schooling and engineering research (year round), as well as biology and bioengineering research (winter only).

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Internship
description: Internship

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Paris University 1
description: Classes in Social Sciences and the Humanities at the Sorbonne University. Offered Autumn Quarter only. Minimum language requirement: placed in Intermediate French II.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Paris University 2
description: May be repeated for credit

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Directed Reading A
description: Under certain conditions, students can take an independent study in Paris under the guidance of local French tutors, often in the fields of literature, philosophy and history, for example.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Accelerated First-Year French, Part 1
description: Completes first-year language sequence in two rather than three quarters. All-in-French communicative and interactive approach. Emphasis on the development of French in a contemporary cultural context. Interpretation of diversified materials, written and oral presentations.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Paris through the lens of your Smartphone
description: The aim of this course is to allow students to conceive, produce, direct and edit a short film that explores their experience in Paris using the basic smartphone technology. They will be introduced to the fundamentals of visual storytelling and basic technics of filmmaking and be encouraged to apply those techniques through a variety of practical exercises and training seminars. At the end of the trimester, the students will have acquired basic notions of visual storytelling and directed a short movie allowing them to express their own idiosyncratic vision of the world and their personal experience in a foreign city. Primary language: French

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Intermediate French I
description: Prerequisite: one year of college French if completed within two quarters of arriving in Paris, or FRENLANG 21C

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Intermediate French II
description: Prerequisite: FRENLANG 21C within two quarters of arriving in Paris, or FRENLANG 22C or OSPPARIS 22P

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Spotlights on French Culture and Society
description: This required course is resolutely interdisciplinary in nature, exploring France through historical, political and sociological perspectives.  It offers both a theoretical introduction through a series of lectures/discussion sessions, as well as onsite visits venue and a series of formal presentations by students. Students will come to terms with why France is what it is today: its tensions, aspirations and challenges and enquire how the present has evolved out of the past, and how the past has led to the present in France of today.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Bon Appétit, Marie Curie! The Science behind Haute Cuisine
description: This course is for anyone who loves food, cooking or science! We will focus on the science and biology behind the techniques and the taste buds. Not a single lecture will pass by without a delicious opportunity - each weekly meeting will include not only lecture, but also a lab demonstration and a chance to prepare classic dishes that illustrate that day's scientific concepts.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Art and Politics in Modern France
description: This course proposes to explore art and politics in France from the revolution to the present. Through a multimedia approach - including sculptures, paintings, prints, commemorative monuments, architecture, street art and photographs - we will retrace the changing forms that some of the most salient political messages have taken in modern French art. The course will follow a chronological progression, from Revolution to Empire, followed by the rise and fall of the IInd Empire, and the resulting thirst for revenge. We will then broach the 20th century, including the politics of the avant-garde, the art of colonialism, the varied aesthetic responses to the rise of totalitarianism, on display at the 1937 World's Fair in Paris, and evident in the art of collaboration and resistance produced in Occupied and Vichy France during the Second World War. The art of 1960s countercultural contestation - anti-capitalist, anti-colonial, feminist, etc.--will then be studied, before examining recent initiatives in the realm of commemorative art and cultural display that approach issues facing contemporary French society today, including terrorism and constructively confronting its colonial legacy.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Accelerated First-Year French, Part 2
description: Continuation of FRENLANG 1A. Completes first-year language sequence in two rather than three quarters.  All-in-French communicative and interactive approach. Emphasis is on the development of French in a contemporary cultural context. Interpretation of diversified materials, written and oral presentations. Prerequisite: French 1A

subject: OSPPARIS
title: The Avant Garde in France through Literature, Art, and Theater
description: Multiple artistic trends and esthetic theories from Baudelaire to the Nouveau Roman, from the Surrealists to Oulipo, from the theater of cruelty to the theater of the absurd, from the Impressionists to Yves Klein. Interdisciplinary approach to reflect on the meaning of avant garde and modernity in general, and on the  question of why revolutionary artists in France remained in search of institutional recognition, nonetheless.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: French Writing Workshop
description: Offered upon request for students who have completed an Advanced French course. Focus on French writing style, enabling students to understand and master the subtleties of French writing.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Studio Art: General
description: The studio art class are offered by a reputed preparatory arts practice school in Paris, the "Ecole d'Arts Plastiques" (EAP). Classes include perspective, sculpture, computer art, art history, among others). The classes are year-long, but given the individual attention offered to Stanford participants by the instructors, our students can begin the classes in the middle of the year. All the studio art classes are primarily intended for students with good language skills who are majoring or minoring in Art, Art History, Product Design, Architecture or STS. These students have priority for attending the class. Auditors are not accepted. Stanford students enrolled at the EAP will participate in collaborative projects with their French counterparts.

subject: OSPPARIS
title: Studio Art: Drawing with Live Model
description: The studio art class are offered by a reputed preparatory arts practice school in Paris, the "Ecole d'Arts Plastiques" (EAP). Classes include perspective, sculpture, computer art, art history, among others). The classes are year-long, but given the individual attention offered to Stanford participants by the instructors, our students can begin the classes in the middle of the year. All the studio art classes are primarily intended for students with good language skills who are majoring or minoring in Art, Art History, Product Design, Architecture or STS. These students have priority for attending the class. Auditors are not accepted. Stanford students enrolled at the EAP will participate in collaborative projects with their French counterparts.
